faqs.question: ¿Cuál es la diferencia entre deontología y consecuencialismo?
faqs.answer: La deontología (Kant) juzga la moralidad de una acción por el deber y las reglas universales, sin importar las consecuencias. El consecuencialismo (utilitarismo de Bentham y Mill) juzga la acción por sus resultados: es buena la acción que produce el mayor bienestar para el mayor número de personas.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es un contraejemplo moral y para qué sirve?
faqs.answer: Es un caso que desafía una teoría ética mostrando una situación donde la teoría da una conclusión contraria a nuestra intuición moral. Sirve para poner a prueba la solidez de una teoría: el caso del tranvía (trolley problem) es un contraejemplo clásico del consecuencialismo ingenuo.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es la ética de las virtudes de Aristóteles?
faqs.answer: Es una teoría que no pregunta '¿qué debo hacer?' sino '¿qué persona debo ser?'. Se centra en el carácter y en cultivar virtudes (coraje, prudencia, justicia) hasta alcanzar la eudaimonia o florecimiento humano, entendido como una vida plena y realizada.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es el problema del 'es y el debe' (is-ought problem) de Hume?
faqs.answer: Hume observó que no se puede derivar lógicamente una conclusión sobre lo que 'debemos' hacer (el ought) solo a partir de hechos sobre lo que 'es' (el is). Separar el descriptive del normative es una de las distinciones centrales de la filosofía moral moderna.

content:
La ética no es solo decidir entre el bien y el mal: es el estudio riguroso de por qué consideramos buenas o malas ciertas acciones, qué principios rigen nuestra conducta y cómo justificamos moralmente nuestras decisiones. En el nivel C1, razonar sobre ética en inglés exige precisión léxica, capacidad de construir argumentos con estructura lógica y habilidad para plantear y responder a contraejemplos. Esta unidad te prepara para discutir filosofía moral con el mismo rigor con el que lo haría un estudiante universitario angloparlante. En esta unidad vas a encontrar tres niveles de dificultad para cada concepto clave. El nivel A2 te ofrece una explicación sencilla para fijar la idea esencial. El nivel B2 añade matices y conectores. El nivel C1 presenta el léxico filosófico preciso y las estructuras argumentativas avanzadas que necesitas dominar. A2: Ethics is about what is right and wrong. Some people think we must follow rules. Other people think we must think about what happens after our actions. Both ideas are important. B2: Ethics examines how we decide what is morally right or wrong. Deontologists argue that we must follow universal duties, whereas consequentialists judge actions by their outcomes. Each framework offers a different lens through which to evaluate moral dilemmas. C1: Ethics, as a branch of philosophy, interrogates the very grounds on which we adjudicate between right and wrong. Deontological frameworks ground moral obligation in universalisable maxims, whereas consequentialist theories evaluate actions purely in terms of their aggregate outcomes. The tension between duty-based and outcome-based reasoning generates the enduring dialectic at the heart of moral philosophy. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 57 C1](/curso-c1/unit-57)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 56 C1: Filosofía de la mente](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-56-filosofia-de-la-mente)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 58 C1: Futuro de la humanidad](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-58-futuro-humanidad)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría: Ética y filosofía moral ### 1. Las tres grandes tradiciones éticas La filosofía moral occidental se articula en torno a tres tradiciones principales: la deontología, el consecuencialismo y la ética de las virtudes. Cada una responde de manera distinta a la pregunta fundamental: ¿qué hace que una acción sea moralmente correcta? A2: There are three main ways to think about ethics. One says follow the rules. Another says look at the results. The third says be a good person. B2: Three major ethical traditions dominate Western moral philosophy. Deontology focuses on duties and rules, consequentialism evaluates outcomes, and virtue ethics emphasises character. Each tradition offers a coherent but competing account of moral rightness. C1: Western moral philosophy is conventionally triangulated around three paradigms: deontology, which grounds moral rightness in adherence to universalisable duties; consequentialism, which adjudicates actions solely by their aggregate outcomes; and virtue ethics, which relocates the locus of moral evaluation from acts to character. These paradigms are not merely complementary perspectives but rival frameworks whose internal logic often yields incompatible verdicts on the same dilemma. ### 2. Deontología: el imperativo categórico de Kant Immanuel Kant sostiene que la moralidad no depende de las consecuencias sino del deber. Su imperativo categórico ordena actuar solo según máximas que uno podría querer que se convirtieran en ley universal. Mentir es siempre inmoral, incluso si la mentira salva una vida, porque universalizar la mentira destruiría la confianza que hace posible la comunicación misma. A2: Kant says we must always tell the truth. We must do our duty because it is the right thing, not because of what happens after. B2: For Kant, moral duty is unconditional. The categorical imperative demands that we act only on principles we could will to become universal laws. This means lying is always wrong, even when it might save a life, because a universal duty to lie would undermine trust itself. C1: Kant's deontology posits that moral obligation is categorically unconditional, deriving not from contingent outcomes but from the rational form of the maxim itself. The categorical imperative commands that one act only on that maxim which one can simultaneously will to be a universal law. This formulation yields a stringent prohibition on lying irrespective of consequences, on the grounds that universalising deceit would self-destructively erode the very fabric of communicative trust upon which rational agency depends. ### 3. Consecuencialismo y utilitarismo El consecuencialismo sostiene que solo los resultados importan moralmente. El utilitarismo, su variante más influyente, desarrollada por Jeremy Bentham y John Stuart Mill, defiende que la acción correcta es aquella que produce la mayor felicidad para el mayor número de personas. La distinción entre utilitarismo de acto y utilitarismo de regla es crucial: el primero evalúa cada acción individualmente, el segundo evalúa la utilidad de seguir reglas generales. A2: Utilitarianism says we should do what makes the most people happy. If an action helps many people, it is good. B2: Utilitarianism, developed by Bentham and Mill, holds that the right action is the one that maximises overall well-being. Act utilitarianism evaluates each action individually, whereas rule utilitarianism assesses the consequences of following general rules. C1: Consequentialism, in its utilitarian variant elaborated by Bentham and Mill, maintains that the sole morally relevant consideration is the aggregate welfare produced by an action. The distinction between act utilitarianism, which calibrates each individual action by its marginal contribution to overall utility, and rule utilitarianism, which evaluates the expected value of internalising general rules, is pivotal for resolving the theory's most stubborn objections. ### 4. Ética de las virtudes: Aristóteles y la eudaimonia Aristóteles desplaza el foco ético desde la acción hacia el carácter. La pregunta no es qué debo hacer, sino qué persona debo ser. La eudaimonia, traducida imperfectamente como florecimiento o bienestar, es el fin último de la vida humana. Se alcanza cultivando virtudes mediante la práctica habitual hasta que se vuelven disposiciones estables del carácter. A2: Aristotle says we should try to be a good person. A good person has good habits. When we practice good things, we become good. B2: Aristotle's virtue ethics shifts the focus from actions to character. Rather than asking what we should do, it asks what kind of person we should become. Eudaimonia, or flourishing, is achieved by cultivating virtues through habitual practice until they become stable dispositions. C1: Aristotle's virtue ethics effects a decisive shift from the act-centred framing of deontology and consequentialism toward a character-centred moral ontology. The governing question is not which action to perform but which dispositions to cultivate, with eudaimonia, inadequately rendered as happiness or flourishing, posited as the telos of human life, attained through the habitual exercise of virtuous capacities until they consolidate into stable traits of character. ### 5. El caso del tranvía: dilema clásico El trolley problem, formulado por Philippa Foot y desarrollado por Judith Jarvis Thomson, es el dilema ético más discutido del siglo XX. Un tranvía sin control se dirige hacia cinco personas. Puedes desviar la vía para que mate a una persona en su lugar. ¿Es correcto hacerlo? El dilema revela la tensión entre el consecuencialismo, que autoriza el desvío, y la deontología, que prohíbe usar a una persona como medio. A2: The trolley problem is a famous story. A train will hit five people. You can change the track so it hits one person instead. Is that okay? B2: The trolley problem asks whether it is permissible to divert a runaway trolley, killing one person to save five. Consequentialists say yes, because five lives outweigh one. Deontologists often say no, because actively killing one person treats them as a mere means to an end. C1: The trolley problem, inaugurated by Foot and refined by Thomson, functions as the exemplary stress test for competing ethical frameworks. The consequentialist verdict, that diverting the trolley is obligatory given the aggregate utility of five lives preserved over one, collides with the deontological prohibition on instrumentalising a person as a mere means, thereby exposing the structural fault line between outcome-based and duty-based reasoning. ### 6. Contraejemplos: la navaja metodológica de la ética Un contraejemplo es un caso que desafía una teoría mostrando una situación donde la teoría produce una conclusión contraria a nuestra intuición moral. El trolley problem es un contraejemplo del consecuencialismo ingenuo. El caso del tranvía gordo y el violinista de Thomson son contraejemplos diseñados para mostrar los límites de teorías éticas específicas. A2: A counterexample is a story that shows a theory might be wrong. If the theory says something we feel is bad, maybe the theory has a problem. B2: A counterexample challenges a theory by presenting a case where its conclusion clashes with our moral intuition. Philosophers construct counterexamples deliberately to expose the limits of a framework. The trolley problem and Thomson's violinist case are classic instances. C1: A counterexample operates as a methodological scalpel in moral philosophy, isolating a case in which a theory's prescribed verdict diverges sharply from considered moral judgement. The deliberate construction of counterexamples, exemplified by the fat man variant and Thomson's violinist thought experiment, serves not to refute a theory outright but to map its counterintuitive implications and thereby force its refinement or abandonment. ### 7. El violinista de Thomson y el argumento del aborto Judith Jarvis Thomson propone un experimento mental: despiertas conectada a un violinista famoso que necesita tus riñones para sobrevivir nueve meses. ¿Estás obligada a mantenerlo conectado? Thomson argumenta que no, aunque reconozcas su derecho a la vida. Este caso pretende mostrar que el derecho a la vida no implica el derecho a usar el cuerpo de otra persona, un argumento influyente en el debate sobre el aborto. A2: Thomson asks: if someone needs your body to live, must you help them? She says maybe you are kind if you help, but you do not have to. B2: Thomson's violinist thought experiment imagines you waking up connected to a famous violinist who needs your kidneys for nine months. She argues that even if the violinist has a right to life, he has no right to use your body without your consent, a parallel she draws to debates about abortion. C1: Thomson's violinist case constructs a carefully calibrated analogy: you awaken medically attached to an unconscious violinist whose survival depends on nine months of circulatory support from your body. The case is engineered to demonstrate that the right to life, even when conceded, does not entail a derivative right to commandeer another person's bodily resources, thereby furnishing a prima facie justification for permissive abortion policy that bypasses the contested status of the foetus. ### 8. El dilema de Heinz: las etapas morales de Kohlberg Lawrence Kohlberg usa el dilema de Heinz, un hombre que roba medicamento para salvar a su esposa, para estudiar el desarrollo moral. Identifica seis etapas en tres niveles: preconvencional, convencional y postconvencional. Carol Gilligan critica que el modelo privilegia el razonamiento ético masculino basado en la justicia sobre el femenino centrado en el cuidado. A2: Kohlberg tells a story about a man who steals medicine for his wife. He asks people if the man was right. He finds people think about morality in different ways as they grow up. B2: Kohlberg used the Heinz dilemma to map six stages of moral development across three levels: preconventional, conventional, and postconventional. Carol Gilligan objected that his framework privileged a justice-oriented reasoning stereotypically male over a care-oriented perspective stereotypically female. C1: Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma furnished the empirical scaffolding for a six-stage model of moral development stratified into preconventional, conventional and postconventional levels. Gilligan's critique exposed the model's gendered bias, arguing that its hierarchical valorisation of justice-based reasoning over care-based reasoning systematically marginalised the relational moral voice predominantly articulated by women. ### 9. Ética aplicada: bioética, ética empresarial y ambiental La ética aplicada traslada los principios teóricos a problemas concretos. La bioética aborda la eutanasia, la experimentación con animales y la justicia en la distribución de recursos sanitarios. La ética empresarial examina la responsabilidad corporativa y los conflictos de interés. La ética ambiental cuestiona si tenemos obligaciones morales hacia seres no humanos y ecosistemas futuros. A2: Applied ethics looks at real problems. It asks questions like: is it okay to help someone die? Should companies be fair? Should we protect nature? B2: Applied ethics translates abstract principles into concrete dilemmas. Bioethics addresses euthanasia and animal research. Business ethics examines corporate responsibility. Environmental ethics asks whether we owe moral duties to non-human beings and to future generations. C1: Applied ethics mediates between abstract normative theory and concrete practical deliberation. Bioethics adjudicates disputes ranging from euthanasia and animal experimentation to the equitable allocation of scarce medical resources. Business ethics interrogates the scope of corporate moral agency, whilst environmental ethics interrogates the very extension of the moral community to encompass non-human organisms and as-yet-unrealised future generations. ### 10. El relativismo moral frente al universalismo El relativismo moral sostiene que la moralidad es culturalmente relativa: lo correcto en una sociedad puede ser incorrecto en otra. El universalismo moral defiende que existen principios éticos válidos para todos los seres humanos independientemente de la cultura. El debate tiene profundas implicaciones para los derechos humanos y la justicia internacional. A2: Some people think what is right depends on your country. Other people think some things are right or wrong everywhere. B2: Moral relativism holds that right and wrong are culturally determined, so no universal standard exists. Moral universalism insists that certain ethical principles hold for all humans regardless of culture. This debate shapes how we think about human rights. C1: Moral relativism contends that normative standards are irreducibly culture-bound, precluding any cross-cultural adjudication of moral claims. Moral universalism, by contrast, maintains that certain ethical principles possess trans-cultural validity derivable from rational or human nature itself. The dispute carries far-reaching implications for the legitimacy of universal human rights regimes and the coherence of international justice. ### 11. El problema del es y el debe: la guillotina de Hume David Hume observó que muchos filósofos pasan inadvertidamente de descripciones fácticas (el es) a prescripciones normativas (el debe) sin justificación lógica. Esta guillotina de Hume establece que no se puede derivar un ought puramente de un is, separando el plano descriptivo del normativo, una distinción fundacional de la metaética contemporánea. A2: Hume said we cannot jump from what is true to what we should do. Just because something is a certain way does not mean it should be that way. B2: Hume observed that philosophers often slide unnoticed from descriptive claims about what is the case to normative claims about what ought to be. The is-ought gap insists that no purely logical inference can bridge the descriptive and the normative. C1: Hume's guillotine, articulated in the Treatise, diagnoses an endemic fallacy whereby philosophers imperceptibly transition from descriptive premises concerning what is the case to normative conclusions concerning what ought to be. The resultant is-ought distinction enforces a logical barrier between the descriptive and the normative, a demarcation that remains constitutive of contemporary metaethical debate. ### 12. Intuicionismo y escepticismo moral El intuicionismo moral sostiene que conocemos ciertas verdades morales básicas por intuición directa, análogas a la percepción sensorial. El escepticismo moral niega que existan hechos morales objetivos. El no cognitivismo, una variante escéptica, defiende que los juicios morales no expresan creencias verdaderas o falsas, sino actitudes o prescripciones. A2: Some people think we just know what is right by feeling it. Other people think there are no real moral facts, only opinions. B2: Moral intuitionism claims we grasp basic moral truths through direct intuition. Moral scepticism denies that objective moral facts exist. Non-cognitivism, a sceptical variant, argues that moral judgements express attitudes rather than truth-apt beliefs. C1: Moral intuitionism, in its contemporary revival, posits that certain foundational moral truths are apprehended through non-inferential intellectual seeming, analogous to perceptual acquaintance. Moral scepticism, in its non-cognitivist incarnation, denies the truth-aptness of moral discourse altogether, construing moral utterances as expressions of conative attitudes or prescriptions rather than as propositions susceptible to truth-conditional analysis. ### 13. Justicia y equidad: Rawls y el velo de ignorancia John Rawls propone un experimento mental para fundamentar la justicia: el velo de ignorancia. Si diseñaras los principios de la sociedad sin saber qué posición ocuparías en ella, elegirías reglas que protegieran incluso a los más desfavorecidos. Sus dos principios de justicia priorizan las libertades básicas y permiten desigualdades solo si benefician a los menos aventajados. A2: Rawls asks: if you did not know if you would be rich or poor, what rules would you choose? You would probably choose fair rules. B2: Rawls's veil of ignorance asks us to design society's rules without knowing our future position. Rational agents behind the veil would choose principles that protect the worst off. His two principles of justice prioritise basic liberties and permit inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged. C1: Rawls's original position, operationalised through the veil of ignorance, solicits the principles of justice that rational agents would converge upon under a deliberate deprivation of knowledge regarding their eventual social placement. The resultant two principles lexically prioritise equal basic liberties and authorise socio-economic inequalities only insofar as they maximise the position of the least advantaged, a constraint dubbed the difference principle. ### 14. Lenguaje y argumentación ética en inglés C1 A nivel C1, debes construir argumentos morales con estructuras precisas. Expresiones como it might be objected that, on the contrary, this reasoning is flawed because, a counterexample would be, the implication of this view is que permiten articular objeciones y refutaciones. Los conectores lógicos, por tanto, son cruciales: nevertheless, moreover, insofar as, notwithstanding, provided that. A2: When we talk about ethics, we can use phrases like "I think this is wrong because" and "but other people say." B2: At an advanced level, you can structure moral arguments with phrases like it might be objected that, this reasoning is flawed because, and a counterexample would be. These expressions help you present and respond to objections clearly. C1: At C1, ethical argumentation demands mastery of meta-discursive markers such as it might be objected that, this reasoning rests on a dubious premise, a decisive counterexample would be, and the implication of this view is. Logical connectors including nevertheless, moreover, insofar as, notwithstanding and provided that enable the precise articulation of concessive, additive and conditional relations essential to rigorous moral reasoning. ### 15. Colocaciones y léxico filosófico-moral El léxico ético del inglés C1 incluye colocaciones estables que debes dominar: to act on principle, to weigh the consequences, to draw a distinction, to mount an objection, to concede a point, to rebut an argument, to uphold a duty, to breach a moral rule, to universalise a maxim, to maximise aggregate welfare, to cultivate a virtue, to possess moral standing, to derive an ought from an is. A2: Here are some useful phrases: to do the right thing, to think about what happens, to be a good person. B2: Useful collocations include to act on principle, to weigh the consequences, to mount an objection and to universalise a maxim. Learning these fixed expressions makes your ethical vocabulary sound natural and precise. C1: The C1 ethical lexicon comprises entrenched collocations whose acquisition is indispensable for idiomatic philosophical discourse: to act on principle, to weigh the consequences, to draw a distinction, to mount an objection, to concede a point, to rebut an argument, to uphold a duty, to breach a moral rule, to universalise a maxim, to maximise aggregate welfare, to cultivate a virtue, to possess moral standing, and to derive an ought from an is. ## Parte II — Ejercicios ### Ejercicio 1 Completa la frase con el término ético correcto: A philosopher who believes that the morality of an action depends only on its results is called a ______.
Ver solución consequentialist
### Ejercicio 2 Traduce al inglés: "Debemos actuar solo según máximas que podamos querer que se conviertan en ley universal."
Ver solución We must act only on maxims that we can will to become universal law.
### Ejercicio 3 Reescribe usando un conector C1 avanzado: Consequentialism says outcomes matter. Deontology says duties matter. They disagree.
Ver solución Whereas consequentialism holds that outcomes matter, deontology maintains that duties matter; the two frameworks thus diverge fundamentally.
### Ejercicio 4 Completa con la colocación correcta: The utilitarian aims to ______ aggregate welfare across all affected parties.
Ver solución maximise
### Ejercicio 5 Identifica la falacia ética en este razonamiento: "Lying is sometimes beneficial, therefore lying is morally permissible."
Ver solución This commits a naturalistic fallacy (or violates Hume's is-ought distinction): it derives a normative conclusion (lying is permissible) purely from a descriptive premise (lying is sometimes beneficial) without an independent moral principle bridging the gap.
### Ejercicio 6 Traduce al inglés: "El velo de ignorancia de Rawls requiere que diseñemos la sociedad sin saber qué posición ocuparemos."
Ver solución Rawls's veil of ignorance requires that we design society without knowing which position we will occupy.
### Ejercicio 7 Completa la frase: According to virtue ethics, the central question is not "what should I do?" but "______?"
Ver solución what kind of person should I become?
### Ejercicio 8 Construye un contraejemplo al siguiente principio consecuencialista: "Siempre es correcto sacrificar a una persona para salvar a cinco."
Ver solución One counterexample: imagine the five people saved are responsible for a future atrocity, while the one sacrificed is an innocent child. If the principle is purely consequentialist, it would still demand sacrificing the child, a verdict that clashes with most people's moral intuition that one should not kill an innocent to save five culpable individuals.
### Ejercicio 9 Reescribe con un registro C1 más formal: This theory is wrong because it has problems.
Ver solución This theory is untenable insofar as it harbours unresolved internal tensions. (Also acceptable: This framework is defensible only with difficulty, given the objections it leaves unanswered.)
### Ejercicio 10 Completa con el término adecuado: The view that moral judgements express attitudes rather than truth-apt beliefs is called ______.
Ver solución non-cognitivism
### Ejercicio 11 Traduce al inglés: "El imperativo categórico prohíbe tratar a las personas como medios meros."
Ver solución The categorical imperative prohibits treating persons as mere means.
### Ejercicio 12 Identifica el marco ético implicado: "Debemos cumplir nuestras promesas incluso cuando hacerlo reduzca la felicidad general."
Ver solución This reflects a deontological framework, since it prioritises the duty to keep promises over the consequences (general happiness). A strict consequentialist would arguably permit breaking the promise if doing so maximised overall welfare.
### Ejercicio 13 Reescribe usando insofar as: Ethics is important. It helps us decide how to live.
Ver solución Ethics is important insofar as it furnishes the principles by which we adjudicate how to live.
### Ejercicio 14 Completa la colocación: A serious objection can be ______ against this view.
Ver solución mounted
### Ejercicio 15 Traduce al inglés: "La ética ambiental se pregunta si tenemos obligaciones hacia las generaciones futuras."
Ver solución Environmental ethics asks whether we owe moral duties to future generations.
### Ejercicio 16 Explica en inglés C1 la diferencia entre act utilitarianism y rule utilitarianism.
Ver solución Act utilitarianism evaluates each individual action by its direct contribution to aggregate welfare, whereas rule utilitarianism evaluates actions by the consequences of adopting the general rule under which the action falls. Consequently, a rule utilitarian might condemn an act that an act utilitarian would permit, on the grounds that endorsing such behaviour as a general rule would be welfare-diminishing in the long run.
### Ejercicio 17 Reescribe con un conector concesivo C1: Consequentialism has problems. Many philosophers still defend it.
Ver solución Notwithstanding the well-documented objections to consequentialism, a significant number of philosophers continue to defend it.
### Ejercicio 18 Completa con la preposición correcta: She acted ______ principle, even though the outcome was unfortunate.
Ver solución on
### Ejercicio 19 Redacta en inglés C1 (60-80 palabras) un breve argumento sobre si el relativismo moral es compatible con los derechos humanos universales.
Ver solución Moral relativism and universal human rights sit in deep tension. If moral standards are irreducibly culture-bound, then no trans-cultural norms can ground rights claims that bind all societies alike. Proponents of universal rights must therefore reject thoroughgoing relativism, invoking instead principles derivable from human nature or rational agency itself. That said, a moderated relativism can accommodate local variation in how universal principles are instantiated, provided the core entitlements remain non-negotiable.
## Resumen de la unidad En esta unidad has explorado las tres grandes tradiciones de la filosofía moral: la deontología de Kant, el consecuencialismo utilitarista y la ética de las virtudes de Aristóteles. Has aprendido a construir y a responder a contraejemplos morales como el trolley problem y el violinista de Thomson, a distinguir el es del debe según Hume y a razonar sobre justicia con el velo de ignorancia de Rawls. A nivel lingüístico, has consolidado colocaciones filosóficas como to mount an objection, to universalise a maxim y to derive an ought from an is, junto con conectores lógicos avanzados como insofar as y notwithstanding. Con los 19 ejercicios has practicado la argumentación ética en inglés C1 con la precisión léxica y la estructuración lógica que exige el nivel avanzado. En la siguiente unidad, la 58, trasladarás esta capacidad de razonamiento cauteloso al futuro de la humanidad, donde la especulación prudente se convierte en la herramienta central.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es el 'mind-body problem' y qué posturas principales incluye?
faqs.answer: Es el problema de la relación entre la mente (consciencia, pensamiento) y el cuerpo (materia física). Incluye dualism (la mente y el cuerpo son sustancias distintas), physicalism (todo es físico), functionalism (los estados mentales se definen por su función) y panpsychism (la consciencia es una propiedad fundamental de la materia).

faqs.question: ¿Qué es el 'hard problem of consciousness' de Chalmers?
faqs.answer: Es la dificultad de explicar por qué y cómo los procesos físicos del cerebro dan lugar a la experiencia subjetiva (qualia). A diferencia de los 'easy problems' (explicar funciones cognitivas), el hard problem pregunta por qué hay algo que se siente al procesar información.

faqs.question: ¿Cómo se usa la metáfora con precisión en filosofía de la mente?
faqs.answer: La metáfora conceptual (the mind as a computer, the brain as a machine) es inevitable pero debe usarse con conciencia de sus límites: distinguir el modelo explicativo de la realidad explicada, señalar dónde la analogía se rompe y evitar reificar la metáfora hasta el punto de confundirla con la teoría.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es la 'intencionalidad' en filosofía de la mente?
faqs.answer: Es la propiedad de los estados mentales de estar 'acerca de' algo, de representar o dirigirse hacia un objeto (pensar en un árbol, creer que lloverá). Es la 'aboutness' de la mente, y la cuestión de si puede reducirse a propiedades físicas es uno de los debates centrales.

content:
La filosofía de la mente es uno de los territorios más fascinantes del pensamiento contemporáneo, y argumentar en él con propiedad exige una destreza singular: el manejo de la metáfora con precisión conceptual. No basta con decir que *the mind is like a computer* o que *the brain produces thoughts*; hay que distinguir *dualism* de *physicalism*, *qualia* de *functional states*, *intentionality* de *aboutness*, y usar las metáforas explicativas \u2014the mind as a machine, consciousness as an emergent property\u2014 con la conciencia de sus límites que el rigor filosófico demanda. En esta unidad del curso de inglés C1 gratis exploramos cómo los hablantes avanzados manejan el léxico de la filosofía de la mente, cómo emplean la metáfora como instrumento de explicación sin confundirla con la teoría y cómo argumentan sobre la consciencia y el problema cuerpo-mente con la precisión que uno de los debates más difíciles de la filosofía exige. Es un terreno donde el lenguaje debe ser a la vez imaginativo y riguroso: la metáfora ilumina, pero el hablante C1 sabe dónde deja de iluminar. Para situar el nivel, observa cómo el mismo debate se expresa en tres niveles. En **A2** diríamos: *The brain thinks. The mind is inside the head. It is hard to understand.* Es claro pero plano, sin vocabulario filosófico ni matices. En **B2** subiríamos un peldaño: *Some philosophers think the mind and the body are different. Others think they are the same. Consciousness is still a mystery.* Aquí ya hay posiciones y problema, pero le falta densidad conceptual y conciencia metalingüística. En **C1** alcanzamos la precisión necesaria: *While the metaphor of the mind as a computer has proven heuristically indispensable in organising the functionalist's account of cognition, its very fruitfulness carries a risk that the philosophically careful user must keep in view: that the analogy between software and mental states, however illuminating as a model of information processing, may seduce us into treating as solved the question that the hard problem of consciousness actually poses \u2014 namely, why there is anything it is like to be in such a state at all, a question that no amount of functional decomposition, however complete, appears even to address, let alone to answer.* Esta unidad te enseña a producir ese tercer nivel de forma natural. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 56 C1](/curso-c1/unit-56)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 55 C1: Libre albedrío y determinismo](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-55-libre-albedrio-determinismo)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 57 C1: Ética y filosofía moral](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-57-etica-filosofia-moral)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Léxico fundamental de la filosofía de la mente La filosofía de la mente se articula en torno a un léxico fundamental: *mind* (mente), *brain* (cerebro), *consciousness* (consciencia), *mental states* (estados mentales), *qualia* (qualia, las cualidades subjetivas de la experiencia), *intentionality* (intencionalidad, la propiedad de estar "acerca de" algo), *subjective experience* (experiencia subjetiva), *phenomenal character* (carácter fenoménico), *the what-it-is-like* (el "cómo se siente"). Un hablante C1 escribe *the distinction between the functional aspects of a mental state \u2014 what it does, what role it plays in the cognitive economy \u2014 and its phenomenal character \u2014 what it is like, from the inside, to be in that state \u2014 is the distinction that the hard problem of consciousness exploits, for the former admits, in principle, of a complete functional account while the latter, by its very nature, seems to resist any account that does not, at some point, presuppose the very thing it sets out to explain.* Distinguir estos niveles de descripción es la condición previa de cualquier argumento serio. ### 2. El problema cuerpo-mente El *mind-body problem* (problema cuerpo-mente) es la cuestión central: *substance dualism* (dualismo de sustancias, mente y cuerpo son sustancias distintas, de Descartes), *property dualism* (dualismo de propiedades, una sustancia con propiedades físicas y mentales), *physicalism* o *materialism* (fisicalismo o materialismo, todo es físico), *monism* (monismo, una sola sustancia), *epiphenomenalism* (epifenomenalismo, los estados mentales existen pero no causan), *interaction problem* (problema de la interacción, cómo interactúan sustancias distintas). Un hablante C1 escribe *the interaction problem that has dogged substance dualism since Descartes \u2014 how two substances as different in kind as mind and matter could causally affect one another \u2014 is not merely a technical difficulty but a structural one, for the very intelligibility of causal interaction seems to presuppose some common currency between cause and effect that the radical heterogeneity of the two substances appears to rule out by definition.* El problema de la interacción es el talón de Aquiles del dualismo cartesiano. ### 3. El hard problem de la consciencia El *hard problem of consciousness* (problema duro de la consciencia) de Chalmers distingue los *easy problems* (explicar funciones cognitivas: atención, integración de información, control) del *hard problem*: por qué hay experiencia subjetiva en absoluto. Léxico: *explanatory gap* (brecha explicativa), *zombie argument* (argumento del zombi, un ser funcionalmente idéntico sin experiencia), *the knowledge argument* (argumento del conocimiento, de Mary la neurocientífica que ve color por primera vez), *Mary's room* (la habitación de Mary). Un hablante C1 escribe *the hard problem, as Chalmers frames it, is not the difficulty of explaining any particular cognitive function \u2014 those are the easy problems, challenging but in principle tractable \u2014 but the question of why the performance of those functions should be accompanied by subjective experience at all, a question whose very formulation suggests that no account framed entirely in functional terms, however complete, will touch the explanandum, for the explanandum is precisely the non-functional residue that the functional account, by its nature, leaves out.* El hard problem apunta a lo que el funcionalismo, por definición, no aborda. ### 4. Funcionalismo y sus variantes El *functionalism* (funcionalismo) define los estados mentales por su función, no por su material: *functional role* (papel funcional), *multiple realisability* (realizabilidad múltiple, el mismo estado mental en sustratos distintos), *computational theory of mind* (teoría computacional de la mente), *machine functionalism* (funcionalismo de máquina), *psychofunctionalism* (psicofuncionalismo), *representational theory* (teoría representacional). Un hablante C1 escribe *the functionalist's appeal to multiple realisability \u2014 the thought that a mental state is individuated by its causal role rather than by the physical substrate that implements it, so that pain in a human, a Martian and a silicon system could, in principle, be the same state \u2014 is at once the theory's greatest strength and the source of its most serious difficulty, for in severing the mental from any particular physical realisation it risks severing it from the physical altogether, a consequence that the physicalist functionalist must somehow prevent without abandoning the very consideration that made functionalism attractive.* La realizabilidad múltiple es el arma de doble filo del funcionalismo. ### 5. La metáfora en filosofía de la mente: el modelo y la realidad El uso de la metáfora (*metaphor*) en filosofía de la mente exige distinguir el *model* (modelo explicativo) de la *reality modelled* (la realidad modelada): *the mind as a computer* (la mente como ordenador), *the brain as a machine* (el cerebro como máquina), *consciousness as an emergent property* (la consciencia como propiedad emergente), *the mind as a theatre* (la mente como teatro, del Cartesian theatre de Dennett), *the brain as a prediction machine* (el cerebro como máquina de predicción). Un hablante C1 escribe *the metaphor of the Cartesian theatre \u2014 the picture, which Dennett attributes to our intuitive self-understanding, of a homunculus seated in the mind observing the stream of experience projected on an inner screen \u2014 is not a theory anyone explicitly endorses but a picture that, Dennett argues, covertly structures much of our thinking about consciousness, which is why exposing it as a metaphor rather than a model is a necessary preliminary to any account that would dispense with the inner spectator it presupposes.* La conciencia metalingüística sobre la metáfora es la marca del C1 en este campo. ### 6. Conectores de precisión conceptual La precisión conceptual emplea conectores que calibran la afirmación: *to be precise* (para ser preciso), *in the strict sense* (en sentido estricto), *properly speaking* (en propiedad), *in the relevant sense* (en el sentido relevante), *strictly construed* (estrictamente interpretado), *as distinct from* (a diferencia de), *not to be confused with* (no debe confundirse con). Un hablante C1 escribe *consciousness, in the strict sense that the hard problem targets, is not to be confused with the cluster of cognitive functions \u2014 attention, access, reportability \u2014 that the easy problems address, for while those functions may be necessary conditions of conscious experience in the creatures we know, they are not identical with it, and the tendency to slide between the two is one that the philosophical literature exists in large part to resist.* Estos conectores previenen la equivocación que arruinaría el argumento. ### 7. Intencionalidad y aboutness La *intentionality* (intencionalidad) es la *aboutness* (el estar "acerca de") de los estados mentales: *intentional state* (estado intencional), *representational content* (contenido representacional), *directedness* (direccionalidad hacia un objeto), *intentional inexistence* (inexistencia intencional, de Brentano), *propositional attitude* (actitud proposicional: creer que, desear que), *mental representation* (representación mental). Un hablante C1 escribe *the Brentanian thesis that intentionality is the mark of the mental \u2014 that what distinguishes mental states from physical ones is their directedness towards an object, their being about something \u2014 raises the question of whether intentionality can be naturalised, that is, explained in terms that do not themselves presuppose the mentality they set out to account for, a question whose difficulty is compounded by the existence of states, like beliefs about non-existent entities, that have intentionality without an object.* La naturalización de la intencionalidad es uno de los grandes desafíos. ### 8. Qualia y el argumento del conocimiento El debate sobre los *qualia* (cualidades subjetivas): *qualia* (qualia), *raw feel* (sensación bruta), *phenomenal properties* (propiedades fenoménicas), *inverted qualia* (qualia invertidos: mi rojo es tu verde), *the knowledge argument* (argumento del conocimiento), *what Mary didn't know* (lo que Mary no sabía), *phenomenal concepts* (conceptos fenoménicos). Un hablante C1 escribe *the knowledge argument, through the thought experiment of Mary \u2014 the colour scientist who knows every physical fact about colour vision but has never seen colour, and who, upon first seeing red, appears to learn something new \u2014 purports to show that there are facts about experience that escape the physicalist's inventory, for if Mary knew all the physical facts and yet learns something on leaving the room, then what she learns is, by construction, non-physical, a conclusion the physicalist must rebut by arguing that what Mary acquires is not new knowledge but a new way of accessing knowledge she already had.* El argumento de Mary ataca al fisicalismo desde la primera persona. ### 9. Emergencia y reducción El debate entre *emergence* (emergencia) y *reduction* (reducción): *emergent property* (propiedad emergente), *reductionism* (reduccionismo), *supervenience* (superveniencia, los cambios mentales dependen de cambios físicos), *identity theory* (teoría de la identidad, los estados mentales son estados cerebrales), *anomalous monism* (monismo anómalo, de Davidson), *reductive vs non-reductive physicalism* (fisicalismo reductivo vs no reductivo). Un hablante C1 escribe *the doctrine of supervenience \u2014 that there can be no mental difference without a physical difference, so that the mental depends on the physical without, in the non-reductive physicalist's view, being reducible to it \u2014 occupies an attractive but unstable position between reductive physicalism, which it is too weak to entail, and property dualism, from which it must struggle to distinguish itself, for if the mental supervenes on the physical but is not reducible to it, one owes an account of what the irreducibility consists in that does not collapse into the dualism it was meant to avoid.* La superveniencia es una posición intermedia y discutida. ### 10. Eliminativismo y relajación del vocabulario mental El *eliminativism* (eliminativismo) cuestiona el vocabulario mental mismo: *folk psychology* (psicología popular, las creencias y deseos del sentido común), *eliminative materialism* (materialismo eliminativo), *propositional attitudes* (actitudes proposicionales), *theory theory* (teoría de la teoría, la psicología popular como teoría), *simulation theory* (teoría de la simulación). Un hablante C1 escribe *the eliminativist's claim that folk psychology is a theory \u2014 and a theory that, like phlogiston or caloric, may turn out to be radically mistaken about its domain \u2014 is not the modest observation that we sometimes misattribute beliefs but the radical thesis that the categories of belief and desire may not carve the cognitive reality at its joints, a thesis whose plausibility depends on whether the predictive and explanatory success of folk psychology is the kind of success that a fundamentally mistaken theory could enjoy.* El eliminativismo es una de las posiciones más radicales del debate. ### 11. Conectores de matización metafórica La matización metafórica emplea conectores que señalan los límites de la analogía: *in a sense* (en cierto sentido), *up to a point* (hasta cierto punto), *with the caveat that* (con la salvedad de que), *the analogy breaks down at* (la analogía se rompe en), *the metaphor should not be pressed too far* (la metáfora no debe tomarse demasiado literalmente), *only in a qualified sense* (solo en un sentido cualificado), *to the extent that* (en la medida en que). Un hablante C1 escribe *the computational metaphor is illuminating, up to a point, insofar as it captures the way in which mental states can be individuated by their functional roles; with the caveat, however, that the analogy breaks down at the point where consciousness is concerned, for while a computer processes information, there is nothing it is like, from the inside, to be that processing \u2014 a disanalogy that the metaphor, if pressed too far, obscures precisely where the philosophically interesting question lies.* Estos conectores calibran la extensión de la metáfora. ### 12. La primera persona y el acceso privilegiado El debate sobre la *first-person perspective* (perspectiva de primera persona) y el *privileged access* (acceso privilegiado): *introspection* (introspección), *first-person authority* (autoridad de primera persona), *incorrigibility* (incorregibilidad), *transparency of the mental* (transparencia de lo mental), *self-knowledge* (autoconocimiento), *the subjective stance* (postura subjetiva). Un hablante C1 escribe *the first-person authority that we ordinarily accord to a subject's avowals of her own mental states \u2014 the presumption that, if she sincerely says she is in pain, she is, barring rare exceptions, right \u2014 is a feature of our epistemic practice that any philosophy of mind must accommodate, though the explanation of that authority is itself contested, with some accounts grounding it in a special mode of access and others in the constitutive role that the avowal plays in fixing the state avowed.* El acceso privilegiado es un dato que toda teoría debe explicar. ### 13. Consciencia de acceso y consciencia fenoménica La distinción entre *access consciousness* (consciencia de acceso, la disponibilidad para el control verbal y la acción) y *phenomenal consciousness* (consciencia fenoménica, la experiencia subjetiva): *access consciousness* (Block), *phenomenal consciousness* (Block), *global workspace theory* (teoría del espacio de trabajo global, de Baars), *integrated information theory* (teoría de la información integrada, de Tononi), *higher-order theories* (teorías de orden superior). Un hablante C1 escribe *the distinction between access and phenomenal consciousness, if sound, allows the functionalist to account for the former \u2014 which is, by construction, a matter of information availability \u2014 while conceding that the latter poses the hard problem, a division of labour that is attractive to the functionalist precisely because it confines the explanandum that resists functional analysis to a domain that the functionalist can, without inconsistency, leave to one side.* La distinción permite una división del trabajo explicativo. ### 14. Encarnación y cognición extendida El *embodied cognition* (cognición encarnada) y la *extended mind* (mente extendida): *embodiment* (encarnación), *extended mind thesis* (tesis de la mente extendida, de Clark y Chalmers), *cognitive extension* (extensión cognitiva), *active externalism* (externalismo activo), *coupled system* (sistema acoplado), *4E cognition* (cognición 4E: embodied, embedded, enacted, extended). Un hablante C1 escribe *the extended mind thesis \u2014 that cognitive processes can, under certain conditions, loop out into the environment, so that a notebook used reliably for memory counts, by parity of reasoning, as part of the mind \u2014 challenges the tacit assumption that the boundaries of the cognitive are coextensive with the boundaries of the skin, though whether the parity argument establishes that the external resource is part of the mind or merely that the boundary between mind and world is less sharp than we assumed is a question its proponents and critics continue to contest.* La mente extendida desafía la localización tradicional de lo cognitivo. ### 15. Cohesión en ensayos de filosofía de la mente La cohesión en ensayos de filosofía de la mente combina precisión conceptual, matización metafórica y conectores lógicos: *the question, properly framed, is* (la pregunta, bien formulada, es), *the distinction that matters is between* (la distinción que importa es entre), *on one construal* (en una interpretación), *on another* (en otra), *the upshot is that* (el resultado es que), *the metaphor is apt insofar as* (la metáfora es adecuada en la medida en que). Un hablante C1 escribe *the question, properly framed, is not whether the mind is like a computer \u2014 a metaphor whose aptness is, in any case, contestable \u2014 but whether the computational model, insofar as it captures the functional individuation of mental states, can address the phenomenal residue that the hard problem identifies, and the upshot is that it can, at best, clarify the former while leaving the latter precisely where it was, which is why the metaphor, however useful as a heuristic, should not be mistaken for a solution to the problem it so elegantly reorganises.* La cohesión filosófica hace visible tanto la estructura del argumento como los límites de la metáfora que lo articula. ## Parte II — Ejercicios **Ejercicio 1.** Completa con el término correcto del léxico fundamental: *qualia*, *intentionality*, *phenomenal character*, *mental states*. 1. The subjective "what-it-is-like" quality of an experience is its ______. 2. The property of mental states of being "about" something is ______. 3. The felt qualities of experience, such as the redness of red, are called ______. 4. Beliefs, desires and sensations are collectively referred to as ______.
Ver solución 1. phenomenal character 2. intentionality (or aboutness) 3. qualia 4. mental states These four terms map the foundational vocabulary: *mental states* is the genus, *intentionality* is one mark of the mental (directedness), *phenomenal character* is another (subjective feel), and *qualia* are the individual felt qualities that compose the phenomenal character. Distinguishing them is the precondition of clear argument in this domain.
**Ejercicio 2.** Completa con la posición en el problema cuerpo-mente: *substance dualism*, *physicalism*, *property dualism*, *epiphenomenalism*. 1. The thesis that mind and body are two distinct substances is ______. 2. The thesis that everything that exists is physical is ______. 3. The thesis that there is one substance with two kinds of properties is ______. 4. The thesis that mental states exist but have no causal power is ______.
Ver solución 1. substance dualism 2. physicalism (or materialism) 3. property dualism 4. epiphenomenalism Note the relationships: *property dualism* is a compromise between *substance dualism* and *physicalism* \u2014 it keeps one substance but two kinds of property. *Epiphenomenalism* can be combined with property dualism: mental properties are real but causally inert, like the steam from a train's whistle that does not affect the train's motion.
**Ejercicio 3.** Reescribe esta afirmación simple como un argumento C1 con precisión conceptual: "The mind is like a computer. So consciousness is just information processing."
Ver solución *While the metaphor of the mind as a computer has proven heuristically indispensable in organising the functionalist's account of cognition, its very fruitfulness carries a risk that the philosophically careful user must keep in view: that the analogy between software and mental states, however illuminating as a model of information processing, may seduce us into treating as solved the question that the hard problem of consciousness actually poses \u2014 namely, why there is anything it is like to be in such a state at all, a question that no amount of functional decomposition, however complete, appears even to address, let alone to answer.* The rewrite distinguishes the heuristic value of the metaphor from its explanatory limits: *heuristically indispensable* concedes the usefulness, *its very fruitfulness carries a risk* signals the danger, and *seduce us into treating as solved the question that... actually poses* names the specific error. The final clause \u2014 *no amount of functional decomposition... appears even to address* \u2014 explains why the metaphor cannot do the work the simple version asks of it.
**Ejercicio 4.** Traduce al inglés C1 con precisión conceptual: "La distinción entre los aspectos funcionales de un estado mental y su carácter fenoménico es la que explota el problema duro de la consciencia."
Ver solución *The distinction between the functional aspects of a mental state \u2014 what it does, what role it plays in the cognitive economy \u2014 and its phenomenal character \u2014 what it is like, from the inside, to be in that state \u2014 is the distinction that the hard problem of consciousness exploits, for the former admits, in principle, of a complete functional account while the latter, by its very nature, seems to resist any account that does not, at some point, presuppose the very thing it sets out to explain.* Key vocabulary: *functional aspects*, *phenomenal character*, *the hard problem of consciousness*, *a complete functional account*, *presuppose the very thing it sets out to explain*. The structure distinguishes the two levels of description and explains why the hard problem targets the second: the functional level is tractable, the phenomenal level seems to presuppose consciousness in its own explanation.
**Ejercicio 5.** Reescribe usando conectores de precisión conceptual (*in the strict sense*, *not to be confused with*, *as distinct from*): "Consciousness is just attention. They are the same thing."
Ver solución *Consciousness, in the strict sense that the hard problem targets, is not to be confused with attention \u2014 as distinct from the cluster of access functions that attention involves \u2014 for while attention may be a necessary condition of certain forms of conscious experience in the creatures we know, it is not identical with the phenomenal character that consciousness, in the relevant sense, denotes, and the tendency to slide between the two is one that the philosophical literature exists in large part to resist.* The connectors do precision work: *in the strict sense* scopes the term, *not to be confused with* flags the distinction, *as distinct from* elaborates what attention actually is. The rewrite distinguishes a necessary condition (attention) from the phenomenon itself (phenomenal consciousness), preventing the conflation that the simple version commits.
**Ejercicio 6.** Completa con léxico del funcionalismo: *functional role*, *multiple realisability*, *machine functionalism*, *computational theory of mind*. 1. The idea that a mental state is individuated by what it does, not what it is made of, is the ______. 2. The thesis that the same mental state can be implemented in different substrates is ______. 3. The view that the mind is a computer running programmes is the ______. 4. The broader thesis that cognition is computation is the ______.
Ver solución 1. functional role 2. multiple realisability 3. machine functionalism 4. computational theory of mind These terms form a nested hierarchy: *functional role* is the core idea, *multiple realisability* is its key implication, *machine functionalism* is one specific implementation (the mind as a Turing machine), and the *computational theory of mind* is the broader thesis that cognition is computation. Understanding their relations is essential for arguing within the functionalist framework.
**Ejercicio 7.** Escribe una frase en C1 que presente el argumento del zombi contra el fisicalismo, usando precisión conceptual y conectores lógicos.
Ver solución *The zombie argument \u2014 the thought experiment of a being functionally and physically identical to a conscious human yet devoid of any inner experience \u2014 purports to show that phenomenal consciousness is not entailed by the physical facts, for if such a being is conceivable without contradiction, then the physical facts do not, by logical necessity, include the phenomenal ones, from which it follows, if the conceivability is genuine, that physicalism is false, a conclusion the physicalist must rebut by arguing either that the zombie is not genuinely conceivable or that conceivability does not entail possibility.* The logical structure: the zombie is *conceivable without contradiction* \u2014 *if... then the physical facts do not... include the phenomenal ones* \u2014 *from which it follows... that physicalism is false*. The final clause (*the physicalist must rebut by arguing either... or...*) identifies the two lines of response. The argument turns conceivability into a challenge to physicalist entailment.
**Ejercicio 8.** Reescribe con matización metafórica, señalando dónde la analogía se rompe: "The brain is a prediction machine. It works just like a computer predicting things."
Ver solución *The metaphor of the brain as a prediction machine is illuminating, up to a point, insofar as it captures the way in which neural processing can be modelled as the minimisation of prediction error across hierarchical levels; with the caveat, however, that the analogy breaks down at the point where the question of why the prediction is accompanied by experience is concerned, for while a prediction machine processes error signals, there is nothing it is like, from the inside, to be that processing \u2014 a disanalogy that the metaphor, if pressed too far, obscures precisely where the philosophically interesting question lies.* The maturation: *illuminating, up to a point, insofar as* concedes the heuristic value; *with the caveat, however, that the analogy breaks down at* signals the limit; *there is nothing it is like... to be that processing* names the disanalogy; *obscures precisely where the philosophically interesting question lies* explains the danger. The rewrite uses the metaphor without being used by it.
**Ejercicio 9.** Completa con léxico de qualia y el argumento del conocimiento: *qualia*, *the knowledge argument*, *what Mary didn't know*, *phenomenal concepts*. 1. The thought experiment about the colour scientist who learns something new on seeing red is ______. 2. The subjective qualities of experience that Mary appears to gain knowledge of are ______. 3. The argument that there are facts about experience that escape the physical inventory is ______. 4. Concepts that pick out experiences by their felt quality, not their physical basis, are ______.
Ver solución 1. what Mary didn't know (or Mary's room) 2. qualia 3. the knowledge argument 4. phenomenal concepts The argument's structure: Mary knows all the physical facts (*the knowledge argument*), yet on seeing red she appears to learn about *qualia*; this is *what Mary didn't know*; the physicalist's reply is that she gains *phenomenal concepts* (a new mode of access) rather than new facts. Understanding the argument and the reply is essential for engaging with the physicalism debate.
**Ejercicio 10.** Reescribe esta afirmación sobre el eliminativismo con la precisión y la abstracción de un C1: "Beliefs aren't real. Folk psychology is wrong, like old science."
Ver solución *The eliminativist's claim that folk psychology is a theory \u2014 and a theory that, like phlogiston or caloric, may turn out to be radically mistaken about its domain \u2014 is not the modest observation that we sometimes misattribute beliefs but the radical thesis that the categories of belief and desire may not carve the cognitive reality at its joints, a thesis whose plausibility depends on whether the predictive and explanatory success of folk psychology is the kind of success that a fundamentally mistaken theory could enjoy, or whether that success is, rather, evidence that the categories it deploys correspond, at least roughly, to real features of the cognitive system.* The rewrite distinguishes the modest thesis (we sometimes misattribute) from the radical one (the categories may not carve reality at its joints), and frames the evaluation as turning on a specific epistemological question: could a fundamentally mistaken theory enjoy the predictive success folk psychology enjoys? The everyday claim becomes a philosophical thesis embedded in the debate about theoretical success and reference.
**Ejercicio 11.** Escribe una frase en C1 que explique el problema de la interacción del dualismo cartesiano, usando conectores lógicos.
Ver solución *The interaction problem that has dogged substance dualism since Descartes \u2014 how two substances as different in kind as mind and matter could causally affect one another \u2014 is not merely a technical difficulty but a structural one, for the very intelligibility of causal interaction seems to presuppose some common currency between cause and effect that the radical heterogeneity of the two substances appears to rule out by definition, which is to say that the difficulty is not that we have not yet found the mechanism of interaction but that the very notion of a mechanism, as something that operates in physical space, is one that the immateriality of the mind puts beyond reach.* The logical structure: the problem is *not merely a technical difficulty but a structural one* (escalation), *for... seems to presuppose some common currency... that the... heterogeneity... appears to rule out by definition* (the structural reason), *which is to say that...* (reformulation that deepens). The argument shows the problem is not empirical (we haven't found the mechanism) but conceptual (the notion of mechanism is incompatible with immateriality).
**Ejercicio 12.** Traduce al inglés C1: "La tesis de la mente extendida desafía el supuesto tácito de que los límites de lo cognitivo coinciden con los de la piel."
Ver solución *The extended mind thesis \u2014 that cognitive processes can, under certain conditions, loop out into the environment, so that a notebook used reliably for memory counts, by parity of reasoning, as part of the mind \u2014 challenges the tacit assumption that the boundaries of the cognitive are coextensive with the boundaries of the skin, though whether the parity argument establishes that the external resource is part of the mind or merely that the boundary between mind and world is less sharp than we assumed is a question its proponents and critics continue to contest.* Key vocabulary: *extended mind thesis*, *loop out into the environment*, *parity of reasoning*, *coextensive with the boundaries of the skin*. The structure presents the thesis, identifies what it challenges, and then complicates the evaluation: does parity show the external is *part of the mind*, or merely that the *boundary is less sharp*? This refusal to resolve the interpretive question is characteristic of C1 philosophical writing.
**Ejercicio 13.** Completa con léxico de emergencia y reducción: *supervenience*, *emergent property*, *identity theory*, *anomalous monism*. 1. The thesis that mental states are identical to brain states is the ______. 2. The dependence of the mental on the physical without reducibility is ______. 3. A property of a system that is not a property of its parts is an ______. 4. Davidson's view that every mental event is physical but mental descriptions are irreducible is ______.
Ver solución 1. identity theory (type identity theory) 2. supervenience 3. emergent property 4. anomalous monism The relationships: *identity theory* is the strongest reductive claim (mental = physical), *supervenience* is weaker (mental depends on physical but may not be reducible), *emergent properties* are system-level properties not present in the parts, and *anomalous monism* (Davidson) holds that every event is physical (monism) but there are no strict psychophysical laws (anomalous), making it a form of non-reductive physicalism. These positions form a spectrum of commitment to reduction.
**Ejercicio 14.** Reescribe esta afirmación sobre el acceso privilegiado con la precisión de un C1: "I know my own mind perfectly. No one can correct me about what I feel."
Ver solución *The first-person authority that we ordinarily accord to a subject's avowals of her own mental states \u2014 the presumption that, if she sincerely says she is in pain, she is, barring rare exceptions, right \u2014 is a feature of our epistemic practice that any philosophy of mind must accommodate, though the explanation of that authority is itself contested, with some accounts grounding it in a special mode of access and others in the constitutive role that the avowal plays in fixing the state avowed, a divergence that turns, in the final analysis, on whether self-knowledge is a form of observation or a form of creation.* The rewrite replaces the absolute claim (*I know my mind perfectly*) with the calibrated notion of *first-person authority* as a feature of epistemic practice, acknowledges that it admits of *rare exceptions*, and frames the explanation as a contested question (is self-knowledge observation or creation?). The everyday certainty becomes a philosophical datum with competing theoretical explanations.
**Ejercicio 15.** Escribe una frase en C1 que distinga consciencia de acceso de consciencia fenoménica, explicando por qué la distinción es estratégica para el funcionalista.
Ver solución *The distinction between access and phenomenal consciousness, if sound, allows the functionalist to account for the former \u2014 which is, by construction, a matter of information availability for verbal report and rational control \u2014 while conceding that the latter poses the hard problem, a division of explanatory labour that is attractive to the functionalist precisely because it confines the explanandum that resists functional analysis to a domain that the functionalist can, without inconsistency, leave to one side, though whether the distinction is sound \u2014 whether access and phenomenal consciousness can in fact come apart, as the dissociation cases are invoked to show \u2014 is a question that the functionalist's critics contest precisely because the strategy's success depends on it.* The structure: *the distinction... if sound, allows* (the strategic benefit), *a division of explanatory labour that is attractive... because it confines... to a domain the functionalist can leave aside* (why it's attractive), *though whether the distinction is sound... is a question that... critics contest precisely because the strategy's success depends on it* (the vulnerability). The sentence explains both why the functionalist wants the distinction and why it is the point at which critics attack.
**Ejercicio 16.** Usa la estructura cohesiva *the question, properly framed, is not X but Y; the metaphor is apt insofar as Z; the upshot is that W* para articular el límite de la metáfora computacional.
Ver solución *The question, properly framed, is not whether the mind is like a computer \u2014 a metaphor whose aptness is, in any case, contestable \u2014 but whether the computational model, insofar as it captures the functional individuation of mental states, can address the phenomenal residue that the hard problem identifies; the metaphor is apt insofar as it illuminates the functional level of description, where the analogy between software and mental states organises a genuine insight about role-based individuation; the upshot, however, is that the model can, at best, clarify that functional level while leaving the phenomenal residue precisely where it was, which is why the metaphor, however useful as a heuristic, should not be mistaken for a solution to the very problem it so elegantly reorganises.* The cohesive structure performs three moves: *the question, properly framed, is not... but...* (reframes the question from the metaphor's aptness to its explanatory reach), *the metaphor is apt insofar as* (concedes the legitimate scope), *the upshot, however, is that* (delivers the limit). The sentence uses the metaphor as a heuristic while marking precisely where it ceases to illuminate \u2014 the C1 stance on explanatory metaphors.
**Ejercicio 17.** Reescribe esta afirmación sobre la intencionalidad con la abstracción filosófica de un C1: "Thoughts are about things. But how does the brain do that?"
Ver solución *The Brentanian thesis that intentionality is the mark of the mental \u2014 that what distinguishes mental states from physical ones is their directedness towards an object, their being about something \u2014 raises the question of whether intentionality can be naturalised, that is, explained in terms that do not themselves presuppose the mentality they set out to account for, a question whose difficulty is compounded by the existence of states, like beliefs about non-existent entities, that have intentionality without an object, which is to say that the very feature that marks the mental also generates the puzzle of how a physical system can be about something at all.* The rewrite moves from the everyday observation (*thoughts are about things*) to the Brentanian thesis (*intentionality as the mark of the mental*), formulates the philosophical question (*can intentionality be naturalised?*), defines the challenge (*without presupposing the mentality it sets out to explain*), and deepens it with the case of *intentionality without an object* (beliefs about non-existent entities). The simple question becomes a layered philosophical problem.
**Ejercicio 18.** Escribe un párrafo breve (4-5 frases) en C1 que articule el debate entre fisicalismo reductivo, no reductivo y dualismo de propiedades, usando precisión conceptual y conectores lógicos.
Ver solución *The spectrum of positions on the mind-body problem \u2014 from reductive physicalism, through non-reductive physicalism, to property dualism \u2014 turns, in the final analysis, on a single question: whether the mental, if it supervenes on the physical, is thereby reducible to it, or whether supervenience leaves a residue that resists reduction without amounting to the distinct substance of the Cartesian dualist. The reductive physicalist holds that the mental just is the physical, properly described, so that a complete physical description would, in principle, leave nothing mental unaccounted for; the non-reductive physicalist concedes the dependence but denies the identity, holding that the mental supervenes on the physical without being reducible to it. The difficulty for the non-reductive position is to specify what the irreducibility consists in: if it is merely epistemic \u2014 a matter of our descriptive categories \u2014 it threatens to collapse into the reductive view the non-reductivist meant to resist, whereas if it is ontic \u2014 a matter of the properties themselves \u2014 it threatens to collapse into the property dualism it was meant to avoid. The upshot, then, is that the non-reductive physicalist occupies an attractive but unstable middle ground, one whose coherence depends on drawing a distinction \u2014 between epistemic and ontic irreducibility \u2014 that is, on the available arguments, more easily asserted than established, which is why the debate, for all its technical refinement, remains as live as it is.* Conceptual vocabulary: *reductive physicalism*, *non-reductive physicalism*, *property dualism*, *supervenience*, *reducible*, *epistemic vs ontic irreducibility*. Logical connectors: *in the final analysis*, *if... then... whereas if... then...*, *the upshot, then, is that*. The paragraph maps the spectrum, explains the middle position's difficulty, and identifies the distinction on which its coherence turns.
**Ejercicio 19.** Escribe un párrafo breve (4-5 frases) en inglés C1 que argumente sobre el papel de la metáfora en filosofía de la mente, usando matización metafórica, precisión conceptual y conectores de cohesión.
Ver solución *The role of metaphor in the philosophy of mind is, to put the matter carefully, both indispensable and dangerous \u2014 indispensable because the subject matter, being in part the subjective character of experience, resists the literal vocabulary that suffices for the physical sciences, and dangerous because a metaphor that illuminates at one level of description can obscure at another, seducing us into mistaking the model for the reality modelled. The computational metaphor, to take the paradigmatic case, is apt insofar as it captures the functional individuation of mental states \u2014 the insight that what makes a state the state it is, is the role it plays rather than the material that realises it \u2014 yet the analogy breaks down, with the caveat that this is not a minor disanalogy but a decisive one, at the point where the question of phenomenal consciousness is concerned, for while a computer processes information, there is nothing it is like, from the inside, to be that processing, and the metaphor, if pressed beyond its legitimate scope, obscures precisely the explanandum \u2014 the subjective residue \u2014 that the hard problem identifies. The upshot is not that the metaphor should be abandoned, for its heuristic value at the functional level is genuine, but that it should be used with the awareness that its illumination is, in the relevant sense, partial: it organises one level of description while leaving another untouched, and the philosophically serious user is the one who can deploy it for what it illuminates without letting it dictate what it cannot. This discipline \u2014 the capacity to use a metaphor and, at the same time, to see where it ceases to apply \u2014 is, in the final analysis, not merely a stylistic virtue but an epistemic one, for the history of the philosophy of mind is in no small part the history of confusions that arose when a useful picture was mistaken for a settled theory. The honest position, then, is that we cannot do without metaphors in this domain, but we can \u2014 and the C1 speaker must \u2014 do with them consciously, marking their scope, signalling their limits, and resisting the perennial temptation to let the elegance of the model substitute for the rigour of the argument it was meant to organise.* Matización metafórica: *apt insofar as*, *the analogy breaks down, with the caveat that*, *if pressed beyond its legitimate scope*, *partial illumination*. Precisión conceptual: *functional individuation*, *phenomenal consciousness*, *the explanandum*, *the subjective residue*. Conectores de cohesión: *to put the matter carefully*, *in the relevant sense*, *the upshot is not that... but that*, *in the final analysis*, *the honest position, then, is that*. The paragraph enacts the very discipline it advocates: it uses the computational metaphor to illustrate a point about metaphor while rigorously marking where that illustration ceases to apply.
## Resumen de la unidad En esta unidad hemos construido el andamiaje lingüístico para argumentar sobre la filosofía de la mente con la precisión conceptual y la conciencia metalingüística que exige el nivel C1. Has aprendido a distinguir *dualism* de *physicalism*, *qualia* de *functional states*, *access consciousness* de *phenomenal consciousness*, y a manejar el léxico del problema cuerpo-mente \u2014*substance dualism*, *property dualism*, *epiphenomenalism*\u2014, el del hard problem \u2014*explanatory gap*, *zombie argument*, *the knowledge argument*\u2014 y el del funcionalismo \u2014*functional role*, *multiple realisability*, *computational theory of mind*. Has incorporado el vocabulario de la intencionalidad \u2014*aboutness*, *propositional attitudes*, *mental representation*\u2014, de la emergencia \u2014*supervenience*, *emergent property*, *identity theory*\u2014 y de la cognición encarnada \u2014*embodied cognition*, *extended mind*, *4E cognition*. Has ejercitado la matización metafórica \u2014*apt insofar as*, *the analogy breaks down at*, *if pressed too far*\u2014 como disciplina epistémica, la precisión conceptual \u2014*in the strict sense*, *not to be confused with*, *as distinct from*\u2014 como higiene argumentativa, y la cohesión filosófica que hace visible tanto la estructura del argumento como los límites de la metáfora que lo articula. La destreza central de esta unidad es el uso consciente de la metáfora: la capacidad de emplear los modelos explicativos \u2014la mente como ordenador, la consciencia como propiedad emergente\u2014 para lo que iluminan, al tiempo que se señala con precisión dónde dejan de iluminar, resistiendo la tentación, tan común en este campo, de confundir la elegancia del modelo con la solución del problema. Esa elegancia metalingüística es la marca distintiva del hablante C1 cuando se enfrenta a uno de los debates donde el lenguaje debe ser a la vez imaginativo y riguroso, y donde la diferencia entre una metáfora que ilumina y una que engaña es, literalmente, la diferencia entre filosofía y confusión.

title: Ejercicios de Libre Albedrío y Determinismo C1
author: linguafly-team
excerpt: Aprende a manejar el lenguaje abstracto del debate sobre el libre albedrío y el determinismo, a usar conectores lógicos con precisión y a argumentar sobre filosofía de la acción con rigor. Teoría detallada y 19 ejercicios para dominar la abstracción argumentativa en inglés.
description: En esta unidad del curso de inglés C1 gratis aprendes a manejar el lenguaje abstracto del debate sobre el libre albedrío y el determinismo, a usar...
alt: Bifurcación de caminos en un laberinto lógico, con engranajes deterministas y una silueta humana decidiendo
keywords: Ejercicios de Libre Albedrío y Determinismo C1
argumentar sobre free will en inglés

faqs.question: ¿Qué diferencia hay entre 'free will', 'determinism' y 'compatibilism' en inglés C1?
faqs.answer: Free will es la capacidad de elegir libremente; determinism es la tesis de que todo evento está causalmente determinado por eventos anteriores; compatibilism sostiene que ambos son compatibles si se redefine el libre albedrío como acción libre de coacción externa, aunque causalmente determinada.

faqs.question: ¿Qué conectores lógicos usa un hablante C1 al argumentar sobre filosofía?
