# Unidad 11 C1: cleft sentences, educación y aprendizaje En una conversación sencilla podemos decir: *The teacher identified the problem*. En un ensayo o una presentación académica quizá queramos destacar quién lo identificó, qué problema se detectó o cuándo ocurrió. Las **cleft sentences**, también llamadas oraciones escindidas, nos permiten reorganizar la información para que un elemento reciba un foco claro. - *It was the teacher who identified the problem.* - *It was the problem that the teacher identified.* - *What the teacher identified was a gap in the students’ reasoning.* El hecho general es parecido, pero la perspectiva cambia. En la Unidad 11 C1 aplicamos estas estructuras al tema de **Education and Learning**: autonomía docente, evaluación, pensamiento crítico, aprendizaje autodirigido, educación progresiva y acceso a la universidad. El objetivo es aprender a controlar el foco sin crear frases artificiales. Las clefts son especialmente útiles al responder preguntas. Si alguien pregunta *Who made the mistake?*, podemos contestar *It was the teacher who made the mistake*. Si pregunta *What did the teacher identify?*, podemos decir *What the teacher identified was a gap in reasoning*. La estructura ayuda a que la respuesta conecte exactamente con la información solicitada. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 11 C1](/curso-c1/unit-11)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 10 C1: repaso, ética y futuro](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-10-repaso-etica-futuro)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 12 C1: complex noun phrases](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-22-biodiversidad-conservacion)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Qué es el foco informativo En una oración neutra, varios elementos comparten la atención del lector: - *The professor changed the assessment because the final exam measured performance under pressure.* Si queremos corregir una posible interpretación, podemos destacar una parte: - *It was the professor who changed the assessment, not the students.* - *It was the assessment that the professor changed, not the curriculum.* - *It was because the final exam measured performance under pressure that the assessment was changed.* El foco depende de la pregunta o del contraste. Una cleft no es simplemente una forma “más avanzada” de decir lo mismo. Si no hay una razón para destacar un elemento, la oración normal suele ser más natural. La cleft aporta valor cuando el escritor quiere corregir, contrastar, resumir o responder con precisión. En educación, el foco puede cambiar la interpretación: - *The school introduced continuous assessment.* - *It was the school that introduced continuous assessment.* La escuela, y no otra institución, es el foco. - *It was continuous assessment that the school introduced.* El tipo de evaluación es el foco. - *What the school introduced was continuous assessment.* La nueva medida es el foco del comentario. ### 2. It-cleft: estructura básica La estructura principal es: > **It + is/was + focus + that/who + clause** Usamos **is** para una situación presente o general y **was** para un hecho pasado: - *It is the feedback that shapes the learner’s next step.* - *It was the feedback that changed her approach.* - *It is the teacher who notices the pattern first.* - *It was the teacher who noticed the error.* **Who** se usa habitualmente para personas y **that** para objetos, ideas, tiempos o lugares: - *It was the tutor who encouraged independent research.* - *It was the deadline that created unnecessary pressure.* - *It was in the library that the students found the relevant source.* - *It was during the final semester that her confidence improved.* En el inglés hablado, *who* y *that* pueden variar, pero en escritura académica la elección debe ser clara. No confundas el tiempo de *is/was* con el tiempo de la cláusula posterior. La oración puede combinar un foco presente con una acción pasada si el contexto lo exige: - *It is the early intervention that helped her regain confidence.* Sin embargo, muchas veces *it was* resulta más coherente si todo el evento pertenece al pasado: - *It was the early intervention that helped her regain confidence.* ### 3. Enfocar el sujeto Para destacar quién realiza la acción, colocamos la persona o grupo después de *it is/was*: - Orden neutro: *The teacher made the mistake.* - It-cleft: *It was the teacher who made the mistake, not the students.* - Orden neutro: *The students challenged the assumption.* - It-cleft: *It was the students who challenged the assumption.* La cláusula relativa conserva el orden normal de la oración. No decimos *It was the teacher who did made the mistake*. Después de *who*, usamos el verbo correspondiente: *who made*, *who noticed*, *who had suggested*. La negación también es posible: - *It was not the teacher who made the mistake.* - *It wasn’t the students who requested the change.* En una pregunta, la cleft mantiene la inversión propia de la pregunta principal: - *Was it the teacher who made the mistake?* - *Is it the assessment that needs revision?* La cleft puede incluir un contraste explícito con *not* o *rather than*: - *It was the lack of feedback, rather than the difficulty of the task, that discouraged learners.* ### 4. Enfocar el objeto Para destacar un objeto, usamos **that** o una cláusula que retoma el objeto: - *It was the final exam that the students found stressful.* - *It was the research method that the supervisor questioned.* - *It was the assumption of equal access that the report challenged.* La oración subyacente es *The students found the final exam stressful*. El objeto aparece en la posición de foco y deja una posición vacía en la cláusula: *that the students found __ stressful*. En inglés formal esta estructura es correcta. Con ciertos verbos y preposiciones, la preposición puede permanecer al final: - *It was Oxford that she enrolled at, not Cambridge.* - *It was the source that the essay referred to.* En un registro muy formal puede adelantarse: - *It was at Oxford that she enrolled.* - *It was to this source that the essay referred.* Elige la opción más natural para el contexto. No fuerces una preposición delante de *which* si una cleft con *that* produce una oración más clara. ### 5. Enfocar tiempo, lugar y causa El foco no tiene que ser una persona o un objeto. También puede ser un momento, un lugar o una causa: - *It was in the first year that the achievement gap became visible.* - *It was after the policy change that attendance improved.* - *It was because the test rewarded memorisation that critics opposed it.* - *It is through sustained practice that learners develop fluency.* Estas estructuras son útiles en explicaciones históricas y análisis de políticas educativas. La cleft hace que la relación causal o temporal sea visible, pero no garantiza que la causa sea correcta. Si la relación es una interpretación, añade cautela: - *It may have been the change in curriculum that improved participation.* ### 6. What-clefts o pseudo-clefts Una **what-cleft** empieza con **what** y contiene una cláusula completa. Su estructura básica es: > **What + subject + verb + is/was + focus** - *What matters is sustained practice.* - *What the teacher noticed was a gap in reasoning.* - *What surprised the panel was the consistency of the results.* - *What learners need is meaningful feedback.* La cláusula con *what* significa “lo que”. No uses una pregunta directa dentro de ella: - Correcto: *What did the teacher notice?* como pregunta directa. - Correcto: *What the teacher noticed was a gap in reasoning.* como what-cleft. - Incorrecto: *What did the teacher notice was a gap in reasoning.* El verbo dentro de la what-clause va antes del foco y mantiene el orden declarativo. La frase posterior identifica la información que queremos presentar como respuesta. ### 7. What-clefts con tiempos verbales El tiempo de *is/was* depende del momento del análisis: - *What matters is whether students can apply the concept.* - *What mattered was whether students could apply the concept.* - *What the assessment reveals is a difference in preparation.* - *What the assessment revealed was a difference in preparation.* La cláusula interna puede tener cualquier tiempo necesario: - *What the researchers found was that attendance had improved.* - *What the teacher is examining is how learners respond to feedback.* - *What the committee will decide is whether the exam should remain.* Una what-cleft puede contener una cláusula con *that* o *whether*: - *What the evidence shows is that teacher autonomy matters.* - *What remains uncertain is whether continuous assessment reduces anxiety.* ### 8. What-cleft como respuesta y resumen Las what-clefts son muy útiles para resumir información: - Pregunta: *What did the Finnish model rely on?* - Respuesta: *What it relied on was trust in teachers and a commitment to equity.* - Pregunta: *What concerns the professor about summative assessment?* - Respuesta: *What concerns her is that a final test captures only a snapshot of performance.* - Pregunta: *What should the school change?* - Respuesta: *What the school should change is the balance between testing and feedback.* También pueden iniciar un párrafo argumentativo: > *What is often overlooked is that assessment shapes learning behaviour. If students are rewarded only for recalling information, they may devote less time to evaluating evidence or formulating original arguments.* La estructura crea una transición natural desde el foco hacia la explicación. No abuses de ella en cada frase: una cadena de what-clefts puede resultar monótona. ### 9. It-cleft frente a what-cleft Ambas estructuras pueden expresar un foco similar, pero su organización retórica es diferente: - *It was the teacher who identified the error.* Destaca al agente y responde a “¿quién?”. - *What the teacher identified was the error.* Destaca el contenido y responde a “¿qué?”. - *It was the final exam that caused anxiety.* Destaca la causa. - *What caused anxiety was the final exam.* Presenta la causa como respuesta. - *It was in the library that they found the source.* Destaca el lugar. - *What they found in the library was the source.* Destaca el objeto encontrado. Usa **it-cleft** cuando el elemento enfocado contrasta con otro elemento. Usa **what-cleft** cuando quieres presentar una pregunta, una conclusión o un comentario sobre una situación. ### 10. Clefts negativas y contrastivas Las clefts pueden corregir una suposición: - *It wasn’t the workload that caused the problem; it was the lack of support.* - *What the policy changed was not access, but the way access was measured.* - *It was not memorisation that the teacher wanted to assess, but critical thinking.* El paralelismo ayuda a que la oposición sea clara. Si el foco aparece en singular, el verbo puede concordar con él: - *What matters is feedback.* - *What matter are the practical consequences.* En usos complejos, algunos hablantes prefieren mantener *what matters is* como fórmula fija y reformular el foco plural: *What matters most is the practical consequences for learners* puede oírse, pero en escritura cuidada es más seguro decir *What matters most are the practical consequences* o *The main issue is the practical consequences*. Mantén la concordancia que tu análisis necesita. ### 11. Clefts en escritura académica Las clefts pueden reforzar una tesis o una transición: - *It is the interaction between autonomy and accountability that determines the success of a school reform.* - *What this comparison demonstrates is that equity and excellence need not be opposites.* - *It was the lack of longitudinal evidence that limited the original conclusion.* También ayudan a introducir una limitación: - *What the study does not establish is whether the improvement will persist.* - *It is not the size of the effect that matters most, but its relevance to daily learning.* Una cleft resulta más eficaz cuando el foco tiene una función discursiva. Si solo añade palabras sin organizar la argumentación, una estructura simple puede ser mejor: - Directa: *Teacher autonomy improves motivation.* - Con foco necesario: *It is teacher autonomy that the comparison identifies as the key factor.* ### 12. Vocabulario de educación y aprendizaje - **blended learning:** aprendizaje que combina clases presenciales, recursos digitales y trabajo independiente. - **pedagogical approach:** enfoque pedagógico. - **self-directed study:** estudio autodirigido. - **critical thinking:** pensamiento crítico. - **scrutinise evidence:** examinar pruebas de forma crítica. - **shed new light on:** aportar una comprensión nueva o más clara. - **teacher autonomy:** autonomía docente. - **equity:** equidad, igualdad justa de oportunidades. - **academic rigour:** rigor académico. - **standardised testing:** evaluación estandarizada. - **summative assessment:** evaluación sumativa al final de un curso o periodo. - **formative feedback:** retroalimentación durante el proceso de aprendizaje. - **learning outcome:** resultado de aprendizaje. - **achievement gap:** brecha de rendimiento o logro. - **higher education:** educación superior. - **undergraduate:** estudiante o nivel de grado universitario. - **curriculum:** plan de estudios. - **enrolment:** matriculación. - **retention:** permanencia de estudiantes o empleados. - **lifelong learning:** aprendizaje permanente. Colocaciones útiles son **adopt a pedagogical approach**, **combine traditional lectures with self-directed study**, **scrutinise evidence**, **evaluate an argument**, **shed new light on a topic**, **measure learning outcomes**, **provide formative feedback**, **close the achievement gap**, **promote equity**, **maintain academic rigour**, **cultivate critical thinking** y **widen access to higher education**. ### 13. Evaluación y clefts El contraste entre evaluación sumativa y formativa ofrece contextos naturales: - *It is the depth of understanding that continuous feedback can reveal.* - *What a final exam captures is a snapshot of performance under pressure.* - *It was the absence of formative feedback that made the course difficult to adjust.* - *What matters is whether students can transfer knowledge to a new problem.* No presentes una conclusión universal si los datos no la justifican. Una buena frase puede incluir distancia o limitación: - *What the evidence appears to suggest is that formative feedback supports revision, although its effect depends on how students use it.* La cleft organiza el foco; *appears to suggest* controla la fuerza de la afirmación; *although* introduce la condición que limita la conclusión. ### 14. Errores frecuentes - *It was the teacher which made the mistake.* → **It was the teacher who made the mistake.** - *It was Oxford where she enrolled at.* → **It was Oxford that she enrolled at** o **It was at Oxford that she enrolled.** - *What did the study show was a gap.* → **What the study showed was a gap.** - *What the students need it is feedback.* → **What the students need is feedback.** - *It was the exam that the students were anxious.* → **It was the exam that made the students anxious** o **It was the exam that the students were anxious about.** - *What matters are sustained practice.* → **What matters is sustained practice.** - *It was not the teacher who made it, but the student.* → Comprueba el referente: **It was not the teacher who made the mistake, but the student.** - *The reason why the policy failed was because...* → En registro formal: **The reason why the policy failed was that...** La revisión final consiste en identificar la pregunta implícita, localizar el foco, comprobar *is/was*, elegir *who/that* y mantener el orden declarativo dentro de la cláusula con *what*. ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Identifica el foco Indica qué elemento se destaca. 1. *It was the teacher who made the mistake.* 2. *It was the mistake that the teacher made.* 3. *What the teacher identified was a gap in reasoning.* 4. *It was in the library that the students found the source.*
Ver solución 1. **The teacher**, la persona responsable. 2. **The mistake**, el objeto de la acción. 3. **A gap in reasoning**, el contenido identificado. 4. **In the library**, el lugar.
### Ejercicio 2 — It-cleft básica Combina las frases destacando el elemento entre paréntesis. 1. The teacher noticed the error. (the teacher) 2. The students found the source. (the source) 3. The policy changed attendance. (the policy) 4. They began the project in September. (in September)
Ver solución 1. **It was the teacher who noticed the error.** 2. **It was the source that the students found.** 3. **It was the policy that changed attendance.** 4. **It was in September that they began the project.**
### Ejercicio 3 — Who o that Elige el relativo correcto. 1. It was the tutor ___ encouraged independent research. 2. It was the deadline ___ created unnecessary pressure. 3. It was the students ___ challenged the assumption. 4. It was the method ___ the supervisor questioned.
Ver solución 1. **who**; 2. **that**; 3. **who**; 4. **that**. En clefts, *who* es la opción habitual para personas y *that* para cosas o ideas.
### Ejercicio 4 — What-clefts Completa. 1. ___ matters ___ sustained practice. 2. ___ the teacher noticed ___ a gap in reasoning. 3. ___ surprised the panel ___ the consistency of the results. 4. ___ learners need ___ meaningful feedback.
Ver solución 1. **What matters is**. 2. **What the teacher noticed was**. 3. **What surprised the panel was**. 4. **What learners need is**.
### Ejercicio 5 — Orden declarativo Corrige las what-clefts. 1. *What did the study show was a gap in access.* 2. *What does the teacher need is more feedback.* 3. *What did the panel find was unexpected variation.*
Ver solución 1. **What the study showed was a gap in access.** 2. **What the teacher needs is more feedback.** 3. **What the panel found was unexpected variation.** Dentro de una what-clause no usamos el orden de una pregunta directa.
### Ejercicio 6 — Presente o pasado Elige **is** o **was**. 1. It ___ the feedback that changed her approach last term. 2. What ___ important now is whether students can apply the concept. 3. It ___ the teacher who notices the pattern first in this course. 4. What ___ most striking in the survey was the gap in access.
Ver solución 1. **was**; 2. **is**; 3. **is**; 4. **was**. El verbo de la cleft sigue el momento de referencia.
### Ejercicio 7 — Contraste Reescribe usando una cleft. *The problem was not the workload. It was the lack of support.*
Ver solución **It wasn’t the workload that caused the problem; it was the lack of support.** También: **What caused the problem was not the workload, but the lack of support.**
### Ejercicio 8 — Vocabulario educativo Completa con **blended, scrutinise, equity, formative feedback** o **academic rigour**. 1. The university uses a ___ approach combining lectures and online study. 2. Critical thinkers ___ evidence before accepting a claim. 3. The policy aims to improve ___ rather than simply raise average scores. 4. Teachers use ___ to help learners revise during the course. 5. The programme maintains high levels of ___ .
Ver solución 1. **blended**; 2. **scrutinise**; 3. **equity**; 4. **formative feedback**; 5. **academic rigour**.
### Ejercicio 9 — Reading Lee el texto y responde. > The Finnish model of education, widely admired for its consistently high outcomes, rests not on standardised testing or competitive ranking, but on deep trust in teachers as autonomous professionals and a firm belief that equity and excellence are not mutually exclusive. What underpins the model is a combination of teacher autonomy, carefully trained professionals and a commitment to support rather than punish struggling learners. It was this balance, rather than the absence of assessment, that attracted international attention. Critics of progressive education nevertheless argue that creativity and personal development can come at the expense of academic rigour if expectations are not made explicit. 1. What does the model rest on? 2. What underpins it according to the text? 3. What attracted international attention? 4. What concern do critics raise?
Ver solución 1. **Trust in teachers and a belief that equity and excellence can coexist.** 2. **Teacher autonomy, trained professionals and support for struggling learners.** 3. **The balance between autonomy, support and expectations, rather than the absence of assessment.** 4. **That creativity and personal development may weaken academic rigour if expectations are unclear.**
### Ejercicio 10 — Listening guiado Guion: “What concerns me about purely summative assessment is that it captures a snapshot of performance under pressure rather than the depth of understanding developed over time. It is the lack of regular feedback that makes the system difficult to adjust. What students need is an opportunity to revise their thinking before the final grade is awarded.” Identifica dos what-clefts y una it-cleft.
Ver solución What-clefts: **What concerns me about purely summative assessment is...** y **What students need is...**. It-cleft: **It is the lack of regular feedback that makes the system difficult to adjust.**
### Ejercicio 11 — Relativo y preposición Completa o corrige. 1. It was Oxford ___ she enrolled ___, not Cambridge. 2. It was the source ___ the essay referred ___ . 3. It was the teacher ___ the students spoke ___ after class.
Ver solución 1. **that; at**: *It was Oxford that she enrolled at.* También: **It was at Oxford that she enrolled.** 2. **that; to**: *It was the source that the essay referred to.* 3. **who; to**: *It was the teacher who the students spoke to.* En registro muy formal: *It was to the teacher whom the students spoke*, aunque la versión con preposición final es más natural.
### Ejercicio 12 — Cleft y registro académico Reescribe con una cleft: *The study does not establish whether the improvement will persist.*
Modelo **What the study does not establish is whether the improvement will persist.** La what-cleft convierte la limitación en el foco del argumento.
### Ejercicio 13 — Corrige el párrafo > What did the assessment reveal was a difference in preparation. It was the final exam which caused anxiety, not the feedback. The students needed it was more time to revise.
Ver solución **What the assessment revealed was a difference in preparation. It was the final exam that caused anxiety, not the feedback. What the students needed was more time to revise.**
### Ejercicio 14 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **Should final exams be replaced by continuous assessment?** Incluye una it-cleft, una what-cleft, una concesión y vocabulario educativo.
Modelo It is the purpose of assessment that should determine its format. If a school wants to measure long-term understanding, continuous assessment may provide more useful evidence than a single final exam. What summative testing captures is a snapshot of performance under pressure, whereas formative feedback can reveal how learners respond to guidance and revise their thinking. Nevertheless, it would be an oversimplification to dismiss examinations entirely. It was the structure of a timed exam that helped some students develop synthesis and time-management skills, although the same structure may disadvantage learners who perform poorly under pressure. A balanced pedagogical approach could combine a final task with regular opportunities to scrutinise evidence, receive feedback and demonstrate progress. What matters most is not whether one method is universally superior, but whether the assessment measures the intended learning outcomes and promotes equity. Schools should therefore use different forms of evidence rather than relying on a single score.
### Ejercicio 15 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre el aprendizaje autodirigido. Usa **What matters is**, **It is... that**, **who** y una concesión.
Pista y modelo **What matters is whether learners can set realistic goals and evaluate their progress. It is the learner who must take responsibility for regular practice, although teachers still provide structure and formative feedback. It is not the amount of material that guarantees progress, but the quality of attention given to it.**
### Ejercicio 16 — Traducción controlada Traduce al inglés. 1. Fue el profesor quien detectó el error. 2. Lo que necesitan los alumnos es retroalimentación significativa. 3. No fue la dificultad de la tarea lo que desanimó a los estudiantes, sino la falta de apoyo.
Ver solución 1. **It was the teacher who noticed the error.** 2. **What the students need is meaningful feedback.** 3. **It wasn’t the difficulty of the task that discouraged the students, but the lack of support.**
### Ejercicio 17 — Edición avanzada Mejora el registro de esta afirmación: *The school’s new system is good because students learn more.*
Modelo **What the available evidence appears to suggest is that the school’s new assessment system may support deeper learning. It is the opportunity to receive formative feedback that seems to have helped students revise their work, although further monitoring is needed before a definitive conclusion can be drawn.**
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > ___ was the teacher ___ identified the problem. ___ the assessment captured was a snapshot of performance, whereas ___ matters most ___ sustained understanding. ___ was not the lack of ability ___ caused the gap, but unequal access to support.
Ver solución **It; who; What; what; is; It; that.** El texto completo es: **It was the teacher who identified the problem. What the assessment captured was a snapshot of performance, whereas what matters most is sustained understanding. It was not the lack of ability that caused the gap, but unequal access to support.**
### Ejercicio 19 — Dos focos, dos respuestas Responde a cada pregunta usando la estructura indicada. Después explica qué elemento queda en primer plano. 1. **Who changed the assessment?** Usa una it-cleft y destaca *the supervisor*. 2. **What did the supervisor change?** Usa una what-cleft y destaca *the feedback schedule*. 3. **When did attendance improve?** Usa una it-cleft y destaca *after the timetable was revised*. 4. **What remains uncertain?** Usa una what-cleft y destaca *whether the improvement will last*.
Ver solución 1. **It was the supervisor who changed the assessment.** El foco es la persona responsable. 2. **What the supervisor changed was the feedback schedule.** El foco es el objeto de la acción. 3. **It was after the timetable was revised that attendance improved.** El foco es el momento o la condición temporal. 4. **What remains uncertain is whether the improvement will last.** El foco es la cuestión que todavía no tiene respuesta. Una it-cleft suele responder a “¿quién, qué, cuándo o dónde?” mediante un elemento que se contrasta. Una what-cleft presenta una pregunta o conclusión como sujeto y coloca la información relevante después de *is/was*. Ambas pueden ser correctas, pero la elección depende de la organización del discurso.
### Ejercicio 20 — Edición de un párrafo académico Reescribe este párrafo para que tenga un registro C1 claro y cohesionado. Debes usar una cleft, una what-clause, una concesión y vocabulario de evaluación. > The exam is bad because it makes students nervous. The school should change it. Some teachers disagree. They say students need exams for their future.
Modelo **It is the pressure created by a single high-stakes exam that concerns many students. What the school should consider is whether continuous assessment could provide a fairer picture of learning. Although some teachers argue that examinations prepare students for future demands, the available evidence does not necessarily show that one timed test measures critical thinking or long-term understanding. A blended assessment model could therefore combine academic rigour with formative feedback.** La versión sustituye *bad* por una descripción precisa, transforma la idea principal en una it-cleft y usa una what-clause para formular la decisión que debe estudiar la escuela. *Although* introduce la postura contraria y *does not necessarily show* evita una generalización excesiva.
## Resumen de la unidad Usa **It is/was + foco + that/who + clause** para destacar una persona, cosa, lugar, momento o causa. Usa **What + clause + is/was + foco** para presentar “lo que” importa, lo que se descubrió o lo que sigue sin resolverse. Recuerda mantener el orden declarativo dentro de la what-clause: *What the study showed was...*, no *What did the study show was...*. Usa *who* para personas y *that* para objetos e ideas, y comprueba que el verbo de la cleft concuerde con el momento de referencia. En escritura académica, las clefts son más útiles cuando responden a una pregunta implícita o establecen un contraste. Combínalas con *although, whereas, nevertheless* y expresiones de cautela para distinguir resultados, interpretaciones y limitaciones. Cuando unas estas estructuras a colocaciones como *provide formative feedback*, *scrutinise evidence*, *promote equity* y *cultivate critical thinking*, podrás argumentar sobre educación con precisión, cohesión y control propio del nivel C1.

faqs.question: ¿Qué son los mixed conditionals?
faqs.answer: Son condicionales que combinan tiempos distintos, por ejemplo una condición irreal pasada con una consecuencia presente: If the city had invested earlier, traffic would be lighter now.

faqs.question: ¿Cómo se forma el mixed conditional pasado-presente?
faqs.answer: Se forma con if más past perfect y would, could o might más infinitivo: If they had planned better, the neighbourhood would be safer now.

faqs.question: ¿Cuándo se usa el mixed conditional presente-pasado?
faqs.answer: Se usa cuando una situación hipotética presente explica un resultado pasado: If the city were more compact, fewer residents would have needed cars.

faqs.question: ¿La Unidad 12 incluye ejercicios resueltos?
faqs.answer: Sí. Incluye gramática, vocabulario urbano, reading, listening, writing y speaking con respuestas y modelos.

content:
# Unidad 12 C1: mixed conditionals, ciudad y arquitectura Las ciudades son el resultado visible de decisiones tomadas durante décadas. Una línea de metro que no se construyó, una zona verde que fue protegida o una política de vivienda que se retrasó pueden explicar la situación actual. Para expresar esas relaciones entre decisiones pasadas y consecuencias presentes, el inglés utiliza los **mixed conditionals**. - *If the city had invested in public transport decades ago, traffic would not be so severe today.* - *If the neighbourhood were more affordable, fewer families would have moved away last year.* En la primera frase, la condición pertenece al pasado y el resultado al presente. En la segunda, una condición presente o permanente se relaciona con una consecuencia pasada. La Unidad 12 combina estas estructuras con el vocabulario de **Urban Life and Architecture**: gentrification, urban sprawl, smart cities, mixed-use buildings, pedestrianisation, architectural heritage, affordable housing y public transport. El objetivo no es aprender una fórmula mecánica. Debes identificar los dos momentos de la relación, elegir el auxiliar correcto y explicar si la consecuencia es un estado, una actividad, una posibilidad o un resultado pasivo. También aprenderás a presentar propuestas urbanas con precisión y a reconocer que casi toda decisión de planificación implica **trade-offs**, es decir, beneficios y costes que deben equilibrarse. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 12 C1](/curso-c1/unit-12)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 11 C1: cleft sentences](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-11-cleft-education)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 13 C1: viajes e intercambio cultural](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-14-subjuntivo-gastronomia)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Dos relojes en una condicional Una oración condicional relaciona una condición con una consecuencia. En las condicionales más habituales, las dos partes pertenecen al mismo marco temporal: - *If the council approves the plan, construction will begin next year.* - *If the council approved the plan, construction would begin next year.* - *If the council had approved the plan, construction would have begun last year.* El mixed conditional aparece cuando la condición y el resultado no comparten tiempo. La combinación más frecuente es: > **If + past perfect, would/could/might + base verb** Se usa para una causa o decisión pasada que tiene una consecuencia actual: - *If the city had built the tram network, commuters would spend less time in traffic now.* - *If the council had protected the old quarter, the city would have more architectural heritage today.* - *If she had studied urban planning, she would be a city planner now.* La otra combinación importante es: > **If + past simple/were, would/could/might have + past participle** Se usa cuando una condición presente, una característica estable o una situación hipotética explica un resultado pasado: - *If the city were more compact, fewer residents would have needed cars last year.* - *If the district were less expensive, more families could have stayed.* - *If the planning process were more transparent, the proposal might have attracted wider support.* ### 2. Pasado hacia presente Este patrón expresa arrepentimiento, análisis causal o una comparación con una realidad actual. La condición utiliza **past perfect** porque se refiere a algo que no ocurrió o que ocurrió de otra manera: - *If the authorities had invested earlier, the neighbourhood would be safer now.* - *If the city had introduced congestion charges, air quality might be better today.* - *If the developers had included affordable housing, the area could be more socially diverse now.* El resultado puede ser un estado con **would be**, una posesión con **would have**, una actividad con **would be + -ing** o una pasiva con **would be + participle**: - *The streets would be quieter now.* - *The district would have better cycle routes.* - *Residents would be using public transport more often.* - *More historic buildings would be protected today.* La palabra *now* o *today* ayuda a identificar el tiempo, pero no siempre es necesaria. En *If I had accepted the job, I would live near the station*, el resultado actual se entiende por *would live*. Con **could** enfatizamos una capacidad u oportunidad que existiría ahora: - *If the city had planned the junction properly, pedestrians could cross safely now.* Con **might** presentamos una consecuencia posible, no segura: - *If the council had consulted residents, the plan might be more widely accepted today.* ### 3. Presente hacia pasado El patrón inverso comienza con una condición presente o hipotética. Puede describir una característica actual de una ciudad, una política que todavía no existe o una situación estructural: - *If the city were less dependent on cars, fewer people would have suffered from pollution during the heatwave.* - *If housing were more affordable, the young professionals would not have left the centre.* - *If the planning system were more flexible, the developer could have adapted the proposal sooner.* La condición no tiene por qué ser literalmente “de ahora” en un sentido puntual. *If the city were more compact* describe una realidad urbana general. El resultado pasado lleva **would/could/might have + past participle**: - *would have reduced* - *could have prevented* - *might have improved* - *would have been protected* Este patrón es útil para evaluar políticas desde la situación actual. Podemos observar un resultado pasado y preguntarnos qué habría ocurrido si el sistema actual o ideal hubiera estado presente: - *If the approval process were more transparent, the residents might have trusted the decision.* ### 4. Mixed frente a second y third conditional El error más frecuente es elegir la forma por el aspecto visual de la frase, sin fijarse en el tiempo del resultado. Compara: - **Second:** *If the city were more compact, traffic would be lighter.* Condición y resultado hipotéticos presentes o futuros. - **Third:** *If the city had invested earlier, traffic would have been lighter last year.* Condición y resultado pasados. - **Mixed:** *If the city had invested earlier, traffic would be lighter now.* Condición pasada y resultado presente. Otro grupo: - **Second:** *If housing were affordable, families would stay in the centre.* Hipótesis general presente. - **Third:** *If housing had been affordable, families would have stayed last year.* Condición y resultado pasados. - **Mixed presente-pasado:** *If housing were affordable, fewer families would have moved away last year.* Condición estructural presente, resultado pasado. Busca señales temporales como *now, today, at present, still* frente a *last year, during the project, at the time, in 2018*. También observa el verbo: *would be* suele apuntar al presente; *would have been* mira hacia el pasado. ### 5. Estados, actividades y consecuencias La forma **would be** puede representar diferentes tipos de resultado: - Estado: *The square would be safer now.* - Identidad o situación: *She would be an architect now.* - Actividad en progreso: *Residents would be cycling to work.* - Pasiva: *The station would be connected to the airport.* Para actividades en progreso, usamos **would be + -ing**: - *If the city had preserved the cycle lanes, more commuters would be cycling now.* - *If the building had been designed for mixed use, residents would be living closer to services.* Para resultados pasados en progreso, podemos usar **would have been + -ing**, aunque la forma es más pesada: - *If the route were safer, commuters would have been cycling along it during the previous summer.* A menudo una reformulación es más clara. Lo importante es que el auxiliar de la consecuencia refleje su tiempo. ### 6. Pasivas en mixed conditionals La pasiva centra la atención en el edificio, la calle, el plan o la comunidad afectada: - *If the old quarter had been protected, fewer historic buildings would be threatened now.* - *If the housing scheme were more inclusive, more low-income families could have been accommodated.* - *If the bridge had been reinforced, it would be open to pedestrians today.* La estructura es: - Resultado presente pasivo: **would/could/might + be + V3**. - Resultado pasado pasivo: **would/could/might + have been + V3**. No confundas *would be protected now* con *would have been protected last year*. La primera sitúa la protección actual; la segunda la sitúa en el pasado. ### 7. Inversión condicional formal En informes y propuestas formales, se puede omitir *if* y utilizar inversión: - *Had the city invested in public transport, congestion would be lower now.* - *Were the district more affordable, fewer families would have moved away.* - *Had the council consulted residents, the plan might be more acceptable today.* **Had + subject + past participle** equivale a *if + subject + had + past participle*. **Were + subject** equivale a *if + subject + were*. La inversión aporta concisión y registro formal, pero no altera el tiempo de la consecuencia. También aparece **if it weren’t for** para una condición presente: - *If it weren’t for the new tram line, the centre would be even more congested.* Y **if it hadn’t been for** para una condición pasada: - *If it hadn’t been for the community campaign, the theatre would have been demolished.* ### 8. Causalidad y responsabilidad Los mixed conditionals son útiles para el análisis, pero no prueban una relación causal por sí solos. *If the council had acted earlier, the neighbourhood would be safer now* propone una explicación contrafactual. No demuestra que esa única decisión hubiera producido el resultado. Para escribir con prudencia, añade expresiones como: - *would probably be* - *might have been* - *could have contributed to* - *there is no guarantee that* - *although other factors would also have mattered* - *If the council had acted earlier, the neighbourhood might be safer now, although housing demand would still have created pressure.* El nivel C1 exige reconocer variables múltiples. En urbanismo, el transporte, el precio del suelo, el empleo, la regulación y las decisiones privadas interactúan. La gramática debe reflejar esa complejidad. ### 9. Vocabulario de vida urbana - **urbanisation:** crecimiento y expansión de las ciudades. - **urban sprawl:** expansión urbana dispersa y poco compacta. - **gentrification:** transformación de un barrio por la llegada de residentes con mayor poder adquisitivo, normalmente con aumento de precios y desplazamiento de habitantes. - **suburbanisation:** traslado de población y actividades hacia zonas periféricas. - **pedestrianisation:** conversión de una zona para priorizar el tránsito peatonal. - **congestion:** congestión de tráfico. - **public transport:** transporte público. - **affordable housing:** vivienda asequible. - **social fabric:** relaciones y cohesión de una comunidad. - **liveability:** calidad de vida que ofrece un lugar. - **density:** densidad de población o construcción. - **green space:** espacio verde. - **smart city:** ciudad que usa datos y tecnología para gestionar servicios y recursos. - **mixed-use development:** desarrollo con usos residenciales, comerciales y de ocio combinados. - **infrastructure:** infraestructura urbana. - **zoning:** división del suelo según usos permitidos. - **heritage:** patrimonio arquitectónico o cultural. - **public realm:** espacios accesibles y compartidos de la ciudad. - **walkability:** facilidad y seguridad para desplazarse a pie. - **cycle network:** red de carriles o rutas ciclistas. Colocaciones importantes son **reduce congestion**, **expand public transport**, **preserve architectural heritage**, **provide affordable housing**, **manage urban density**, **combat urban sprawl**, **improve walkability**, **invest in infrastructure**, **protect green space**, **promote mixed-use development**, **support local communities** y **enhance liveability**. ### 10. Vocabulario de arquitectura - **load-bearing:** que soporta el peso estructural. - **vernacular architecture:** arquitectura propia de una región y sus materiales o tradiciones. - **brutalism:** movimiento caracterizado por hormigón visto y formas geométricas contundentes. - **facade:** fachada. - **floor plan:** plano de distribución. - **retrofitting:** adaptación de un edificio existente para mejorar su rendimiento o seguridad. - **adaptive reuse:** reutilización de un edificio para una nueva función. - **restoration:** restauración. - **demolition:** demolición. - **landmark:** edificio o lugar emblemático. - **public housing:** vivienda pública. - **high-rise:** edificio alto. - **low-rise:** edificio de poca altura. - **building code:** normativa de construcción. - **structural integrity:** integridad estructural. Las colocaciones incluyen **design a building**, **renovate a landmark**, **restore a facade**, **reuse an industrial site**, **meet building codes**, **preserve structural integrity**, **increase residential density**, **incorporate green roofs** y **adapt an existing structure**. ### 11. Smart cities y trade-offs Una smart city puede usar sensores para controlar el tráfico, reducir consumo energético o mejorar la gestión de residuos. Sin embargo, la tecnología no resuelve automáticamente los problemas sociales. Una ciudad puede ser eficiente y seguir siendo inaccesible para familias con ingresos bajos. - *If the city had invested in open data, residents would understand planning decisions better now.* - *If the system were designed around privacy, it might have gained more public trust.* Toda política urbana implica un intercambio: - Más densidad puede reducir desplazamientos, pero aumentar el precio del suelo. - Más carriles de bici pueden mejorar la movilidad, pero restar espacio a coches o aparcamiento. - La restauración puede preservar patrimonio, pero elevar los alquileres. - La vigilancia inteligente puede mejorar la seguridad, pero poner en riesgo la privacidad. Un texto C1 debe reconocer estos trade-offs y evitar soluciones absolutas. Las estructuras *although, whereas, provided that* y *unless* pueden complementar los mixed conditionals para presentar una propuesta equilibrada. ### 12. Cómo escribir una propuesta formal Una propuesta para un ayuntamiento suele incluir propósito, evidencia, beneficios, riesgos y recomendación. Las clefts y los condicionales ayudan a organizarla: - *The aim of this proposal is to improve walkability in the historic centre.* - *It is pedestrian safety that should determine the design of the scheme.* - *If the council had introduced a phased plan earlier, disruption would be lower now.* - *A pilot could be launched provided that local businesses are consulted.* Usa verbos formales como *recommend, propose, outline, address, assess, implement, monitor* y *evaluate*. Evita expresiones vagas como *make the city nicer*. Sustitúyelas por *enhance liveability, reduce congestion, improve access* o *protect the public realm*. ### 13. Errores frecuentes - *If the city would have invested, traffic would be lower.* → **If the city had invested, traffic would be lower.** - *If the district were cheaper, families would have stayed now.* → **... families would stay now** o **would have stayed last year**, según el tiempo. - *If the city were compact, fewer residents would have needed cars last year.* → Correcto: condición presente, resultado pasado. - *Were the city had better transport...* → **If the city had better transport...** o **Were the city better served by public transport...**. - *If the council had consulted residents, the plan would have be accepted.* → **would have been accepted**. - *Had the council acted, congestion will be lower.* → **Had the council acted, congestion would be lower.** - *If it wasn’t for the tram, traffic would be worse.* → En registro formal: **If it weren’t for the tram...**. - *If the building had been mixed-use, residents would have living closer.* → **would have been living** o **would live**, según el sentido. ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Identifica el tipo Indica si cada frase es **second, third** o **mixed conditional**. 1. *If the city had invested earlier, traffic would be lighter now.* 2. *If the city invested more, traffic would be lighter.* 3. *If the city had invested earlier, traffic would have been lighter last year.* 4. *If housing were affordable, fewer families would have moved away.*
Ver solución 1. **Mixed, pasado → presente**. 2. **Second conditional**, condición y resultado hipotéticos presentes. 3. **Third conditional**, condición y resultado pasados. 4. **Mixed, presente → pasado**: la asequibilidad es una condición estructural; la mudanza ocurrió en el pasado.
### Ejercicio 2 — Pasado hacia presente Completa con **would, could** o **might** y la forma correcta del verbo. 1. If the council had protected the old quarter, the city ___ (have) more heritage today. 2. If the tram line had been extended, pedestrians ___ (cross) the centre more safely now. 3. If the developers had included affordable housing, the area ___ (be) more diverse today. 4. If the authority had consulted residents, the plan ___ (be) more widely accepted now.
Ver solución 1. **would have**. 2. **could cross**. 3. **might be**. 4. **might be** o **would be**, según si presentas una posibilidad o una consecuencia más lógica.
### Ejercicio 3 — Presente hacia pasado Completa. 1. If the city were less dependent on cars, fewer people ___ ___ (suffer) from pollution during the heatwave. 2. If housing were more affordable, more families ___ ___ (stay) in the centre. 3. If the planning process were transparent, the proposal ___ ___ (attract) wider support.
Ver solución 1. **would have suffered** o, en negativo según el sentido, **would not have suffered**. 2. **could have stayed**. 3. **might have attracted**.
### Ejercicio 4 — Resultado presente o pasado Elige la opción correcta. 1. If the city had built the metro, commuters (*would spend / would have spent*) less time travelling now. 2. If the district were more walkable, fewer residents (*would have needed / would need*) cars during last year’s disruption. 3. If the council had preserved the theatre, it (*would be / would have been*) open today. 4. If the building were structurally sound, it (*could have been / could be*) restored after the storm.
Ver solución 1. **would spend**. 2. **would have needed**. 3. **would be**. 4. **could have been** si hablamos de una decisión pasada después de la tormenta.
### Ejercicio 5 — Pasiva Transforma. 1. If the council had protected the facade, the developers would not threaten it now. 2. If the housing scheme were inclusive, the authority could have accommodated more families. 3. If the bridge had been reinforced, pedestrians would use it today.
Ver solución 1. **If the council had protected the facade, it would not be threatened by the developers now.** 2. **If the housing scheme were inclusive, more families could have been accommodated.** 3. **If the bridge had been reinforced, it would be used by pedestrians today.**
### Ejercicio 6 — Inversión formal Reescribe sin *if*. 1. If the city had invested in public transport, congestion would be lower now. 2. If the district were more affordable, fewer families would have moved away. 3. If the council had consulted residents, the proposal might be more acceptable today.
Ver solución 1. **Had the city invested in public transport, congestion would be lower now.** 2. **Were the district more affordable, fewer families would have moved away.** 3. **Had the council consulted residents, the proposal might be more acceptable today.**
### Ejercicio 7 — Vocabulario urbano Completa con **gentrification, urban sprawl, smart city, mixed-use** o **pedestrianisation**. 1. The rapid spread of low-density development is known as ___ . 2. The neighbourhood has experienced ___, with rising rents and the displacement of long-term residents. 3. A ___ uses data and technology to manage urban services. 4. The development is ___, combining homes, offices and shops. 5. The ___ of the centre improved walkability but required changes to delivery routes.
Ver solución 1. **urban sprawl**; 2. **gentrification**; 3. **smart city**; 4. **mixed-use**; 5. **pedestrianisation**.
### Ejercicio 8 — Vocabulario arquitectónico Elige el término adecuado: **retrofitting, adaptive reuse, facade, structural integrity** o **vernacular**. 1. The old factory was converted into apartments through ___ . 2. The engineers checked the building’s ___ after the earthquake. 3. The project involves ___ an office block to improve energy efficiency. 4. The front exterior of a building is its ___ . 5. The village is known for its ___ architecture and local materials.
Ver solución 1. **adaptive reuse**; 2. **structural integrity**; 3. **retrofitting**; 4. **facade**; 5. **vernacular**.
### Ejercicio 9 — Reading Lee el texto y responde. > The Riverside district has undergone rapid gentrification since the old warehouses were converted into mixed-use developments. The area is now more attractive to visitors, but long-term residents face rising rents and reduced access to affordable housing. If the council had introduced protections earlier, fewer families would be under pressure now. The planning committee argues that the redevelopment has improved the public realm, whereas community groups contend that the benefits have been distributed unevenly. A proposal to pedestrianise the main street might improve air quality, although local traders are concerned about deliveries. What remains unresolved is whether the district can become more liveable without losing its social fabric. 1. What caused rapid change in Riverside? 2. What problem do long-term residents face? 3. What would be different if protections had been introduced earlier? 4. What do the planning committee and community groups disagree about? 5. What remains unresolved?
Ver solución 1. **The conversion of old warehouses into mixed-use developments.** 2. **Rising rents and reduced access to affordable housing.** 3. **Fewer families would be under pressure now.** 4. **They disagree about whether the benefits of redevelopment have been distributed fairly.** 5. **Whether the district can improve liveability without losing its social fabric.**
### Ejercicio 10 — Listening guiado Guion: “If the city were less dependent on cars, fewer residents would have suffered during last summer’s pollution emergency. Had the council expanded the cycle network earlier, people might be cycling to work more often now. The scheme could improve walkability, but it would create trade-offs for parking and deliveries.” Identifica los dos mixed conditionals y explica el tiempo de cada parte.
Ver solución 1. **If the city were less dependent on cars** es una condición presente; **fewer residents would have suffered** es un resultado pasado. 2. **Had the council expanded the cycle network earlier** es una condición pasada; **people might be cycling... now** es un resultado presente en progreso.
### Ejercicio 11 — Selección de colocaciones Completa con **reduce, preserve, provide, improve** o **manage**. 1. ___ congestion 2. ___ architectural heritage 3. ___ affordable housing 4. ___ walkability 5. ___ urban density
Ver solución 1. **reduce congestion**; 2. **preserve architectural heritage**; 3. **provide affordable housing**; 4. **improve walkability**; 5. **manage urban density**.
### Ejercicio 12 — Corrige los errores 1. *If the city would have planned better, traffic would be lighter now.* 2. *Were the district had more housing, fewer people would have left.* 3. *If the bridge had been reinforced, it would have be open today.* 4. *Had the council consulted residents, the plan will be more acceptable.*
Ver solución 1. **If the city had planned better, traffic would be lighter now.** 2. **If the district had more housing, fewer people would have left** o **Were the district better supplied with housing, fewer people would have left.** 3. **If the bridge had been reinforced, it would be open today.** 4. **Had the council consulted residents, the plan would be more acceptable.**
### Ejercicio 13 — Análisis de trade-offs Completa con una consecuencia lógica. 1. If the city increased density, it might ___, but it could also ___ . 2. If the council pedestrianised the centre, air quality would ___, whereas deliveries might ___ . 3. If the authority introduced smart sensors, services could ___, although privacy might ___ .
Modelo 1. **reduce urban sprawl; increase pressure on housing**. 2. **improve; become more complicated**. 3. **be managed more efficiently; be put at risk**. Hay varias respuestas válidas si mantienen una relación lógica y un registro apropiado.
### Ejercicio 14 — Reformulación académica Convierte esta afirmación absoluta en una frase prudente con mixed conditional: *The council’s earlier decision caused all the current problems.*
Modelo **If the council had made a different decision earlier, some of the current problems might have been less severe, although other factors would also have contributed.** La frase presenta una hipótesis, limita la consecuencia con *some* y reconoce que la ciudad depende de más de una causa.
### Ejercicio 15 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **Should a historic city centre be pedestrianised?** Incluye un mixed conditional, una inversión formal, dos colocaciones urbanas y un trade-off.
Modelo A historic city centre should be pedestrianised gradually rather than transformed overnight. If the council had redesigned delivery routes earlier, traders would be less concerned about disruption now. Had the authority consulted local businesses from the beginning, the proposal might have attracted wider support. Pedestrianisation could reduce congestion, improve walkability and preserve the public realm, but it would also create trade-offs for residents who depend on cars and shops that require frequent deliveries. A pilot scheme would allow the council to monitor air quality, footfall and access before making the arrangement permanent. It would be essential to provide reliable public transport and accessible parking outside the restricted area. The aim should not be to exclude vehicles at any cost, but to create a safer and more liveable centre while protecting local economic activity. If the scheme were introduced with clear exemptions and regular evaluation, it could improve the area without imposing an unfair burden on particular groups.
### Ejercicio 16 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre gentrification. Usa **If the council had...**, **the neighbourhood would... now**, **whereas** y **might have**.
Pista y modelo **If the council had introduced affordable-housing measures earlier, the neighbourhood would be more socially diverse now. New investment has improved some services, whereas long-term residents might have remained under less pressure if rents had been regulated. Gentrification can bring benefits, but it may also weaken the social fabric unless local people are protected.**
### Ejercicio 17 — Traducción controlada Traduce al inglés. 1. Si la ciudad hubiera invertido antes, el tráfico sería menos intenso ahora. 2. Si la vivienda fuera más asequible, menos familias se habrían marchado el año pasado. 3. Si no fuera por el nuevo tranvía, el centro estaría mucho más congestionado.
Ver solución 1. **If the city had invested earlier, traffic would be less intense now.** 2. **If housing were more affordable, fewer families would have moved away last year.** 3. **If it weren’t for the new tram, the centre would be much more congested.**
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > The district is under pressure. If the council ___ (protect) affordable housing earlier, fewer residents ___ (leave) now. ___ the planning process were more transparent, community groups ___ (trust) the proposal last year. The redevelopment may improve liveability, but it will create ___ for parking, deliveries and housing density.
Ver solución **had protected; would be leaving; Were; might have trusted; trade-offs.** El primer condicional conecta una acción pasada con un resultado presente en progreso. El segundo conecta una condición presente con un resultado pasado. *Trade-offs* resume los beneficios y costes que deben equilibrarse.
## Resumen de la unidad Para formar el mixed conditional pasado → presente, usa **if + past perfect** y **would/could/might + infinitivo**: *If the city had planned better, traffic would be lighter now*. Para el patrón presente → pasado, usa **if + past simple/were** y **would/could/might have + participio**: *If housing were affordable, fewer families would have moved away*. Distingue siempre el tiempo de la condición y el del resultado. Usa **would be** para un estado presente, **would be + -ing** para una actividad actual y **would have been + participio** para un resultado pasado en pasiva. En escritura formal puedes invertir la condición: *Had the council acted earlier...* y *Were the district more affordable...*. El vocabulario de urbanismo exige precisión: *gentrification* no es simplemente “mejora del barrio”, *urban sprawl* no es cualquier expansión y *mixed-use* describe una combinación concreta de funciones. Cuando unas estas palabras a colocaciones como *provide affordable housing*, *improve walkability* y *preserve architectural heritage*, podrás analizar las ciudades con la complejidad temporal, léxica y argumentativa propia del nivel C1.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es una participle clause?
faqs.answer: Es una cláusula reducida con participio presente, pasado o perfecto que expresa una relación de tiempo, causa, condición o concesión de forma compacta.

faqs.question: ¿Cuándo se usa Having + participio?
faqs.answer: Se usa para indicar que una acción terminó antes de la acción principal: Having travelled extensively, he understood the cultural nuances.

faqs.question: ¿Qué diferencia hay entre travelling y travelled?
faqs.answer: Travelling suele indicar que el sujeto realiza la acción; travelled o un participio pasado suele expresar una relación pasiva, como the route travelled by traders.
