faqs.question: ¿Para qué sirve do enfático?
faqs.answer: Do, does o did delante del verbo base añade énfasis, contradice una negación previa o refuerza una afirmación: She did train hard.

faqs.question: ¿Qué ocurre después de only al principio?
faqs.answer: Los adverbiales con only al principio suelen provocar inversión entre auxiliar y sujeto: Only through consistent practice did she improve.

faqs.question: ¿Qué diferencia hay entre fronting y cleft?
faqs.answer: Fronting mueve un elemento al principio; una cleft lo presenta dentro de It is/was + foco + that/who, con una estructura escindida.

faqs.question: ¿La Unidad 15 incluye ejercicios resueltos?
faqs.answer: Sí. Incluye práctica de énfasis, fronting, vocabulario deportivo, reading, listening, writing y speaking con respuestas y modelos.

content:
# Unidad 15 C1: énfasis, deporte y rendimiento El inglés tiene varias formas de señalar que una idea es especialmente importante. En una conversación, podemos usar la entonación; en la escritura, podemos utilizar estructuras como **do/did enfáticos**, **fronting** y clefts. Estas formas no cambian necesariamente el hecho, pero sí indican cómo debe interpretarlo el lector o el interlocutor. - *She trained hard for the marathon.* - *She did train hard for the marathon, whatever anyone might say.* - *Only through years of sacrifice did she achieve her ambition.* - *It was her mental resilience that set her apart.* La Unidad 15 aplica estas estructuras al mundo de **Sport, Competition and Performance**. El tema permite debatir sobre rendimiento de élite, preparación psicológica, presión, talento, recursos y meritocracia. El vocabulario incluye *mental resilience, flow, momentum, marginal gains, tactical awareness, endurance, commercialised sport* y *level playing field*. El énfasis debe tener una función. Si utilizamos `did` o una inversión en cada frase, el texto puede resultar teatral. Si escogemos la estructura correcta para corregir una interpretación, destacar un proceso o contrastar dos factores, la prosa gana precisión y fuerza retórica. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 15 C1](/curso-c1/unit-15)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 14 C1: subjuntivo y gastronomía](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-14-subjuntivo-gastronomia)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 16 C1: música y artes escénicas](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-16-pasiva-musica)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Qué es el énfasis gramatical El énfasis aparece cuando el hablante quiere llamar la atención sobre una afirmación, corregir una duda o establecer una oposición. En inglés, la oración neutra suele ser suficiente: - *The athlete trained consistently.* Si alguien ha sugerido que la atleta no se esforzó, podemos reforzar la afirmación: - *The athlete did train consistently.* Si queremos destacar el modo o la condición: - *Only through consistent training did the athlete improve.* Si queremos señalar el factor decisivo: - *It was consistent training that improved her performance.* Cada estructura organiza la información de forma distinta. `Did train` refuerza el verbo; `only through... did` pone una condición en primer plano; la cleft destaca un elemento nominal. El contexto determina cuál es la opción más natural. ### 2. Do y does enfáticos en presente En presente simple, usamos **do** con *I, you, we, they* y **does** con *he, she, it*, seguidos del verbo en forma base: - *I do understand the coach’s concern.* - *They do deserve recognition.* - *She does perform well under pressure.* - *The strategy does work in certain conditions.* El auxiliar puede expresar una contradicción o una confirmación enfática: - A: *The team lacks discipline.* - B: *They do work extremely hard; their problem is tactical coordination.* - *I do believe that access to coaching matters.* Después de `do/does`, el verbo principal no lleva `-s`: - Correcto: *She does train every morning.* - Incorrecto: *She does trains every morning.* La `-s` ya está marcada en **does**. En preguntas y negativas, `do/does` también funciona como auxiliar, pero no siempre tiene valor enfático: - *Does she train every morning?* Pregunta neutral. - *She does train every morning.* Afirmación enfática. La entonación también contribuye al significado. En escritura, el contexto o expresiones como *indeed, certainly, actually* pueden reforzar la lectura enfática. ### 3. Did enfático en pasado Para una afirmación enfática en pasado simple, usamos **did + verbo base**: - *She did train hard for the marathon.* - *The team did deserve to win.* - *He did follow the recovery plan.* - *They did improve after the coaching change.* El verbo vuelve a la forma base porque el pasado está marcado en `did`: - Correcto: *She did train.* - Incorrecto: *She did trained.* `Did` suele contradecir una negación o una duda: - *You didn’t prepare for the final.* - *I did prepare; the problem was that the conditions changed.* También puede confirmar algo con fuerza: - *The athlete did break the national record, despite the injury.* No confundas el `did` enfático con el `did` de una pregunta o negativa: - *Did she compete?* pregunta. - *She didn’t compete.* negativa. - *She did compete.* afirmación enfática. En una reseña o argumento, esta estructura puede ser útil para responder a una crítica, pero no debe sustituir a una evidencia. ### 4. Bare infinitive después de do Tanto en presente como en pasado, el verbo posterior aparece en forma base: - *She does perform consistently.* - *She did perform consistently.* - *They do understand the risks.* - *They did understand the risks.* Con verbos auxiliares modales no necesitamos añadir `do` para enfatizar del mismo modo: - *She must have trained hard.* - *She certainly must have trained hard.* No digas *She did must train*. Si quieres enfatizar una obligación, puedes usar *She really did have to train* o una cleft. Con `be`, el inglés utiliza el verbo `be` directamente: - *She is determined.* - *She really is determined.* - *She was ready.* - *She really was ready.* `Do` enfático se aplica principalmente al presente y pasado simple de verbos léxicos. ### 5. Fronting de adverbiales **Fronting** coloca al principio un adverbial que normalmente aparecería después. Si el elemento inicial contiene **only**, **never**, **rarely**, **seldom**, **under no circumstances** u otra expresión negativa o restrictiva, suele provocar inversión: - Orden neutro: *She achieved her ambition only through years of sacrifice.* - Fronting: *Only through years of sacrifice did she achieve her ambition.* - Orden neutro: *The team had rarely performed so well.* - Fronting: *Rarely had the team performed so well.* - Orden neutro: *Athletes should under no circumstances ignore recovery.* - Fronting: *Under no circumstances should athletes ignore recovery.* La inversión coloca el auxiliar antes del sujeto. Si no hay auxiliar, añadimos `do/does/did`: - *Only then did she realise the importance of sleep.* - *Rarely do coaches consider the social cost of elite competition.* No confundas fronting con una pregunta. *Only then did she realise...* es una oración declarativa, no una interrogación. ### 6. Only, not until y not only Con **only + adverbial** al principio, la inversión se produce en la cláusula principal: - *Only after the injury did the athlete change her training routine.* - *Only by managing sleep can competitors sustain performance.* - *Only when the team improved communication did results change.* La cláusula temporal conserva el orden normal: *after the injury*, *when the team improved*. No inviertas las dos cláusulas. **Not until** funciona de manera similar: - *Not until the final lap did the runner overtake her rival.* - *Not until the pressure increased did the weakness become visible.* **Not only** forma una estructura correlativa: - *Not only did the training improve endurance, but it also reduced injury risk.* - *Not only is the sport commercialised, but it is also increasingly unequal.* La segunda parte debe ser paralela. No digas *Not only did the training improve endurance, but also reduced injury risk* si quieres un paralelismo completo; repite el sujeto o el auxiliar cuando sea necesario. ### 7. Fronting sin inversión No todo elemento frontal provoca inversión. Un complemento preposicional neutro puede aparecer al principio sin cambiar el orden: - *In the final, the team played cautiously.* - *After the injury, the runner changed her technique.* - *Under pressure, many athletes make different decisions.* La inversión depende de la naturaleza del adverbial y del énfasis, no simplemente de que algo aparezca al principio. Compara: - *In the final, the team played cautiously.* Orden normal después del complemento. - *Only in the final did the team play cautiously.* Inversión por `only`. Usar inversión donde no corresponde puede hacer que una frase suene artificial. ### 8. Clefts como estructura de foco Una cleft divide una oración para destacar un elemento: - *It was her mental resilience that set her apart.* - *It was the lack of recovery time that caused the injury.* - *It was the coach who changed the strategy.* - *It was during the final lap that the race changed.* El patrón es **It is/was + focus + that/who + clause**. Usa `who` habitualmente para personas y `that` para objetos, ideas, tiempos y causas. Las pseudo-clefts con `what` tienen esta forma: - *What set her apart was her mental resilience.* - *What the team lacked was tactical awareness.* - *What matters is the ability to recover under pressure.* La cleft suele responder a “¿qué elemento fue decisivo?”; la what-cleft presenta una conclusión o una respuesta. No uses orden interrogativo dentro de la what-clause: - Correcto: *What the team lacked was tactical awareness.* - Incorrecto: *What did the team lack was tactical awareness.* ### 9. Vocabulario de rendimiento - **mental resilience:** capacidad psicológica para gestionar presión y adversidad. - **physical endurance:** capacidad de sostener un esfuerzo físico. - **tactical awareness:** comprensión de decisiones y posiciones estratégicas. - **flow:** estado de absorción total y rendimiento aparentemente effortless. - **momentum:** impulso psicológico o ventaja progresiva durante una competición. - **peak performance:** máximo nivel de rendimiento. - **marginal gains:** pequeñas mejoras acumulativas en nutrición, sueño, técnica o equipamiento. - **recovery:** recuperación física y mental. - **performance plateau:** periodo en el que el rendimiento deja de mejorar. - **competitive pressure:** presión propia de la competición. - **sports psychology:** psicología del deporte. - **injury prevention:** prevención de lesiones. - **training load:** carga de entrenamiento. - **overtraining:** exceso de entrenamiento que perjudica el rendimiento. - **discipline:** capacidad de mantener hábitos y normas. - **self-belief:** confianza en la propia capacidad. - **composure:** calma y control bajo presión. - **grit:** perseverancia ante dificultades prolongadas. - **level playing field:** situación con condiciones de competencia relativamente justas. - **meritocracy:** sistema que supuestamente recompensa talento y esfuerzo. Colocaciones útiles son **maintain focus**, **manage pressure**, **sustain performance**, **build endurance**, **develop resilience**, **gain momentum**, **reach peak performance**, **prevent injury**, **monitor training load**, **reframe anxiety**, **compete at elite level** y **perform under constraint**. ### 10. Deporte, sociedad y meritocracia El deporte de élite suele presentarse como una prueba pura de talento y esfuerzo. Sin embargo, el acceso a entrenamiento, instalaciones, nutrición, descanso, atención médica y apoyo psicológico varía enormemente. Por eso el concepto de **level playing field** debe analizarse con cuidado. - *The narrative of meritocracy may conceal structural inequality.* - *It is access to resources that often determines who can develop talent.* - *Only when young athletes receive comparable support can competition become fairer.* La palabra **commercialised** describe un deporte organizado cada vez más alrededor del beneficio económico. **Professionalised** solo indica que se ha convertido en una actividad profesional; no implica necesariamente una crítica. **Politicised** señala la influencia de intereses políticos. ### 11. Énfasis y contradicción En un debate, `do/did` puede corregir una interpretación, pero el argumento debe seguir siendo específico: - Débil: *The athlete did work hard.* - Mejor: *The athlete did work hard, but access to specialist recovery support also contributed to her progress.* La primera frase enfatiza el esfuerzo; la segunda evita reducir todo el rendimiento a una sola causa. El fronting puede destacar la limitación: - *Only through access to coaching and recovery facilities can talent become consistent performance.* La cleft puede separar dos factores: - *It was not raw talent that determined the outcome, but the quality of preparation available to each competitor.* Este uso es especialmente útil en writing argumentativo, porque permite mostrar concesiones y contrastes con control. ### 12. Errores frecuentes - *She did trained hard.* → **She did train hard.** - *He does performs well.* → **He does perform well.** - *Only through training she improved.* → **Only through training did she improve.** - *Only after the injury did she changed her routine.* → **Only after the injury did she change her routine.** - *Not only did the team improve, but also reduced injuries.* → **Not only did the team improve, but it also reduced injuries.** - *Rarely the coach has seen such resilience.* → **Rarely has the coach seen such resilience.** - *In the final did the team play cautiously.* → **In the final, the team played cautiously.** - *What did the athlete need was rest.* → **What the athlete needed was rest.** - *It was the coach which changed the strategy.* → **It was the coach who changed the strategy.** ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Do y did enfáticos Completa con **do, does** o **did**. 1. She ___ train incredibly hard for the marathon. 2. The team ___ deserve recognition for its recovery. 3. I ___ understand the coach’s concern. 4. The strategy ___ work under certain conditions.
Ver solución 1. **did**; 2. **does**; 3. **do**; 4. **does**. El verbo principal permanece en forma base después del auxiliar.
### Ejercicio 2 — Corrige el verbo 1. *She did trained all winter.* 2. *The athlete does performs consistently.* 3. *They did improved after the coaching change.*
Ver solución 1. **She did train all winter.** 2. **The athlete does perform consistently.** 3. **They did improve after the coaching change.**
### Ejercicio 3 — Only + inversión Reescribe. 1. She achieved her ambition only through years of sacrifice. 2. The team improved only after the coach changed the strategy. 3. Athletes can sustain performance only by managing recovery.
Ver solución 1. **Only through years of sacrifice did she achieve her ambition.** 2. **Only after the coach changed the strategy did the team improve.** 3. **Only by managing recovery can athletes sustain performance.**
### Ejercicio 4 — Not until y not only Completa. 1. Not until the final lap ___ the runner overtake her rival. 2. Not only ___ the training improve endurance, but it also reduced injury risk. 3. Not only is the sport commercialised, but it ___ also increasingly unequal.
Ver solución 1. **did**; 2. **did**; 3. **is**. La inversión aparece después del elemento restrictivo y el paralelismo se mantiene en la segunda parte.
### Ejercicio 5 — Fronting sin inversión Elige la opción correcta. 1. *In the final, the team played / did the team play cautiously.* 2. *Only in the final played the team / did the team play cautiously.* 3. *After the injury, the runner changed / did the runner change her technique.*
Ver solución 1. **the team played**; 2. **did the team play**; 3. **the runner changed**. *In* y *after* son complementos frontales neutros; *only* provoca inversión.
### Ejercicio 6 — Clefts Reescribe destacando el elemento indicado. 1. Her mental resilience set her apart. (mental resilience) 2. The coach changed the strategy. (the coach) 3. The lack of recovery time caused the injury. (lack of recovery time) 4. The race changed during the final lap. (during the final lap)
Ver solución 1. **It was her mental resilience that set her apart.** 2. **It was the coach who changed the strategy.** 3. **It was the lack of recovery time that caused the injury.** 4. **It was during the final lap that the race changed.**
### Ejercicio 7 — What-clefts Completa. 1. ___ set her apart ___ her mental resilience. 2. ___ the team lacked ___ tactical awareness. 3. ___ matters ___ the ability to recover under pressure.
Ver solución 1. **What; was**; 2. **What; was**; 3. **What; is**.
### Ejercicio 8 — Vocabulario Completa con **flow, momentum, mental resilience, marginal gains** o **level playing field**. 1. The athlete entered a state of total absorption known as ___ . 2. Small improvements in sleep and nutrition can produce ___ . 3. The team gained ___ after scoring twice in quick succession. 4. A fair competition requires a reasonably ___ . 5. The ability to recover from pressure demonstrates ___ .
Ver solución 1. **flow**; 2. **marginal gains**; 3. **momentum**; 4. **level playing field**; 5. **mental resilience**.
### Ejercicio 9 — Reading Lee el texto y responde. > The pursuit of sporting excellence increasingly resembles an arms race. Wealthier clubs invest in marginal gains through nutrition, sleep monitoring, specialist coaching and psychological support. These improvements may seem individually minor, but together they can determine whether an athlete performs consistently under pressure. Critics argue that the system entrenches inequality because raw talent is developed differently depending on access to resources. The language of meritocracy therefore requires qualification: effort matters, but effort alone cannot create a level playing field. Only when young athletes receive comparable facilities and recovery support can competition become genuinely fairer. 1. What do wealthy clubs invest in? 2. Why do small improvements matter? 3. What criticism do opponents make? 4. Why does meritocracy require qualification? 5. What condition could make competition fairer?
Ver solución 1. **Nutrition, sleep monitoring, specialist coaching and psychological support.** 2. **Together they can determine consistent performance under pressure.** 3. **That the system entrenches inequality through unequal access to resources.** 4. **Because effort alone cannot create a level playing field when resources differ.** 5. **Comparable facilities and recovery support for young athletes.**
### Ejercicio 10 — Listening guiado Guion: “The athlete did work hard, but it was the quality of her recovery programme that transformed her results. Only after she had reduced her training load did her endurance improve. What separated her from other competitors was not the absence of anxiety, but her ability to reframe it as energy.” Identifica un `did` enfático, una it-cleft, una inversión con `only` y una what-cleft.
Ver solución `Did` enfático: **did work hard**. It-cleft: **it was the quality of her recovery programme that transformed her results**. Inversión: **Only after she had reduced her training load did her endurance improve**. What-cleft: **What separated her from other competitors was...**.
### Ejercicio 11 — Fronting y sentido Explica la diferencia entre: 1. *The team improved only after the coach changed the strategy.* 2. *Only after the coach changed the strategy did the team improve.*
Ver solución El significado básico es el mismo, pero la segunda versión pone la condición temporal en primer plano y utiliza inversión enfática. Es más marcada y adecuada cuando el momento del cambio es el punto central del argumento.
### Ejercicio 12 — Corrección avanzada Corrige el párrafo. > She did trained hard, but rarely the coach recognised her progress. Not only the team improved, but also reduced injuries. What did matter was the access to recovery support.
Ver solución **She did train hard, but rarely did the coach recognise her progress. Not only did the team improve, but it also reduced injuries. What mattered was access to recovery support.**
### Ejercicio 13 — Registro argumentativo Reescribe con énfasis y matiz: *Sport rewards talent equally, but resources are different.*
Modelo **It is not talent alone that determines sporting success; only when athletes have access to comparable coaching, facilities and recovery support can competition approach a level playing field.**
### Ejercicio 14 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **Does competitive sport build character?** Incluye un `did` enfático, una inversión con `only`, una cleft y vocabulario de rendimiento.
Modelo Competitive sport can build character, but its effects depend heavily on the environment in which competition takes place. Athletes do develop discipline and mental resilience through demanding training, yet pressure can also produce anxiety or unhealthy perfectionism. It is not victory alone that builds character; rather, it is the way coaches and teammates respond to setbacks. Only when competitors are encouraged to reflect on failure can they develop genuine composure and self-belief. Elite sport may also expose unequal access to nutrition, facilities and psychological support. Wealthier athletes can accumulate marginal gains, whereas others may struggle to recover between sessions. The language of meritocracy therefore needs qualification. Effort does matter, and athletes do deserve recognition for sustained commitment, but personal dedication cannot create a level playing field by itself. Competitive sport is most likely to foster resilience when it combines high expectations with responsible coaching, adequate recovery and respect for the person behind the performance.
### Ejercicio 15 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre la presión competitiva. Usa `What matters is`, `It is... that`, `only when` y `did` enfático.
Pista y modelo **What matters is how athletes interpret pressure. It is not the absence of anxiety that produces consistent performance, but the ability to manage it. Only when competitors receive appropriate support can they recover effectively. The athlete did work hard, but her progress also depended on coaching and access to facilities.**
### Ejercicio 16 — Traducción controlada Traduce al inglés. 1. Sí que entrenó muchísimo para el maratón. 2. Solo mediante años de sacrificio consiguió su objetivo. 3. Fue la resiliencia mental lo que la distinguió.
Ver solución 1. **She did train incredibly hard for the marathon.** 2. **Only through years of sacrifice did she achieve her ambition.** 3. **It was her mental resilience that set her apart.**
### Ejercicio 17 — Edición de una reseña Mejora esta frase: *The athlete was very good and she tried hard, so she won.* Incluye una cleft y una colocación de rendimiento.
Modelo **It was the athlete’s ability to maintain focus under pressure, combined with her exceptional physical endurance, that enabled her to reach peak performance.**
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > The runner ___ train consistently, but ___ after the injury ___ she changed her recovery plan. ___ was her mental resilience that kept her competing, and ___ matters most ___ the ability to manage pressure rather than the absence of anxiety.
Ver solución **did; only; did; It; what; is.** El texto completo es: **The runner did train consistently, but only after the injury did she change her recovery plan. It was her mental resilience that kept her competing, and what matters most is the ability to manage pressure rather than the absence of anxiety.**
### Ejercicio 19 — Integra el argumento Combina estas ideas en un párrafo formal de 70–90 palabras. Incluye un `did` enfático para corregir una afirmación, una inversión con **only**, una it-cleft y una concesión. > The athlete trained consistently. Her progress was not caused by training alone. She received specialist recovery support. This support became available after she joined an elite programme. Sport can build resilience, but access to resources is unequal.
Ver solución Una respuesta posible es: **The athlete did train consistently, but her progress was not caused by training alone. It was specialist recovery support that made the greatest difference after she joined an elite programme. Only when athletes have access to comparable resources can a competition approach a level playing field. Although sport can build resilience, access to coaching, nutrition and recovery facilities remains unequal.** El párrafo utiliza `did train` para reforzar una afirmación, la it-cleft para destacar el apoyo, la inversión con `only` para expresar una condición y `although` para introducir una concesión. El contenido también evita explicar el éxito mediante una única causa.
Al revisar cualquier respuesta de esta unidad, comprueba tres aspectos. Primero, confirma que `do`, `does` o `did` van seguidos del verbo base. Segundo, localiza la inversión: después de `only` debe aparecer el auxiliar antes del sujeto, mientras que un complemento frontal neutro no exige ese cambio. Por último, pregunta qué factor quieres destacar. Si el énfasis no corrige, contrasta ni organiza una idea, la oración normal suele ser la opción más natural. ## Resumen de la unidad Usa **do/does/did + verbo base** para reforzar una afirmación, confirmar una acción o contradecir una negación. Recuerda que el verbo principal no lleva `-s` ni pasado después del auxiliar: *She does perform*, *she did perform*. Usa **only, not until, never, rarely** y otras expresiones restrictivas al principio para crear fronting e inversión. Si el complemento frontal es neutro, como *in the final* o *after the injury*, normalmente no necesitas inversión. Las clefts con **it was... that/who** y las what-clefts con **what... was...** distribuyen el foco de otra manera. En debates deportivos, estas estructuras ayudan a evitar explicaciones demasiado simples. El esfuerzo importa, pero también cuentan la recuperación, el entrenamiento, la nutrición y el acceso a recursos. Cuando combines *mental resilience*, *marginal gains*, *perform under pressure* y *level playing field* con énfasis gramatical, podrás escribir y hablar sobre rendimiento con la precisión argumentativa propia del nivel C1.

excerpt: Guía C1 sobre voz pasiva avanzada, reporting verbs y causativas con vocabulario de música y artes escénicas, teoría y ejercicios resueltos.
description: Aprende la pasiva impersonal, la pasiva con reporting verbs y las causativas have/get something done en inglés C1. Música, ejemplos y ejercicios resueltos.

keywords: Ejercicios de la Pasiva Avanzada en Inglés C1

faqs.question: ¿Cómo se forma la pasiva impersonal?
faqs.answer: Se forma con It is believed/reported/said that más una cláusula, o con sujeto + is believed/reported/said + to-infinitive.

faqs.question: ¿Qué significa have something done?
faqs.answer: Significa organizar o encargar que otra persona realice un servicio: She had her violin restored by a luthier.

faqs.question: ¿Cuál es la diferencia entre have y get something done?
faqs.answer: Ambas formas son causativas; have suele ser más neutral y get puede sugerir esfuerzo, persuasión o un tono más informal.

faqs.question: ¿La Unidad 16 incluye ejercicios resueltos?
faqs.answer: Sí. Incluye práctica de pasivas, causativas, reporting verbs, vocabulario musical, reading, listening, writing y speaking.

content:
# Unidad 16 C1: pasiva avanzada, música y performance La voz pasiva permite cambiar el foco de una oración. En vez de centrar la atención en la persona que realiza una acción, podemos destacar la obra, el instrumento, el escenario o el resultado. En música y artes escénicas esta elección aparece constantemente: - *The orchestra performed the symphony.* - *The symphony was performed by the orchestra.* - *The symphony is believed to have transformed the composer’s reputation.* La Unidad 16 C1 amplía la pasiva con tres áreas especialmente útiles: **passive reporting**, **causative have/get something done** y pasivas en tiempos y estructuras complejas. También trabaja el vocabulario de interpretación musical, desde *pacing* y *range* hasta *leitmotif, timbre, phrasing* y *interpretive judgement*. Una reseña avanzada no solo describe lo que ocurrió. Puede atribuir una opinión sin asumirla como propia, explicar que un instrumento fue restaurado por un especialista o señalar que una obra está siendo reinterpretada. La gramática ayuda a distinguir agente, resultado, evidencia y valoración. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 16 C1](/curso-c1/unit-16)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 15 C1: énfasis y deporte](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-15-enfasis-deporte)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 17 C1: literatura y storytelling](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-17-literatura-storytelling)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Qué hace la voz pasiva La pasiva transforma el objeto de una oración activa en el sujeto de la nueva oración. La forma general es: > **Subject + be + past participle** - Activa: *The conductor rehearsed the orchestra.* - Pasiva: *The orchestra was rehearsed by the conductor.* El agente con *by* puede omitirse si es desconocido, irrelevante o evidente: - *The stage was redesigned for the production.* - *The score was discovered in an archive.* - *The instruments were tuned before the concert.* La pasiva no es necesariamente más formal, pero es muy frecuente en informes, reseñas y descripciones de procesos. En una crítica, puede ser más importante el efecto que la persona que lo produjo: - *The audience was held in complete stillness by the performance.* En una oración activa, el escritor elegiría el agente como sujeto. En una pasiva, el escritor elige qué resultado merece el primer plano. ### 2. Pasiva en tiempos principales El tiempo verbal se marca en *be*, mientras que el participio principal permanece en V3: - **Present simple:** *The instruments are tuned before every performance.* - **Past simple:** *The hall was renovated last year.* - **Present continuous:** *The stage is being prepared.* - **Past continuous:** *The lighting was being adjusted when the audience arrived.* - **Present perfect:** *The violin has been restored by a specialist.* - **Past perfect:** *The score had been archived before the discovery was announced.* - **Future:** *The new production will be premiered in June.* - **Future perfect:** *The theatre will have been renovated by the opening night.* Compara *is performed* con *is being performed*. La primera puede describir una práctica habitual; la segunda muestra una acción que está ocurriendo ahora. *Has been restored* destaca un resultado actual; *was restored* sitúa el trabajo en un pasado terminado. ### 3. Modal passive Con modales usamos: > **modal + be + past participle** - *The score must be performed from memory.* - *The instruments should be stored in stable conditions.* - *The production can be adapted for a smaller venue.* - *The rights may be renewed next season.* Para una acción pasada usamos: > **modal + have been + past participle** - *The violin should have been inspected before the tour.* - *The contract may have been signed without proper consultation.* - *The recording could have been edited after the broadcast.* - *The mistake can’t have been caused by the new technician.* No confundas *must be performed* con *must have been performed*. La primera expresa obligación o necesidad presente/futura; la segunda expresa una conclusión o posibilidad sobre una acción anterior. ### 4. Passive reporting impersonal La pasiva impersonal permite presentar una opinión o información atribuida sin enfocar una fuente concreta: > **It + be + past participle + that-clause** - *It is believed that the premiere will be a watershed moment.* - *It is reported that the orchestra is facing financial pressure.* - *It has been suggested that the festival should change its funding model.* - *It was widely assumed that the conductor would resign.* Los reporting verbs más habituales son **say, believe, think, report, claim, expect, assume, understand, consider** y **allege**. El adverbio puede mostrar el alcance de la afirmación: *widely, generally, officially, reportedly, privately*. La forma impersonal es útil cuando la fuente es un grupo, una tradición crítica o un conjunto de informes. Si la fuente es relevante, es mejor nombrarla: - Menos específico: *It is believed that the theatre is underfunded.* - Más específico: *The cultural committee believes that the theatre is underfunded.* ### 5. Passive reporting personal La misma información puede reorganizarse para enfocar el sujeto: > **Subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive** - *The young conductor is said to show extraordinary promise.* - *The premiere is expected to attract international attention.* - *The orchestra is believed to be negotiating a new contract.* Si el hecho es anterior al momento del reporte, usamos el **perfect infinitive**: - *The conductor is believed to have changed the interpretation.* - *The score is reported to have been discovered in a private archive.* - *The presenter is said to have been misquoted.* La equivalencia es: - *It is believed that the conductor changed the interpretation.* - *The conductor is believed to have changed the interpretation.* No mezcles ambas formas: *It is believed the conductor to have changed...* no es la estructura estándar. ### 6. Reporting verbs y matiz La elección del participio cambia la relación con la información: - **is said to:** se dice que, atribución relativamente neutral. - **is believed to:** se considera probable. - **is reported to:** una fuente o medio lo ha comunicado. - **is thought to:** se piensa o se interpreta. - **is alleged to:** se acusa, sin confirmación. - **is expected to:** se prevé o espera. - **is understood to:** se entiende según información disponible. - *The singer is alleged to have cancelled the performance for contractual reasons.* - *The singer is expected to return next season.* - *The singer is understood to be negotiating with a new label.* No son intercambiables en todos los contextos. *Alleged* puede sugerir una acusación; *expected* se refiere a una previsión; *understood* mantiene una distancia prudente sin señalar necesariamente conflicto. ### 7. Causative have something done Usamos **have + object + past participle** cuando organizamos que otra persona realice un servicio o acción: - *She had her violin restored by a luthier.* - *The theatre had its acoustics tested before reopening.* - *The orchestra had the costumes repaired before the tour.* - *The composer had the score copied professionally.* La persona o institución que aparece como sujeto no realiza necesariamente la acción. *She had her violin restored* significa que encargó u organizó la restauración. El agente puede aparecer después de *by*, pero normalmente se omite si no es importante. La estructura funciona en muchos tiempos: - *She has had her piano tuned.* - *She had had the piano tuned before the concert.* - *She will have the piano tuned tomorrow.* - *She is having the piano tuned this afternoon.* La combinación *had had* es correcta: el primer *had* es el auxiliar del past perfect y el segundo forma la causativa. ### 8. Get something done **Get + object + past participle** también expresa una acción encargada o conseguida: - *The singer got her microphone repaired before the show.* - *The company got the contract translated overnight.* - *We need to get the stage inspected.* *Get* puede sonar más informal que *have* y a veces sugiere esfuerzo, persuasión o que la persona logró que algo ocurriera: - *She had her costume altered.* Neutral. - *She got her costume altered at short notice.* Enfatiza que consiguió el servicio. En conversación, *get* es muy común. En un informe formal, *have* puede resultar más neutral, aunque ambas son correctas. No confundas la causativa con una pasiva ordinaria: - *The violin was restored by a specialist.* El hecho de la restauración. - *The musician had the violin restored by a specialist.* La músico organizó o encargó el trabajo. ### 9. Causativa con acciones negativas o desagradables La estructura también puede indicar que algo ocurrió a una persona, a menudo sin que lo planificara: - *The performer had her equipment stolen backstage.* - *The theatre got its roof damaged during the storm.* - *The journalist had her recording deleted.* Este uso suele llamarse **causative have** con significado de experiencia adversa. El sujeto no causó deliberadamente el robo, daño o eliminación. El contexto determina si *have* significa “encargar” o “sufrir una experiencia”: - *The theatre had its roof repaired.* El teatro organizó la reparación. - *The theatre had its roof damaged.* El techo sufrió daños. ### 10. Causative activa con infinitivo Con algunos verbos usamos una estructura distinta cuando el sujeto hace que otra persona actúe: - **have + person + bare infinitive:** *The director had the actors repeat the scene.* - **get + person + to-infinitive:** *The director got the actors to repeat the scene.* - **make + person + bare infinitive:** *The director made the actors repeat the scene.* - **let + person + bare infinitive:** *The director let the actors improvise.* Compara: - *The director had the scene repeated.* Encargó o dispuso que la escena se repitiera. - *The director had the actors repeat the scene.* Hizo que los actores la repitieran. Con *get* necesitamos *to*: *got the actors to repeat*, no *got the actors repeat*. Con *make* usamos el infinitivo sin *to*. ### 11. Pasiva con dos objetos Algunos verbos como *give, send, offer, show* y *tell* pueden formar dos pasivas: - Activa: *The conductor gave the soloist a new score.* - Pasiva 1: *The soloist was given a new score.* - Pasiva 2: *A new score was given to the soloist.* Con verbos de reporte y comunicación, el objeto personal suele convertirse en sujeto: - *The audience was told that the performance would be delayed.* - *The performers were sent revised schedules.* La elección depende del foco. Si el lector necesita saber quién recibió la información, usa la primera pasiva. Si el documento o mensaje es el tema, usa la segunda. ### 12. Pasiva con verbos preposicionales La preposición permanece junto al verbo: - *The source was referred to in the programme notes.* - *The performer was spoken to after the rehearsal.* - *The proposal was objected to by several musicians.* - *The audience was provided with translated subtitles.* En registro formal, podemos adelantar la preposición con *which/whom* en una relativa, pero en una pasiva normal no la elimines. *The source was referred* está incompleto; debe ser *was referred to*. ### 13. Música y performance: vocabulario - **pacing:** control del ritmo y progresión de una interpretación. - **timing:** precisión del momento en que se ejecutan acciones o sonidos. - **tempo:** velocidad de una pieza. - **range:** extensión de notas que puede producir una voz o instrumento. - **pitch:** altura de un sonido. - **timbre:** cualidad o color distintivo del sonido. - **phrasing:** forma de agrupar y articular frases musicales. - **leitmotif:** motivo recurrente asociado a una persona, idea o situación. - **cadenza:** pasaje solista, a menudo virtuoso. - **overture:** pieza que abre una ópera o producción. - **pianissimo:** interpretación muy suave. - **fortissimo:** interpretación muy fuerte. - **acoustic:** relativo al sonido y su propagación. - **resonance:** riqueza o prolongación del sonido. - **interpretive judgement:** decisiones sobre cómo dar significado a una obra. - **expressive range:** variedad de matices expresivos. - **technical precision:** exactitud técnica. - **stagecraft:** habilidades y recursos de la puesta en escena. - **watershed moment:** momento decisivo que marca un cambio. - **musicality:** sensibilidad para expresar la estructura y emoción musical. Colocaciones esenciales son **calibrate the pacing**, **maintain a steady tempo**, **expand the vocal range**, **shape a phrase**, **introduce a leitmotif**, **create acoustic resonance**, **make interpretive choices**, **deliver a technically precise performance**, **hold the audience’s attention** y **stage a production**. ### 14. Pasiva en crítica musical Una reseña puede utilizar la pasiva para enfocar la obra: - *The opening theme is gradually transformed throughout the movement.* - *The silence is used to create tension.* - *The final chord is sustained longer than expected.* - *The audience is drawn into the performance through carefully controlled pacing.* La pasiva no elimina siempre al agente. Si la decisión interpretativa importa, nómbralo: - *The pianist shapes the phrase with unusual restraint.* - *The phrase is shaped with unusual restraint by the pianist.* La versión activa suele ser más dinámica; la pasiva puede resultar más analítica. Alternar ambas evita una reseña monótona. ### 15. Registro y responsabilidad La pasiva impersonal puede crear una falsa impresión de objetividad si se usa sin fuente. Compara: - *It is universally accepted that the performance was revolutionary.* - *Several critics have argued that the performance was unusually influential.* La segunda muestra quién sostiene la interpretación. Si no puedes identificar una fuente, *the evidence suggests* o *the performance appears to have* puede ser más honesto que *it is known that*. En una reseña, separa observación y valoración: - Observación: *The tempo was reduced in the final movement.* - Interpretación: *This may have been intended to emphasise the movement’s reflective quality.* - Evaluación: *The decision was largely effective, although the transition became less coherent.* ### 16. Errores frecuentes - *It is believed the premiere to be important.* → **It is believed that the premiere is important** o **The premiere is believed to be important.** - *The conductor is said having changed the score.* → **is said to have changed**. - *She had restored her violin by a luthier.* → **She had her violin restored by a luthier.** - *She got her violin to restore.* → **She got her violin restored** o **She got the luthier to restore her violin.** - *The director made the actors to repeat the scene.* → **made the actors repeat**. - *The score was referred.* → **The score was referred to**. - *It is essential that the instruments are inspected.* → En subjuntivo formal: **that the instruments be inspected**. - *The audience was told the concert delayed.* → **The audience was told that the concert was delayed.** ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Pasiva básica Transforma las frases. 1. The orchestra performed the symphony. 2. The technicians are preparing the stage. 3. The conservator has restored the violin. 4. The archive had stored the score for decades.
Ver solución 1. **The symphony was performed by the orchestra.** 2. **The stage is being prepared by the technicians.** 3. **The violin has been restored by the conservator.** 4. **The score had been stored by the archive for decades.**
### Ejercicio 2 — Modal passive Completa. 1. The score must ___ (perform) from memory. 2. The instruments should ___ (store) in stable conditions. 3. The recording may ___ (edit) after the broadcast. 4. The violin should ___ ___ ___ (inspect) before the tour.
Ver solución 1. **be performed**; 2. **be stored**; 3. **be edited**; 4. **have been inspected**. El modal presente usa *be + V3*; el pasado usa *have been + V3*.
### Ejercicio 3 — Passive reporting Transforma. 1. People believe that the premiere will attract international attention. 2. Critics say that the conductor changed the interpretation. 3. The press reports that the presenter was misquoted.
Ver solución 1. **It is believed that the premiere will attract international attention.** / **The premiere is believed to attract international attention.** 2. **It is said that the conductor changed the interpretation.** / **The conductor is said to have changed the interpretation.** 3. **It is reported that the presenter was misquoted.** / **The presenter is reported to have been misquoted.**
### Ejercicio 4 — Causative have Completa con la forma correcta de **have**. 1. She ___ her violin ___ (restore) before the tour. 2. The theatre is ___ its acoustics ___ (test) this week. 3. They will ___ the costumes ___ (repair) tomorrow. 4. She had ___ the piano ___ (tune) before the concert began.
Ver solución 1. **had her violin restored**; 2. **having its acoustics tested**; 3. **have the costumes repaired**; 4. **had had the piano tuned**.
### Ejercicio 5 — Have, get o pasiva normal Elige la opción adecuada. 1. The musician ___ her microphone repaired before the show. (*had / was*) 2. The microphone ___ repaired by a technician. (*had / was*) 3. The theatre ___ its roof damaged in the storm. (*had / was*) 4. The theatre ___ its roof repaired after the storm. (*had / was*)
Ver solución 1. **had** — la músico organizó el servicio. 2. **was** — pasiva normal: el micrófono recibió la acción. 3. **had** — experiencia adversa: el techo sufrió daños. 4. **had** — la institución organizó la reparación.
### Ejercicio 6 — Get causative Transforma usando **get + object + past participle**. 1. The singer arranged for her costume to be altered. 2. The company arranged for the contract to be translated. 3. We need the stage to be inspected.
Ver solución 1. **The singer got her costume altered.** 2. **The company got the contract translated.** 3. **We need to get the stage inspected.**
### Ejercicio 7 — Causative activa Completa con **had, got** o **made**. 1. The director ___ the actors repeat the scene. 2. The director ___ the actors to repeat the scene after explaining the problem. 3. The director ___ the actors repeat the scene as a punishment.
Ver solución 1. **had**; 2. **got**; 3. **made**. *Have* dispone que alguien haga algo; *get* implica conseguirlo y lleva *to*; *make* expresa obligación o imposición.
### Ejercicio 8 — Música y vocabulario Completa con **pacing, range, timbre, leitmotif** o **phrasing**. 1. The singer’s vocal ___ allowed her to move from pianissimo to fortissimo. 2. The recurring theme functioned as a ___ for the protagonist. 3. The performance’s ___ created tension without rushing the music. 4. The instrument’s distinctive ___ made it immediately recognisable. 5. The pianist’s ___ gave each musical sentence a clear direction.
Ver solución 1. **range**; 2. **leitmotif**; 3. **pacing**; 4. **timbre**; 5. **phrasing**.
### Ejercicio 9 — Reading Lee el texto y responde. > The new production is believed to have been developed over three years. It is reported that the score was substantially revised after the first workshop, and the orchestra is said to have been given additional rehearsal time. The director had the acoustic properties of the theatre tested before the opening, while the performers got their costumes altered to allow greater movement. What distinguishes the production is not technical novelty alone, but the way the leitmotif is gradually transformed as the protagonist’s understanding changes. The pacing is deliberately restrained in the opening scenes, although the final movement is performed with considerable expressive range. 1. How long is the production believed to have been developed? 2. What happened to the score? 3. What additional time was the orchestra given? 4. What did the director have tested? 5. What distinguishes the production?
Ver solución 1. **Three years.** 2. **It was substantially revised after the first workshop.** 3. **Additional rehearsal time.** 4. **The acoustic properties of the theatre.** 5. **The transformation of the leitmotif and the expressive relationship between music and character, not technical novelty alone.**
### Ejercicio 10 — Listening guiado Guion: “The premiere is expected to attract a large audience, but the production is not being presented as a conventional revival. The director is said to have had the score reorchestrated, and several scenes are believed to have been shortened. What matters is that the original emotional arc has not been lost.” Identifica una pasiva de presente, una pasiva continua, una estructura con infinitivo perfecto y una causativa.
Ver solución Pasiva de presente: **is expected to attract**. Pasiva continua: **is not being presented**. Infinitivo perfecto: **is said to have had**. Causativa: **to have had the score reorchestrated**; el director encargó que se hiciera el trabajo.
### Ejercicio 11 — Pasiva con preposición Completa la preposición. 1. The source was referred ___ in the programme notes. 2. The performer was spoken ___ after the rehearsal. 3. The proposal was objected ___ by several musicians. 4. The audience was provided ___ translated subtitles.
Ver solución 1. **to**; 2. **to**; 3. **to**; 4. **with**. Las preposiciones forman parte de la construcción verbal y no pueden eliminarse.
### Ejercicio 12 — Infinitivo perfecto Completa con **to be**, **to have**, **to have been** o **to have been + -ing**. 1. The young conductor is said ___ extraordinary promise. 2. The score is believed ___ discovered in an archive. 3. The presenter is reported ___ misquoted. 4. The orchestra is thought ___ negotiating a new contract.
Ver solución 1. **to show** extraordinary promise; 2. **to have been** discovered; 3. **to have been** misquoted; 4. **to have been** negotiating.
### Ejercicio 13 — Observación o interpretación Clasifica cada frase como **observación**, **atribución** o **interpretación**. 1. *The tempo was reduced in the final movement.* 2. *The conductor is believed to have changed the phrasing.* 3. *The slower tempo may have emphasised the movement’s reflective quality.* 4. *The score was revised after the workshop.*
Ver solución 1. **Observación**; 2. **Atribución**; 3. **Interpretación**; 4. **Observación atribuida al registro del proceso**, si el texto no especifica quién lo revisó.
### Ejercicio 14 — Corrección gramatical Corrige las frases. 1. *It is believed the premiere to be revolutionary.* 2. *She had restored her violin by a luthier.* 3. *The director got the actors repeat the scene.* 4. *The score was referred.*
Ver solución 1. **It is believed that the premiere is revolutionary** o **The premiere is believed to be revolutionary.** 2. **She had her violin restored by a luthier.** 3. **The director got the actors to repeat the scene.** 4. **The score was referred to.**
### Ejercicio 15 — Reformulación crítica Reescribe de forma más prudente: *The performance was emotionally perfect.*
Modelo **The performance appears to have achieved an unusually effective balance between technical precision and emotional expression.** La nueva frase evita una evaluación absoluta y especifica qué aspectos sostienen la valoración.
### Ejercicio 16 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **How can a conductor modernise a classical work without losing its identity?** Incluye una pasiva impersonal, una estructura personal con infinitivo perfecto, una causativa y vocabulario musical.
Modelo A classical work can be modernised without losing its identity if the conductor distinguishes essential structures from historically variable conventions. It is often argued that a new interpretation should respect the original score, but the work is also believed to have survived because performers have continually made different expressive choices. A conductor might have the orchestration revised while preserving the main melodic relationships and leitmotifs. The pacing could be adjusted, although the tempo should not be changed merely to create novelty. It is important that the acoustic balance be tested before the premiere and that the performers be given sufficient rehearsal time. A successful production is likely to refresh the work’s public image when its changes are motivated by interpretation rather than fashion. In my view, the most convincing modernisation allows the audience to hear familiar material differently while retaining the emotional arc, structural coherence and expressive range that make the composition recognisable.
### Ejercicio 17 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre una actuación que recuerdes. Usa **was performed**, **is believed to have**, **had the instrument tuned** y dos palabras de vocabulario musical.
Pista y modelo **The concerto was performed in a small hall with remarkable acoustic resonance. The soloist is believed to have changed the phrasing during the final movement, and she had her instrument tuned immediately before the performance. The pacing was restrained, but the expressive range was extraordinary.**
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > The new opera ___ ___ ___ (believe) to have been revised after the first workshop. The director ___ (have) the stage ___ (inspect) and the singers ___ (get) their costumes ___ (alter). Several scenes ___ (shorten), but the central leitmotif ___ (retain).
Ver solución **is believed; had; inspected; got; altered; were shortened; was retained.** El texto completo es: **The new opera is believed to have been revised after the first workshop. The director had the stage inspected and the singers got their costumes altered. Several scenes were shortened, but the central leitmotif was retained.**
### Ejercicio 19 — Elige el foco adecuado Escribe una versión apropiada para cada intención. 1. Quieres destacar la información atribuida: “People believe the premiere will change contemporary opera.” 2. Quieres destacar el estreno y mantener distancia: “People believe the premiere changed the composer’s reputation.” 3. Quieres decir que la pianista encargó el servicio a otra persona: “A specialist tuned her piano.” 4. Quieres describir una acción que los actores realizaron por orden del director: “The actors repeated the scene.”
Ver solución 1. **It is believed that the premiere will change contemporary opera.** 2. **The premiere is believed to have changed the composer’s reputation.** 3. **The pianist had her piano tuned by a specialist.** 4. **The director had the actors repeat the scene.** La primera frase enfoca la proposición completa; la segunda enfoca el estreno y usa infinitivo perfecto para la anterioridad. La tercera es una causativa pasiva: la pianista organiza el servicio. La cuarta es una causativa activa con *have + person + bare infinitive*, porque los actores son quienes realizan la acción.
## Resumen de la unidad Usa la pasiva para destacar el resultado o el elemento afectado: **be + participio**. Con modales, utiliza **must be performed** para obligación o necesidad presente y **must have been performed** para una conclusión sobre el pasado. En reporting, elige entre **It is believed that...** y **The work is believed to...** según quieras enfocar la información o el sujeto. Las causativas **have/get + object + past participle** indican que alguien organiza un servicio: *She had her violin restored*. Con una persona, usa **have + person + bare infinitive** o **get + person + to-infinitive**: *The director had the actors repeat the scene* y *got the actors to repeat it*. Recuerda que el mismo verbo *have* también puede describir una experiencia adversa, como *have equipment stolen*. En crítica musical, combina observaciones concretas con atribución y evaluación prudente. Las estructuras pasivas organizan el foco; el vocabulario de *pacing, phrasing, timbre, range* y *interpretive judgement* aporta precisión. Una reseña C1 no necesita afirmar que una actuación es “perfecta”: debe explicar qué decisiones fueron tomadas, qué efecto produjeron y qué evidencia permite sostener esa valoración.
