faqs.question: ¿Qué es fronting en inglés?
faqs.answer: Fronting consiste en colocar al principio un elemento que normalmente aparecería después para darle énfasis; ciertos adverbiales negativos provocan inversión entre auxiliar y sujeto.

faqs.question: ¿Cuándo se invierte el sujeto y el auxiliar?
faqs.answer: Después de expresiones como never, rarely, not only, not until y under no circumstances, cuando se colocan al principio de la oración.

faqs.question: ¿Cómo se expresa especulación en inglés C1?
faqs.answer: Con expresiones como might well, could conceivably, there is every chance y it is feasible that, ajustando la fuerza de la hipótesis a la evidencia.

faqs.question: ¿La Unidad 8 incluye ejercicios resueltos?
faqs.answer: Sí. Incluye práctica de fronting, contraste, especulación, vocabulario global, reading, listening, writing y speaking.

content:
# Unidad 8 C1: fronting, contraste y especulación Cuando hablamos de problemas globales necesitamos dos tipos de precisión. Primero, debemos decidir qué información merece ocupar el primer plano: una consecuencia, una limitación, un grupo afectado o una condición. Segundo, debemos distinguir entre hechos comprobados, interpretaciones plausibles y escenarios que solo podemos imaginar. La Unidad 8 trabaja esas capacidades mediante **fronting**, **topicalisation**, estructuras de **contraste** y lenguaje de **especulación**. Compara estas frases: - *The Security Council has rarely been so divided.* - *Rarely has the Security Council been so divided.* La segunda no cambia el hecho, pero coloca *rarely* al frente y crea un énfasis formal mediante inversión. Ahora observa el contraste: - *Developed nations have stabilised inflation, whereas many emerging economies still face debt distress.* Y la especulación: - *The conflict might well intensify if humanitarian access remains restricted.* - *A negotiated settlement could conceivably be reached this year.* El objetivo C1 no es sonar dramático ni categórico. Es organizar la frase para guiar al lector y expresar una hipótesis con un grado de seguridad responsable. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 8 C1](/curso-c1/unit-8)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 7 C1: nominal clauses y reporting verbs](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-7-nominal-reporting-concession-salud)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 9 C1: discourse markers avanzados](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-70-language-lab-cohesion-discursiva)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. Qué es fronting **Fronting** significa mover al principio de la oración un elemento que, en el orden neutro, aparecería más tarde. La intención es ponerlo en foco, crear contraste o preparar el tema del discurso. - Orden neutro: *The committee discussed climate finance in the closing session.* - Con foco: *Climate finance, the committee discussed in the closing session.* La segunda estructura es marcada y debe usarse con un propósito. En inglés formal es más común combinar fronting con una estructura de foco: - *It was climate finance that dominated the closing session.* - *What the committee discussed was climate finance.* - *As for climate finance, the committee treated it as a priority.* El fronting puede afectar al objeto, al complemento adverbial o al tema. No todos los movimientos son igualmente naturales; el contexto y la puntuación ayudan a evitar ambigüedades. ### 2. Adverbiales negativos e inversión Cuando una expresión negativa o restrictiva se coloca al principio, normalmente invertimos el auxiliar y el sujeto. El patrón es: > **Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb** - *Rarely has the Security Council been so divided.* - *Seldom do governments acknowledge the long-term cost.* - *Never have I seen such a fragile ceasefire.* - *Under no circumstances should the mandate be renewed without consent.* La inversión no convierte la frase en pregunta. Es una estructura declarativa enfática. Si ya existe un auxiliar, lo movemos delante del sujeto: *has the council been*, *have I seen*, *should the mandate be*. Si no hay auxiliar en el presente o pasado simple, añadimos **do, does o did** y el verbo principal vuelve a su forma base: - *Rarely do states agree on a common definition.* - *Little did the negotiators realise how serious the dispute was.* No digas *Rarely governments agree* ni *Rarely does governments agree*. El auxiliar debe concordar con el sujeto y el verbo principal no lleva la marca de tiempo cuando aparece *do/does/did*. ### 3. Never, rarely, seldom y little **Never** expresa ausencia total de experiencia o frecuencia. **Rarely** y **seldom** significan “raramente” y suelen aparecer en registros formales. **Little** delante de un verbo significa “en muy poca medida” o “sin darse cuenta de hasta qué punto”: - *Never before has the region faced such severe displacement.* - *Rarely do humanitarian agencies receive unrestricted funding.* - *Seldom has a treaty been negotiated under such pressure.* - *Little did the public know that the agreement was already failing.* La inversión es obligatoria o muy esperable cuando estas expresiones tienen alcance sobre toda la oración y aparecen al principio. Si la expresión permanece en posición media, no hay inversión: - *The region has never faced such severe displacement.* - *Humanitarian agencies rarely receive unrestricted funding.* ### 4. Not only y under no circumstances **Not only** crea una estructura correlativa: > **Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb, but also + clause** - *Not only did the drought reduce harvests, but it also increased food prices.* - *Not only has the policy failed to protect workers, but it has also widened inequality.* - *Not only is the measure expensive, but it is also difficult to enforce.* La segunda parte puede repetir el auxiliar o usar *but also* con una estructura paralela. Evita *Not only the drought reduced harvests*. Si *not only* modifica al sujeto y no a toda la proposición, la inversión puede no aparecer: *Not only the drought but also the flood damaged crops*. El significado y el foco cambian. **Under no circumstances** significa “bajo ninguna circunstancia” y exige una formulación firme: - *Under no circumstances should aid be withheld from civilians.* - *Under no circumstances must the data be used to identify vulnerable families.* En documentos formales también aparecen **on no account**, **at no time**, **in no way** y **not once**: - *On no account should the ceasefire be treated as permanent.* - *At no time did the observers claim that the process was complete.* - *In no way does the measure address the underlying cause.* ### 5. Not until, only then y only after Las expresiones con **not until** y **only** provocan inversión en la oración principal cuando aparecen al principio: - *Not until the treaty was signed did the ceasefire hold.* - *Only after the corridor reopened did aid reach the displaced communities.* - *Only then did negotiators understand the scale of the crisis.* - *Only by investing in local services can governments reduce displacement.* Observa que la cláusula temporal después de *not until* mantiene el orden normal: *the treaty was signed*, no *was the treaty signed*. La inversión está en la principal: *did the ceasefire hold*. Con **only when**, ocurre lo mismo: - *Only when reliable data become available can the policy be evaluated.* No inviertas dos veces. *Only when can reliable data become available can the policy...* es incorrecto. ### 6. Clefts y pseudo-clefts como fronting Las cleft sentences dividen una oración para destacar un elemento: - *It was climate finance that dominated the summit.* - *It was the lack of enforcement that undermined the agreement.* - *It was in the border region that the shortage became most severe.* El patrón es **It is/was + foco + that/who + información**. Usa *who* para personas y *that* para cosas, aunque *that* puede aparecer en muchas clefts. Las pseudo-clefts empiezan con **what**: - *What the planet needs is enforceable regulation.* - *What surprised observers was the speed of the escalation.* - *What governments have failed to address is the root cause.* Estas estructuras permiten presentar un tema y su comentario con claridad. No confundas *what* con *that*: *what* significa “lo que” e incluye el elemento focalizado; *that* introduce una proposición completa. ### 7. Topicalisation y left dislocation En una topicalisation, un elemento se coloca al principio y se retoma o se interpreta desde la cláusula: - *The refugees, many of them unaccompanied minors, the authorities were initially unable to process.* - *Climate finance, few governments have treated as a long-term priority.* En el inglés formal contemporáneo, a menudo es más claro usar una estructura con pronombre: - *As for the refugees, many of them unaccompanied minors, the authorities were initially unable to process them.* - *As for climate finance, few governments have treated it as a long-term priority.* **As for** y **with regard to** introducen el tema sin forzar una estructura marcada: - *As for debt relief, the proposal remains under discussion.* - *With regard to migration, the report recommends regional coordination.* Elige topicalisation cuando el referente sea fácilmente recuperable y la frase gane contraste. Si el lector puede perderse, utiliza *as for*, una cleft o el orden canónico. ### 8. Contraste entre cláusulas El contraste presenta dos ideas diferentes o resultados que no coinciden. Las principales opciones son: - **whereas:** *Whereas developed nations have stabilised inflation, emerging economies face debt distress.* - **while:** *While the policy reduced emissions, it increased energy costs.* - **on the other hand:** *The measure is affordable. On the other hand, enforcement is difficult.* - **by contrast:** *By contrast, manufacturing exports have rebounded sharply.* - **conversely:** *Higher rates may protect savings; conversely, they can restrict investment.* - **in contrast with/to:** *In contrast with earlier agreements, the new treaty includes monitoring.* - **unlike:** *Unlike temporary aid, debt relief can change long-term incentives.* *Whereas* y *while* introducen cláusulas completas. *Despite* e *in spite of* introducen nombres o gerundios: - *Despite economic growth, inequality widened.* - *Despite the economy growing, inequality widened.* - *Although the economy grew, inequality widened.* No digas *despite the economy grew*. Añade *the fact that* si necesitas conservar una cláusula: *despite the fact that the economy grew*. ### 9. Especulación: graduar una hipótesis El lenguaje especulativo permite hablar de posibilidades sin confundirlas con hechos. La fuerza de las expresiones puede organizarse así: | Fuerza | Expresión | Ejemplo | |---|---|---| | Posibilidad moderada | may, might, could | *The conflict might intensify.* | | Posibilidad reforzada | might well, could well | *The policy might well fail without funding.* | | Posibilidad concebible | could conceivably | *A settlement could conceivably be reached.* | | Probabilidad | be likely to, there is every chance | *Prices are likely to rise.* | | Viabilidad | it is feasible/possible that | *It is feasible that the corridor will reopen.* | | Improbabilidad | be unlikely to, there is little chance | *A rapid recovery is unlikely.* | **Might well** no significa certeza: refuerza que la posibilidad es razonable. **Could conceivably** presenta una opción imaginable, no necesariamente probable. **There is every chance** es más optimista que *there is a possibility*. Elige la expresión según la calidad de la evidencia. ### 10. Especulación sobre presente, pasado y futuro Para una situación presente usamos *may/might/could + base* o *be + -ing*: - *The government might reconsider the agreement.* - *The parties could be preparing a new proposal.* Para una situación pasada usamos **may/might/could + have + participle**: - *The negotiators may have underestimated public opposition.* - *The delay could have resulted from a shortage of fuel.* Para atribuir una posibilidad a una voz pasiva: - *The figures may have been manipulated.* - *The aid could be redirected to local organisations.* También podemos usar **must** y **can’t** para deducciones fuertes, pero no son equivalentes a la especulación cautelosa: - *The agreement must have been drafted under pressure.* - *The agreement can’t have addressed every concern.* ### 11. Vocabulario de global issues - **humanitarian mandate:** mandato humanitario. - **ceasefire:** alto el fuego. - **corridor:** corredor, especialmente de ayuda o evacuación. - **displacement:** desplazamiento forzoso. - **unaccompanied minor:** menor no acompañado. - **host-state consent:** consentimiento del Estado anfitrión. - **climate finance:** financiación climática. - **debt distress:** dificultades graves para pagar deuda. - **emerging economy:** economía emergente. - **inflation:** inflación. - **food insecurity:** inseguridad alimentaria. - **humanitarian access:** acceso humanitario. - **aid conditionality:** condicionalidad de la ayuda. - **sanctions:** sanciones. - **governance:** gobernanza. - **enforcement:** aplicación efectiva de una norma. - **accountability:** rendición de cuentas. - **regional disparity:** desigualdad regional. - **migration route:** ruta migratoria. - **debt relief:** alivio o condonación de deuda. - **underlying cause:** causa subyacente. - **vulnerable population:** población vulnerable. Colocaciones útiles son **negotiate a ceasefire**, **secure humanitarian access**, **provide emergency aid**, **address food insecurity**, **ease debt distress**, **impose sanctions**, **strengthen accountability**, **enforce a mandate**, **protect displaced people**, **reduce regional disparities** y **reach a negotiated settlement**. ### 12. Registro y responsabilidad En temas globales, una afirmación demasiado categórica puede ser inexacta o injusta. Compara: - *The sanctions will solve the crisis.* - *The sanctions might well intensify pressure, but they are unlikely to address the underlying cause on their own.* La segunda distingue una posibilidad de una limitación. También es importante no confundir contraste con oposición absoluta: - *Whereas the measure improved access in cities, it had a limited effect in rural areas.* La frase no dice que la política fuera inútil; compara resultados. El fronting puede ayudar a señalar un grupo que no debe desaparecer del análisis: - *As for displaced families, their immediate safety must remain the priority.* ### 13. Errores frecuentes - *Rarely the council has agreed.* → **Rarely has the council agreed.** - *Not until was the treaty signed did the ceasefire hold.* → **Not until the treaty was signed did the ceasefire hold.** - *Not only did the policy fail, but also increased costs.* → **Not only did the policy fail, but it also increased costs.** - *Despite the economy grew, inequality widened.* → **Although the economy grew...** o **Despite economic growth...**. - *The conflict could conceivably will intensify.* → **The conflict could conceivably intensify.** - *Whereas developed countries stabilised, but emerging markets struggled.* → Elimina *but*: **Whereas developed countries stabilised, emerging markets struggled.** - *Under no circumstances the data should be shared.* → **Under no circumstances should the data be shared.** - *It is feasible that a solution could conceivably be possible.* → Elige una expresión clara: **It is feasible that a solution will be found.** La revisión final debe comprobar si el elemento inicial realmente necesita énfasis, si la inversión está en la cláusula correcta, si el conector admite el complemento que sigue y si la especulación refleja la evidencia disponible. ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Inversión con adverbiales negativos Completa con el auxiliar adecuado. 1. Rarely ___ the Security Council been so divided. 2. Seldom ___ governments acknowledge the long-term cost. 3. Never ___ I seen such a fragile ceasefire. 4. Little ___ the negotiators realise how serious the dispute was.
Ver solución 1. **has**; 2. **do**; 3. **have**; 4. **did**. Cuando no hay auxiliar en presente o pasado simple, añadimos *do/does/did* y el verbo vuelve a la forma base.
### Ejercicio 2 — Not only Reescribe con **not only... but also**. *The drought reduced harvests. It increased food prices.*
Ver solución **Not only did the drought reduce harvests, but it also increased food prices.** La inversión aparece después de *not only* y la segunda cláusula mantiene el paralelismo.
### Ejercicio 3 — Not until y only after Completa. 1. Not until the treaty was signed ___ the ceasefire hold. 2. Only after the corridor reopened ___ aid reach the displaced communities. 3. Only when reliable data become available ___ the policy be evaluated.
Ver solución 1. **did**; 2. **did**; 3. **can**. La cláusula temporal mantiene el orden normal; la inversión está en la principal.
### Ejercicio 4 — Fronting o cleft Elige la estructura más adecuada para destacar el elemento indicado. 1. Destacar *climate finance*: *It was climate finance that / Climate finance it was that dominated the summit.* 2. Destacar la necesidad de regulación: *What the planet needs is / That the planet needs is enforceable regulation.* 3. Destacar la región: *It was in the border region that / In the border region it was that the shortage became severe.*
Ver solución 1. **It was climate finance that dominated the summit.** 2. **What the planet needs is enforceable regulation.** 3. **It was in the border region that the shortage became severe.**
### Ejercicio 5 — As for y with regard to Completa con la expresión adecuada. 1. ___ migration, the report recommends regional coordination. 2. ___ debt relief, the proposal remains under discussion. 3. ___ the refugees, their immediate safety must remain the priority.
Ver solución Son posibles **with regard to** y **as for** en los tres casos, con diferencias leves de registro. *With regard to* es más formal; *as for* introduce un cambio o delimitación de tema más marcado.
### Ejercicio 6 — Contraste Elige **whereas, despite, by contrast** o **conversely**. 1. ___ developed nations have stabilised inflation, emerging economies face debt distress. 2. ___ economic growth, inequality widened. 3. The first region improved access. ___, the second saw little change. 4. Lower rates may support borrowers; ___, they can reduce returns for savers.
Ver solución 1. **Whereas**; 2. **Despite**; 3. **By contrast**; 4. **conversely**. *Whereas* introduce una cláusula; *despite* un grupo nominal; los adverbios enlazan dos resultados contrastados.
### Ejercicio 7 — Corrige la concesión Corrige estas frases. 1. *Despite the economy grew, inequality widened.* 2. *Whereas developed nations stabilised, but emerging markets struggled.* 3. *The policy was expensive, however it improved access.*
Ver solución 1. **Although the economy grew, inequality widened** o **Despite economic growth, inequality widened.** 2. **Whereas developed nations stabilised, emerging markets struggled.** 3. **The policy was expensive; however, it improved access.**
### Ejercicio 8 — Especulación presente Elige **might well, could conceivably, is likely to** o **is unlikely to**. 1. Without funding, the programme ___ fail. 2. A negotiated settlement ___ be reached this year, although several obstacles remain. 3. Prices ___ rise if humanitarian access is restricted. 4. The measure ___ solve the underlying cause on its own.
Ver solución 1. **might well**; 2. **could conceivably**; 3. **are likely to**; 4. **is unlikely to**. Cada expresión gradúa la hipótesis de forma distinta.
### Ejercicio 9 — Especulación pasada Completa con el modal perfecto correcto. 1. The negotiators ___ ___ ___ (underestimate) public opposition. 2. The delay ___ ___ ___ (result) from a shortage of fuel. 3. The figures ___ ___ ___ (manipulate). 4. The agreement ___ ___ ___ (address) every concern.
Ver solución 1. **may/might have underestimated**. 2. **could have resulted**. 3. **may/might/could have been manipulated**. 4. **can’t have addressed** si las pruebas muestran que quedan muchas preocupaciones; **might not have addressed** si solo se plantea como posibilidad.
### Ejercicio 10 — Vocabulario global Completa con **ceasefire, displacement, accountability, debt relief** o **humanitarian access**. 1. The parties negotiated a temporary ___ . 2. The conflict caused mass ___ across the region. 3. Aid agencies need secure ___ to reach civilians. 4. The report calls for greater governmental ___ . 5. Several countries requested urgent ___ .
Ver solución 1. **ceasefire**; 2. **displacement**; 3. **humanitarian access**; 4. **accountability**; 5. **debt relief**.
### Ejercicio 11 — Reading Lee el texto y responde. > Rarely has a climate summit produced such a sharp contrast between public ambition and financial commitments. Whereas wealthy states have announced ambitious emissions targets, several emerging economies continue to face debt distress and limited access to climate finance. Only after a new funding mechanism was proposed did negotiators begin to discuss implementation in detail. The mechanism might well improve adaptation capacity, but it is unlikely to succeed unless funding is predictable and local institutions are involved. As for vulnerable communities, the agreement states that their participation must be protected at every stage. 1. What contrast does the text identify? 2. When did negotiators discuss implementation in detail? 3. What might the mechanism improve? 4. What conditions are necessary for success? 5. What does the agreement say about vulnerable communities?
Ver solución 1. **There is a contrast between wealthy states’ public ambition and the financial commitments available to emerging economies.** 2. **Only after a new funding mechanism was proposed.** 3. **It might improve adaptation capacity.** 4. **Funding must be predictable and local institutions must be involved.** 5. **Their participation must be protected at every stage.**
### Ejercicio 12 — Listening guiado Guion: “Under no circumstances should the humanitarian corridor be treated as permanent. The agreement could conceivably hold for several weeks, but it might well collapse if aid deliveries are delayed. By contrast, local ceasefires have tended to last longer when community leaders are involved. Only then can trust develop between the parties.” Identifica una inversión negativa, dos expresiones de especulación y un conector de contraste.
Ver solución Inversión negativa: **Under no circumstances should the humanitarian corridor be treated as permanent.** Especulación: **could conceivably hold** y **might well collapse**. Contraste: **By contrast**. La última frase usa inversión con *only then*: **Only then can trust develop**.
### Ejercicio 13 — Reformulación Reescribe con un registro más académico: *The sanctions will fix the crisis, but they may make things worse.*
Modelo **The sanctions are unlikely to address the underlying cause on their own; conversely, they might well intensify economic pressure on vulnerable populations.** La reformulación evita una promesa absoluta, usa una colocación precisa y añade un contraste lógico.
### Ejercicio 14 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **Should international organisations impose conditions on humanitarian aid?** Incluye una inversión, dos conectores de contraste y tres expresiones de especulación.
Modelo It is often argued that aid should be conditional on improvements in governance. However, such conditions may delay assistance when vulnerable populations are already facing food insecurity. Only when accountability mechanisms are transparent can conditionality be evaluated fairly. Whereas some donors might well consider strict requirements necessary, local organisations could conceivably view them as an obstacle to humanitarian access. By contrast, unrestricted funding is likely to reach communities more quickly, although it may not guarantee responsible implementation. Under no circumstances should civilians lose access to emergency support because political negotiations have stalled. International agencies should therefore distinguish between conditions designed to protect public resources and requirements that merely express donor preferences. A carefully monitored compromise might provide funding immediately while requiring public reporting, independent audits and community participation. Such a system is unlikely to satisfy every actor, but it could balance speed, accountability and local ownership more effectively than a single inflexible rule.
### Ejercicio 15 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre un problema global. Usa **whereas**, **by contrast**, **might well**, **could conceivably** y **as for**.
Pista y modelo **Whereas some countries can invest in climate adaptation, others face debt distress. By contrast, communities with strong local institutions might well respond more effectively to extreme weather. A regional funding mechanism could conceivably reduce the disparity. As for vulnerable families, their immediate access to food and shelter must remain the priority.**
### Ejercicio 16 — Traducción controlada Traduce al inglés. 1. Raramente ha sido tan difícil negociar un alto el fuego. 2. No fue hasta que se firmó el tratado cuando se mantuvo la tregua. 3. El acuerdo podría fracasar si no se garantiza el acceso humanitario.
Ver solución 1. **Rarely has it been so difficult to negotiate a ceasefire.** 2. **Not until the treaty was signed did the ceasefire hold.** 3. **The agreement could fail if humanitarian access is not guaranteed.**
### Ejercicio 17 — Corrección avanzada Corrige el párrafo. > Rarely governments have agreed on climate finance. Despite the proposal was ambitious, it did not address debt distress; however several states supported it. The mechanism could conceivably will improve adaptation, but under no circumstances local communities should be excluded.
Ver solución **Rarely have governments agreed on climate finance. Although the proposal was ambitious, it did not address debt distress; however, several states supported it. The mechanism could conceivably improve adaptation, but under no circumstances should local communities be excluded.** Se corrige la inversión tras *rarely*, la concesión con *although*, la puntuación de *however*, la ausencia de *will* después de *could* y la inversión tras *under no circumstances*.
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > ___ only after the corridor reopened ___ aid reach the displaced population. ___ contrast, the rural route remains unsafe, ___ local leaders have requested additional monitoring. A negotiated settlement ___ well be possible, but it is ___ to address the underlying dispute without sustained diplomacy.
Ver solución **Only; did; By; whereas/while; might; unlikely.** Una versión completa es: **Only after the corridor reopened did aid reach the displaced population. By contrast, the rural route remains unsafe, whereas local leaders have requested additional monitoring. A negotiated settlement might well be possible, but it is unlikely to address the underlying dispute without sustained diplomacy.**
### Ejercicio 19 — Integración final Reescribe el argumento en un solo párrafo formal. Debes incluir una inversión con **rarely**, una comparación con **whereas**, un resultado con **therefore** o **consequently** y una hipótesis con **might well**. > International agreements rarely include effective enforcement. Some governments make ambitious promises, but local institutions receive little funding. A rapid improvement is possible, but it is not certain.
Ver solución **Rarely do international agreements include effective enforcement. Whereas some governments make ambitious promises, local institutions receive little funding; consequently, implementation remains uneven. A rapid improvement might well be possible if reliable funding were secured, although it cannot be guaranteed.** La primera frase usa inversión porque *rarely* aparece al principio. *Whereas* contrasta dos realidades completas, *consequently* introduce el resultado y *might well* presenta una posibilidad razonable sin convertirla en predicción segura.
## Resumen de la unidad Usa **fronting** para poner en primer plano un tema o una circunstancia. Después de adverbiales negativos como **never, rarely, seldom, not only, not until** y expresiones como **under no circumstances**, invierte el auxiliar y el sujeto. Si no hay auxiliar, añade **do, does o did**. Usa clefts como **it was X that...** y pseudo-clefts como **what... is...** para enfocar una idea concreta. Usa **whereas, while, by contrast, conversely** e **in contrast** para comparar resultados sin convertir el análisis en una oposición simplista. Recuerda que **despite** necesita un nombre o gerundio, mientras que **although** introduce una cláusula. Finalmente, el lenguaje especulativo debe reflejar la evidencia. **Might well** expresa una posibilidad razonable, **could conceivably** una posibilidad imaginable, **be likely to** una probabilidad y **be unlikely to** una baja probabilidad. Cuando combines esas formas con colocaciones como *secure humanitarian access*, *ease debt distress* y *reach a negotiated settlement*, podrás hablar de problemas globales con énfasis, equilibrio y rigor propios del nivel C1.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es distancing language?
faqs.answer: Es el lenguaje que permite atribuir o presentar información con distancia, usando allegedly, reportedly, supposedly, it is claimed o estructuras como is said to.

faqs.question: ¿Para qué sirven las construcciones impersonales?
faqs.answer: Permiten informar de una opinión, rumor o evidencia sin centrar la oración en una fuente concreta, algo frecuente en noticias y textos académicos.

faqs.question: ¿Qué es una advanced cleft?
faqs.answer: Es una estructura escindida que reorganiza la oración para destacar una causa, persona, momento o información concreta, como What surprised viewers was the speed of the correction.

faqs.question: ¿La Unidad 9 incluye ejercicios resueltos?
faqs.answer: Sí. Incluye práctica de distancing, impersonales, clefts, vocabulario, reading, listening, writing y speaking con respuestas y modelos.

content:
# Unidad 9 C1: distancing, medios y clefts avanzadas En periodismo, comunicación institucional y análisis académico, no siempre podemos presentar una información como un hecho confirmado. A veces existe una fuente anónima, una declaración interesada, un rumor o una interpretación que todavía debe comprobarse. La Unidad 9 C1 enseña a manejar esa distancia mediante **distancing language**, construcciones impersonales y **cleft sentences** avanzadas. Compara estas frases: - *The footage was staged.* - *It is alleged that the footage was staged.* - *The footage is alleged to have been staged.* - *The footage, which was circulated online, is supposedly authentic.* La primera afirma directamente. Las otras atribuyen, distancian o marcan la información como no confirmada. Esa diferencia es esencial: un texto responsable debe dejar claro qué se ha observado, qué se ha dicho y qué se infiere. Las clefts añaden otra herramienta. En lugar de presentar todos los elementos con el mismo peso, podemos decir: - *It was the timing that raised questions.* - *What raised questions was the timing.* - *The timing was what raised questions.* El hecho básico es parecido, pero cambia el foco. En una noticia o un ensayo, controlar ese foco ayuda a guiar al lector hacia la información más relevante. > **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 9 C1](/curso-c1/unit-9)
> **Unidad anterior:** [Unidad 8 C1: fronting y especulación](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-8-fronting-contraste-global)
> **Siguiente unidad:** [Unidad 10 C1: repaso del módulo](/blog/curso-c1/unidad-48-consolidacion-problemas-globales)
> **Curso completo:** [Inglés C1](/blog/metodos/ingles-c1) ## Parte I — Teoría ### 1. La idea de distancia La distancia lingüística separa al escritor de una afirmación. No significa necesariamente que la información sea falsa; indica que la fuente, la evidencia o el grado de confirmación deben tenerse en cuenta. - **Hecho presentado como confirmado:** *The station corrected the report.* - **Información atribuida:** *The station is reported to have corrected the report.* - **Rumor o afirmación no verificada:** *The station supposedly corrected the report.* - **Interpretación cautelosa:** *The correction appears to have followed public pressure.* En la práctica, un periodista puede distinguir entre lo que sabe directamente y lo que procede de terceros. Un investigador puede distinguir entre el resultado medido y la explicación propuesta. El inglés C1 ofrece recursos precisos para esas diferencias. ### 2. Allegedly, reportedly y supposedly Estos adverbios se colocan normalmente antes del verbo principal o después de un auxiliar: - *The company allegedly manipulated the figures.* - *The company is allegedly manipulating the figures.* - *The company has reportedly withdrawn the advertisement.* - *The presenter supposedly knew about the error.* **Allegedly** suele asociarse con una acusación que no ha sido probada, especialmente en contextos legales o periodísticos. **Reportedly** indica que una fuente o varios medios han informado de algo, sin que el escritor lo confirme personalmente. **Supposedly** puede significar “supuestamente” y a veces transmite escepticismo o ironía. - *The minister allegedly accepted gifts.* Es una acusación atribuida. - *The minister reportedly accepted gifts.* Los medios han informado de ello. - *The minister supposedly accepted gifts.* Se presenta como una versión cuestionable o no comprobada. No trates estos adverbios como sinónimos perfectos. La elección comunica actitud. Si quieres evitar una insinuación excesivamente negativa, puedes usar *according to the report*, *the available evidence suggests* o *the claim remains unverified*. ### 3. Impersonal passive reporting Una estructura muy frecuente es: > **It + be + past participle + that-clause** - *It is alleged that the footage was staged.* - *It is believed that the account was hacked.* - *It has been reported that several witnesses were contacted.* - *It is widely assumed that the headline was misleading.* Los verbos más habituales son **say, believe, think, report, claim, allege, assume, expect, understand, know**. El adverbio puede indicar la extensión o la fuente: *widely, generally, officially, reportedly, privately*. El tiempo del auxiliar sitúa la atribución: - *It is believed that the policy is changing.* - *It was believed that the policy would change.* - *It has been claimed that the figures were altered.* - *It had been reported that the station would close.* La estructura impersonal permite evitar una fuente vaga como *people say*. No obstante, si la fuente es importante, nómbrala: *The regulator stated that...* es más informativo que *It was stated that...*. ### 4. Estructura personal con infinitivo La misma información puede expresarse con un sujeto enfocado y **be + participle + to-infinitive**: > **Subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive** - *The dossier is said to contain fabricated evidence.* - *The presenter is believed to have been misquoted.* - *The staff are reported to have been briefed with a doctored translation.* - *The CEO is alleged to have concealed the conflict of interest.* Usa **to + infinitive** cuando la acción es simultánea o posterior al verbo de reporte: - *The outlet is believed to be expanding.* - *The outlet is expected to publish a correction.* Usa **to have + past participle** para una acción anterior: - *The outlet is believed to have published a misleading headline.* - *The outlet is reported to have removed the article.* Para una situación continua anterior aparece **to have been + -ing**: - *The team is thought to have been monitoring the account.* La transformación entre las dos estructuras es mecánica: - *It is believed that the CEO concealed the conflict.* - *The CEO is believed to have concealed the conflict.* No mezcles las formas: *It is believed the CEO to have concealed...* no es el patrón estándar. Elige *it + that-clause* o *subject + passive reporting + infinitive*. ### 5. There is thought to be Las construcciones impersonales también pueden combinarse con **there**: - *There is thought to be widespread unease about synthetic media.* - *There are believed to be several errors in the translation.* - *There appears to be little consensus on how to label AI-generated images.* La concordancia depende del sustantivo posterior: *there is thought to be a problem*, pero *there are thought to be several problems*. En estilo periodístico, estas formas permiten presentar la existencia de algo sin atribuir la opinión a una persona concreta. Con *appear* es posible usar una construcción más directa: - *There appears to be a conflict of interest.* - *There appear to be three conflicting accounts.* No digas *there is appearing to be* en este uso. *Appear* funciona normalmente en simple. ### 6. Distancing con so-called y what is described as **So-called** puede ser neutral o crítico. Presenta una etiqueta que quizá no aceptamos completamente: - *The so-called reform failed to change the ownership structure.* - *The so-called experts had no relevant qualifications.* **What is described as**, **what has been presented as** y **what was billed as** atribuyen una caracterización: - *What was described as a technical update became a major redesign.* - *The event, billed as a public debate, allowed no questions.* - *The campaign has been presented as a transparency measure.* Estas estructuras crean distancia entre el escritor y la etiqueta. Si el tono debe ser neutral, puedes usar *the measure described by the ministry as...*. Si quieres señalar discrepancia, *so-called* lo hace de forma más evidente. ### 7. Impersonal constructions en medios Además de la pasiva de reporte, aparecen estructuras con **one, people, it** y **there**: - *One tends to assume that information is neutral.* - *People are known to share headlines without reading them.* - *It is often difficult to distinguish satire from misinformation.* - *There is little evidence to support the claim.* **One** es formal y generalizador, aunque puede sonar distante o rígido. **People** es más natural, pero menos impersonal. **It is** permite presentar una evaluación; **there is/are** presenta existencia o ausencia de evidencia. Para no generalizar demasiado, usa *tend to, are likely to, may, can sometimes*: - *Readers may interpret a headline differently depending on context.* - *Users tend to share emotionally striking content.* ### 8. Cleft sentences para el foco Una cleft divide una oración en dos partes para destacar un elemento: > **It is/was + focus + that/who + clause** - *It was the timing that raised questions.* - *It was the editor who approved the headline.* - *It is the lack of context that makes the clip misleading.* - *It was after the correction that the story gained attention.* La parte focalizada puede ser una persona, objeto, tiempo, lugar o causa. **Who** se usa habitualmente con personas; **that** puede usarse con objetos y situaciones. En una cleft negativa o interrogativa, el verbo conserva la forma correspondiente: - *Was it the source that the editor had failed to check?* - *It was not the headline that caused the dispute.* La cleft no añade información nueva por sí sola. Cambia la distribución del énfasis y puede contrastar un elemento con otros. ### 9. What-clefts y pseudo-clefts La estructura **what-cleft** es: > **What + clause + be + focus** - *What surprised viewers was the speed of the correction.* - *What the investigation revealed was a pattern of undisclosed sponsorship.* - *What matters is whether the evidence can be independently verified.* - *What the public wants to know is who approved the campaign.* El verbo dentro de la *what-clause* sigue el orden declarativo: *what the investigation revealed*, no *what did the investigation reveal*. La parte posterior identifica el foco. También es posible invertir el orden: - *The speed of the correction was what surprised viewers.* - *Who approved the campaign is what the public wants to know.* La versión con *what* al principio suele presentar una pregunta implícita o un tema que se desarrolla. Es útil para organizar una explicación: *What the report does not establish is whether the error was deliberate.* ### 10. The reason why y the thing that Otras clefts avanzadas son: - *The reason why the story spread is that it confirmed existing fears.* - *The reason the story spread was its emotional appeal.* - *The thing that concerned viewers was the absence of a correction.* - *The point that the editor was making was that context matters.* En muchos casos, *the reason why* es correcto, aunque *the reason* puede ser más conciso. Evita mezclar dos estructuras: *The reason why the story spread was because...* aparece en el habla, pero en escritura formal suele preferirse *The reason why the story spread was that...*. ### 11. Clefts frente a inversión y fronting Estas tres técnicas cambian el foco de maneras distintas: - **Cleft:** *It was the lack of context that misled readers.* Divide la oración y destaca la causa. - **What-cleft:** *What misled readers was the lack of context.* Presenta una relación “lo que... fue...”. - **Fronting:** *The lack of context, the editor failed to address.* Coloca el objeto al inicio, con una estructura marcada. La cleft suele ser la opción más clara para un ensayo o una presentación. El fronting puede sonar literario o enfático y requiere más control. No uses una técnica marcada simplemente para parecer avanzado: el foco debe mejorar la comunicación. ### 12. Vocabulario de media and information - **dossier:** expediente o conjunto de documentos. - **footage:** imágenes grabadas, normalmente de vídeo. - **eyewitness:** testigo presencial. - **doctored translation:** traducción manipulada. - **chyron:** texto superpuesto en pantalla. - **synthetic media:** contenido generado o alterado digitalmente. - **misinformation:** información falsa o inexacta sin prueba de intención. - **disinformation:** información falsa difundida deliberadamente. - **source verification:** comprobación de una fuente. - **editorial oversight:** supervisión editorial. - **conflict of interest:** conflicto de intereses. - **undisclosed sponsorship:** patrocinio no revelado. - **media literacy:** alfabetización mediática. - **public broadcaster:** radiodifusor público. - **regulatory body:** organismo regulador. - **correction:** rectificación. - **retraction:** retirada formal de un artículo o afirmación. - **public backlash:** reacción pública negativa. - **clickbait:** contenido diseñado para atraer clics mediante titulares llamativos. - **fact-checking:** verificación de hechos. Colocaciones importantes son **verify a source**, **publish a correction**, **issue a retraction**, **distort the context**, **fabricate evidence**, **broadcast footage**, **circulate a claim**, **disclose sponsorship**, **raise questions**, **trigger a backlash**, **challenge a narrative**, **assess credibility** y **combat disinformation**. ### 13. Cómo escribir de forma responsable Un texto de medios debe distinguir tres capas: 1. **Observación:** *The video was uploaded at 9:14.* 2. **Atribución:** *The account is reported to have removed it later.* 3. **Interpretación:** *The timing may suggest an attempt to limit scrutiny.* No conviertas la tercera capa en la primera. *The timing proves censorship* es mucho más fuerte que la evidencia descrita. Una redacción responsable puede decir: *The timing appears to have raised questions, although it does not establish deliberate censorship.* También debes distinguir entre **alleged**, que marca una acusación, y **confirmed**, que afirma que una autoridad o investigación ha verificado algo. *The alleged error* y *the confirmed error* no tienen la misma carga. Si una persona podría resultar dañada por una afirmación, atribuye la información y especifica su estado. ### 14. Errores frecuentes - *The dossier is said having been compiled.* → **The dossier is said to have been compiled.** - *It is alleged the footage to be staged.* → **It is alleged that the footage was staged.** - *There are thought to be a problem.* → **There is thought to be a problem.** - *Rarely the source is verified.* → Si se busca inversión: **Rarely is the source verified.** - *What did the report reveal was...* → **What the report revealed was...** - *It was the editor which approved the headline.* → **It was the editor who approved the headline.** - *The reason why it spread was because it was emotional.* → En registro formal: **The reason why it spread was that it was emotional.** - *The so-called verified account* cuando solo quieres informar de su etiqueta oficial. → **The account described as verified** puede ser más neutral. ## Parte II — Ejercicios con soluciones ### Ejercicio 1 — Passive reporting Completa con **is alleged to have been**, **is alleged having been** o **alleged to be**. 1. The footage ___ staged before the leak. 2. The presenter ___ misquoted in the headline. 3. The account is ___ controlled by an overseas company.
Ver solución 1. **is alleged to have been** — la puesta en escena es anterior a la atribución. 2. **is alleged to have been** — *misquoted* ocurrió antes del momento actual. 3. **alleged to be** — después de *is* ya aparece la estructura personal; la frase completa es **The account is alleged to be controlled...**.
### Ejercicio 2 — Impersonal o personal Transforma. 1. It is believed that the dossier contains fabricated evidence. 2. It was reported that the staff had been briefed with a doctored translation. 3. It is thought that there is little consensus about the label.
Ver solución 1. **The dossier is believed to contain fabricated evidence.** 2. **The staff were reported to have been briefed with a doctored translation.** 3. **There is thought to be little consensus about the label.**
### Ejercicio 3 — Tiempo del infinitivo Elige **to be**, **to have been** o **to have + participle**. 1. The outlet is believed ___ expanding rapidly. 2. The outlet is believed ___ removed the article. 3. The outlet is believed ___ under pressure before the correction.
Ver solución 1. **to be** — situación simultánea o en desarrollo. 2. **to have removed** — acción anterior. 3. **to have been** — estado anterior.
### Ejercicio 4 — Adverbios de distancia Completa con **allegedly, reportedly, supposedly** o **according to the report**. 1. The minister ___ accepted gifts from the company. 2. The broadcaster has ___ withdrawn the programme. 3. The ___ independent review was funded by the organisation itself. 4. ___, several witnesses were contacted before publication.
Ver solución 1. **allegedly** — acusación no probada. 2. **reportedly** — información difundida por medios o fuentes. 3. **supposedly** — etiqueta que el escritor mira con escepticismo. 4. **According to the report** — atribución explícita a una fuente documental.
### Ejercicio 5 — There is/are thought to be Completa con la concordancia correcta. 1. There ___ thought to be a conflict of interest. 2. There ___ believed to be several errors in the translation. 3. There ___ appears to be little evidence for the claim. 4. There ___ appear to be three conflicting accounts.
Ver solución 1. **is**; 2. **are**; 3. **appears**; 4. **appear**. El verbo concuerda con el sustantivo posterior en las estructuras con *there*.
### Ejercicio 6 — It-clefts Reescribe destacando el elemento entre paréntesis. 1. The timing raised questions. (the timing) 2. The editor approved the headline. (the editor) 3. The story gained attention after the correction. (after the correction) 4. The lack of context made the clip misleading. (the lack of context)
Ver solución 1. **It was the timing that raised questions.** 2. **It was the editor who approved the headline.** 3. **It was after the correction that the story gained attention.** 4. **It was the lack of context that made the clip misleading.**
### Ejercicio 7 — What-clefts Completa con **What** y el orden correcto. 1. ___ surprised viewers ___ the speed of the correction. 2. ___ the investigation revealed ___ a pattern of undisclosed sponsorship. 3. ___ matters ___ whether the evidence can be independently verified.
Ver solución 1. **What surprised viewers was**. 2. **What the investigation revealed was**. 3. **What matters is**. La cláusula con *what* mantiene el orden declarativo: *what the investigation revealed*, no *what did the investigation reveal*.
### Ejercicio 8 — Distancing y tono Explica qué cambia en el tono. 1. *The footage was staged.* 2. *The footage is alleged to have been staged.* 3. *The footage may have been staged.* 4. *The footage appears to have been staged.*
Ver solución 1. Presenta la afirmación como hecho. 2. Atribuye una acusación a una fuente o contexto externo. 3. Presenta una posibilidad abierta. 4. Presenta una interpretación basada en indicios, con distancia moderada.
### Ejercicio 9 — Vocabulario Completa con **misinformation, disinformation, retraction, clickbait** o **media literacy**. 1. Deliberately false content designed to influence voters is ___ . 2. Inaccurate content shared without clear intent is ___ . 3. The journal issued a formal ___ after discovering fabricated evidence. 4. A sensational headline designed to attract clicks is ___ . 5. The ability to evaluate sources is part of ___ .
Ver solución 1. **disinformation**; 2. **misinformation**; 3. **retraction**; 4. **clickbait**; 5. **media literacy**.
### Ejercicio 10 — Reading Lee y responde. > The account was reportedly created shortly before the video circulated widely. It is alleged to have used footage from an unrelated event, although the original source has not yet been verified. What surprised viewers was not the speed of the upload but the absence of an immediate correction. There appears to be little consensus about whether the error resulted from editorial oversight or deliberate disinformation. The broadcaster has issued a statement and is believed to be conducting an internal review. As for the audience, media-literacy groups have warned users not to share the clip without checking its context. 1. When was the account reportedly created? 2. What is alleged about the footage? 3. What surprised viewers? 4. What remains uncertain? 5. What has the broadcaster done?
Ver solución 1. **Shortly before the video circulated widely.** 2. **It is alleged to have come from an unrelated event.** 3. **The absence of an immediate correction.** 4. **Whether the error resulted from editorial oversight or deliberate disinformation.** 5. **It has issued a statement and is believed to be conducting an internal review.**
### Ejercicio 11 — Listening guiado Guion: “The campaign was billed as a public debate, but it supposedly allowed no questions from the audience. It is widely believed that the format was designed to protect the speakers from scrutiny. What the organisers have not explained is why the transcript was published three days late. There are thought to be several discrepancies between the recording and the written version.” Identifica una expresión de distancia, una impersonal, una what-cleft y una construcción con *there*.
Ver solución Distancia: **supposedly** o **was billed as**. Impersonal: **It is widely believed that...**. What-cleft: **What the organisers have not explained is...**. There-construction: **There are thought to be several discrepancies...**.
### Ejercicio 12 — Corrección gramatical Corrige estas frases. 1. *It is alleged the video to be manipulated.* 2. *The CEO is believed having concealed the conflict.* 3. *What did the investigation reveal was a sponsorship pattern.* 4. *It was the reporter which found the discrepancy.*
Ver solución 1. **It is alleged that the video was manipulated.** 2. **The CEO is believed to have concealed the conflict.** 3. **What the investigation revealed was a sponsorship pattern.** 4. **It was the reporter who found the discrepancy.**
### Ejercicio 13 — Neutraliza la acusación Reescribe con un registro periodístico responsable: *The broadcaster deliberately hid the error.*
Modelo **The broadcaster is alleged to have withheld information about the error, although the available evidence does not establish whether the omission was deliberate.** La versión atribuye la acusación y añade el límite de la evidencia.
### Ejercicio 14 — Writing Escribe 150–180 palabras sobre: **How should news organisations handle an unverified viral video?** Incluye una impersonal passive, una estructura personal con infinitivo perfecto, una cleft y tres términos de medios.
Modelo When an unverified video goes viral, it is essential that news organisations distinguish evidence from speculation. The footage may be authentic, but it may also have been taken out of context or digitally altered. It is often reported that the first account to share a clip has already disappeared; however, this does not prove who created the material. The account is sometimes believed to have circulated the video for political purposes, although that interpretation requires independent verification. What matters most is whether the source, date and location can be confirmed. Editors should therefore delay publication until they have conducted source verification and checked the footage against reliable records. If an error occurs, the organisation should issue a visible correction rather than quietly changing the headline. Media literacy also matters: readers need enough context to recognise clickbait and distinguish misinformation from deliberate disinformation. A cautious process may reduce speed, but it protects editorial credibility and public trust.
### Ejercicio 15 — Speaking Habla durante un minuto sobre una noticia controvertida. Usa **allegedly**, **reportedly**, **what matters is** y una cleft con *who* o *that*.
Pista y modelo **The company allegedly funded the campaign, although the payment was reportedly made through an intermediary. What matters is whether the documents can be verified. It was the lack of disclosure that raised questions, rather than the campaign’s content itself. The organisation may have breached the rules, but the available evidence is not yet conclusive.**
### Ejercicio 16 — Traducción controlada Traduce al inglés. 1. Se cree que el expediente contiene pruebas fabricadas. 2. Lo que sorprendió a los espectadores fue la rapidez de la rectificación. 3. Hay varios errores en la traducción, según se informa.
Ver solución 1. **The dossier is believed to contain fabricated evidence.** 2. **What surprised viewers was the speed of the correction.** 3. **There are reportedly several errors in the translation.** También: **There are said to be several errors in the translation.**
### Ejercicio 17 — Edición avanzada Mejora este párrafo para que sea formal, claro y prudente: > The so-called independent report proves that the broadcaster lied. The reporter which wrote it is believed having received money. What did the report show was a big conflict.
Modelo **The report, described as independent, claims that the broadcaster misrepresented several facts. The reporter who wrote it is alleged to have received undisclosed funding. What the report appears to show is a significant conflict of interest, although further verification is required.** Se evita presentar las acusaciones como hechos confirmados, se corrigen *which* y el infinitivo, y se forma correctamente la what-cleft.
### Ejercicio 18 — Mini-test final Completa el texto. > The footage ___ ___ ___ have been edited before publication. ___ is alleged that the original file was shorter. ___ surprised investigators was the unexplained delay in the correction. There ___ thought to be several discrepancies, ___ the broadcaster maintains that the error was accidental.
Ver solución **is alleged to; It; What; are; although.** La versión completa es: **The footage is alleged to have been edited before publication. It is alleged that the original file was shorter. What surprised investigators was the unexplained delay in the correction. There are thought to be several discrepancies, although the broadcaster maintains that the error was accidental.**
## Resumen de la unidad Usa **allegedly, reportedly, supposedly, it is claimed** y las estructuras con **is said/believed/reported to** para marcar que una información procede de una fuente o no está completamente confirmada. Si la acción es anterior, utiliza **to have + participio**; si la situación es simultánea, usa **to be** o **to be + -ing**. Las construcciones con **there is/are thought to be** presentan la existencia de una opinión, problema o discrepancia. Las clefts con **it was X that/who** y **what... was...** reorganizan el foco y ayudan a responder preguntas implícitas: qué ocurrió, quién lo hizo, cuándo sucedió o qué aspecto resulta relevante. En medios e información, la gramática debe ir unida a la responsabilidad. Distingue hechos, atribuciones e interpretaciones; no conviertas una alegación en una certeza. Cuando combines esa precisión con colocaciones como *verify a source*, *issue a correction*, *assess credibility* y *combat disinformation*, podrás escribir textos C1 claros, matizados y fiables.

content:
Este artículo reúne **los ejercicios de la Unidad 41 del curso A1** (*At the Airport*) con **soluciones comentadas**. Corresponde a las lecciones del curso: gramática, vocabulario, reading, listening y writing.

> **Guía teórica:** [At the Airport A1](/blog/curso-a1/unidad-41-aeropuerto-must-should)  
> **Practica en el curso:** [Unidad 41 — At the Airport](/curso-a1/unit-41)

Haz cada bloque **sin mirar** la solución. Luego comprueba y lee la explicación.

![Must / should at the airport](/blog/curso-a1/unit-41/a1-unit41-must-should.png)

**Contenido de la unidad:**
1. [Lección 1 — Gramática: must / should](#leccion-1--gramatica-must--should)
2. [Lección 2 — Vocabulario: aeropuerto](#leccion-2--vocabulario-aeropuerto)
3. [Lección 3 — Reading: At the airport](#leccion-3--reading-at-the-airport)
4. [Lección 4 — Listening: Check-in](#leccion-4--listening-check-in)
5. [Lección 5 — Writing: Airport tips](#leccion-5--writing-airport-tips)

---

## Lección 1 — Gramática: must / should

**Objetivo:** *must* (obligación) y *should* (consejo) en el aeropuerto.

### Ejercicios 1–5 — Completa

1. You ____ show your passport at check-in. → *must / should / canning*  
2. You ____ go to the gate early. → *should / musts / going*  
3. You ____ have your ticket. → *must / shoulding / are*  
4. You ____ arrive early for your flight. → *should / musts / do*  
5. You ____ show your boarding pass. → *must / shoulds / am*

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

1. **must** — obligación.  
2. **should** — consejo.  
3. **must**  
4. **should**  
5. **must**

</details>

### Ejercicios 6–10 — Elige

6. *Must* shows ____. → a) obligation · b) only a wish · c) past tense  
7. *Should* shows ____. → a) advice or recommendation · b) only past · c) a sport  
8. After *must* / *should* we use ____. → a) base verb · b) -ing only · c) past participle only  
9. You ____ your passport. → a) must show · b) must showing · c) musts show  
10. Check-in is ____. → a) where you get your boarding pass · b) the plane seat · c) the hotel

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

6. **a) obligation**  
7. **a) advice or recommendation**  
8. **a) base verb**  
9. **a) must show**  
10. **a) where you get your boarding pass**

</details>

### Ejercicios 11–13 — Ordena

11. You / must / show / your / passport / at check-in.  
12. Go / to / gate / number / ten.  
13. You / should / arrive / early / for / your / flight.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

11. You must show your passport at check-in.  
12. Go to gate number ten.  
13. You should arrive early for your flight.

</details>

### Ejercicios 14–15 — Verdadero o falso

14. *Must* + base verb: *You must show your passport.* → True / False  
15. *Should* gives advice: *You should go early.* → True / False

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

14. **True**  
15. **True**

</details>

---

## Lección 2 — Vocabulario: aeropuerto

**Objetivo:** *passport, ticket, check-in, boarding pass, gate, boarding, luggage, suitcase, flight*.

### Ejercicios 1–5 — Elige el significado

1. *Passport* = ____. → a) document for travel · b) a gate number · c) a suitcase only  
2. *Ticket* = ____. → a) document for the flight · b) only luggage · c) a gate  
3. *Check-in* = ____. → a) where you get your boarding pass · b) the plane seat · c) customs only  
4. *Gate* = ____. → a) where you board the plane · b) the hotel desk · c) a restaurant  
5. *Boarding* = ____. → a) getting on the plane · b) buying food · c) sleeping

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

1. **a) document for travel**  
2. **a) document for the flight**  
3. **a) where you get your boarding pass**  
4. **a) where you board the plane**  
5. **a) getting on the plane**

</details>

### Ejercicios 6–7 — Empareja

6. Empareja: passport / boarding pass / gate / luggage / flight → travel document · get at check-in · board the plane · bags · plane trip  
7. Empareja: ticket / check-in / boarding / suitcase / passport → for the flight · desk · get on the plane · luggage · show at the airport

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

6. **passport → travel document** · **boarding pass → get at check-in** · **gate → board the plane** · **luggage → bags** · **flight → plane trip**  
7. **ticket → for the flight** · **check-in → desk** · **boarding → get on the plane** · **suitcase → luggage** · **passport → show at the airport**

</details>

### Ejercicios 8–10 — Completa

8. You must show your ____. → *passport / passportsing / gate*  
9. Gate ____ ten. → *number / numbers / numbering*  
10. Have a good ____! → *flight / flightsing / gate*

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

8. **passport**  
9. **number**  
10. **flight**

</details>

### Ejercicios 11–13 — Definiciones

11. *Luggage* means ____. → a) bags you take when you travel · b) only a ticket · c) a gate  
12. A *boarding pass* is ____. → a) a document to get on the plane · b) a hotel key · c) a menu  
13. Where do you get your boarding pass? → a) At check-in. · b) On the plane seat only · c) At home never

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

11. **a) bags you take when you travel**  
12. **a) a document to get on the plane**  
13. **a) At check-in.**

</details>

### Ejercicios 14–15 — Verdadero o falso

14. You show your passport and ticket at check-in. → True / False  
15. The gate is where you board the plane. → True / False

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

14. **True**  
15. **True**

</details>

---

## Lección 3 — Reading: At the airport

**Objetivo:** leer un texto sobre el aeropuerto con *must* y *should*.

### Texto

<audio controls preload="none" src="/audio/blog/curso-a1/unit-41/reading-airport.mp3" title="🔊 Reading: At the airport"></audio>

> I am at the airport today. My flight is at ten o'clock. I must show my passport and my ticket at check-in. After that, I get my boarding pass. I should go to the gate early. Boarding starts at half past nine. I have one suitcase. My luggage is not heavy.

### Ejercicios 1–5 — Elige la respuesta correcta

1. Where is the writer? → a) At the airport. · b) At home. · c) At school.  
2. What time is the flight? → a) At ten o'clock. · b) At nine o'clock. · c) At midnight.  
3. What must the writer show? → a) Passport and ticket. · b) Only a book. · c) Only food.  
4. Where does the writer show them? → a) At check-in. · b) At the hotel. · c) At school.  
5. When does boarding start? → a) At half past nine. · b) At ten. · c) At noon.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

1. **a) At the airport.**  
2. **a) At ten o'clock.**  
3. **a) Passport and ticket.**  
4. **a) At check-in.**  
5. **a) At half past nine.**

</details>

### Ejercicios 6–10 — Comprensión

6. How many suitcases does the writer have? → a) One. · b) Five. · c) Zero.  
7. Is the luggage heavy? → a) No. · b) Yes. · c) The text doesn't say.  
8. The writer should go to the gate ____. → a) Early. · b) Late. · c) Never.  
9. Where do you get the boarding pass? → a) Check-in. · b) The plane seat. · c) The park.  
10. A boarding pass is ____. → a) A document to board the plane. · b) A suitcase. · c) A gate number only.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

6. **a) One.**  
7. **a) No.**  
8. **a) Early.**  
9. **a) Check-in.**  
10. **a) A document to board the plane.**

</details>

### Ejercicios 11–15 — Detalles

11. The text is about ____. → a) The airport and a flight. · b) Only food. · c) Only sports.  
12. *Must show* means ____. → a) An obligation to show something. · b) A wish only. · c) Past tense.  
13. The *gate* is ____. → a) The place where you board. · b) The hotel room. · c) The ticket price.  
14. *Luggage* means ____. → a) Bags and suitcases. · b) Only tickets. · c) Only gates.  
15. The main topic is ____. → a) What to do at the airport. · b) Cooking. · c) School subjects.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

11. **a) The airport and a flight.**  
12. **a) An obligation to show something.**  
13. **a) The place where you board.**  
14. **a) Bags and suitcases.**  
15. **a) What to do at the airport.**

</details>

---

## Lección 4 — Listening: Check-in

**Objetivo:** escuchar indicaciones en el aeropuerto.

### Audio y guion

<audio controls preload="none" src="/audio/blog/curso-a1/unit-41/listening-check-in.mp3" title="🔊 Listening: Check-in"></audio>

> **A:** Where is the check-in?  
> **B:** Over there. You must show your passport and ticket.  
> **A:** Thank you. What gate is the flight to London?  
> **B:** Gate twenty-two. You should go now; boarding starts in ten minutes.  
> **A:** I have my boarding pass.  
> **B:** Perfect. Have a good flight!

### Ejercicios 1–5 — Comprensión

1. A's first question is ____. → a) “Where is the check-in?” · b) “Where is the hotel?” · c) “What time is lunch?”  
2. What must A show? → a) Passport and ticket. · b) Only food. · c) Only a book.  
3. What gate is the London flight? → a) Gate twenty-two. · b) Gate two. · c) Gate ten.  
4. When does boarding start? → a) In ten minutes. · b) In one hour. · c) Tomorrow.  
5. Does A have a boarding pass? → a) Yes. · b) No. · c) The audio doesn't say.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

1. **a) “Where is the check-in?”**  
2. **a) Passport and ticket.**  
3. **a) Gate twenty-two.**  
4. **a) In ten minutes.**  
5. **a) Yes.**

</details>

### Ejercicios 6–10 — Detalles

6. B says A should ____. → a) Go now. · b) Wait three hours. · c) Go home.  
7. Where is check-in? → a) Over there. · b) Outside the city. · c) At school.  
8. “Have a good flight!” is ____. → a) A wish for a good trip. · b) A refusal. · c) A ticket.  
9. The dialogue is ____. → a) At the airport. · b) At home. · c) In a park.  
10. The flight is ____. → a) A plane to London. · b) A bus to London. · c) A train only.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

6. **a) Go now.**  
7. **a) Over there.**  
8. **a) A wish for a good trip.**  
9. **a) At the airport.**  
10. **a) A plane to London.**

</details>

### Ejercicios 11–15 — Forma

11. *Must* here shows ____. → a) An obligation. · b) Only a hobby. · c) Past simple.  
12. *Boarding* means ____. → a) Getting on the plane. · b) Buying lunch. · c) Sleeping.  
13. After the gate information, A says ____. → a) “Thank you.” · b) “Goodbye forever.” · c) “I refuse.”  
14. The *gate* is ____. → a) The place where you board. · b) The suitcase. · c) The passport.  
15. The dialogue gives ____. → a) Airport instructions. · b) Cooking recipes. · c) Sports scores.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

11. **a) An obligation.**  
12. **a) Getting on the plane.**  
13. **a) “Thank you.”**  
14. **a) The place where you board.**  
15. **a) Airport instructions.**

</details>

---

## Lección 5 — Writing: Airport tips

**Objetivo:** escribir instrucciones y tips con *must* / *should*.

### Ejercicios 1–5 — Completa

1. You ____ show your passport. → *must / shoulds / am*  
2. You ____ go to the gate early. → *should / musts / are*  
3. You ____ your ticket at check-in. → *must show / must showing / musts*  
4. Go ____ the gate now. → *to / for / at*  
5. You ____ have your boarding pass. → *must / shoulding / do*

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

1. **must**  
2. **should**  
3. **must show**  
4. **to**  
5. **must**

</details>

### Ejercicios 6–8 — Ordena

6. You / must / show / your / passport / at check-in.  
7. My / flight / is / at / ten o'clock.  
8. You / should / go / to / the / gate / early.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución</summary>

6. You must show your passport at check-in.  
7. My flight is at ten o'clock.  
8. You should go to the gate early.

</details>

### Ejercicios 9–15 — Escribe (modelos)

9. Escribe una obligación con *must* en el aeropuerto.  
10. Escribe un consejo con *should*.  
11. Dos frases: gate + hora del vuelo.  
12. Pregunta y respuesta: *Where is check-in?*  
13. Párrafo corto (3–4 frases) sobre check-in y gate.  
14. Dos tips: *must* + *should*.  
15. Lista: qué *must* / *should* llevar o hacer.

<details>
<summary>Ver solución (ejemplos)</summary>

9. You must show your passport at check-in.  
10. You should arrive early for your flight.  
11. My gate is number fifteen. My flight is at nine o'clock.  
12. Where is check-in? Over there.  
13. I must show my passport and ticket at check-in. Then I get my boarding pass. I should go to the gate early.  
14. You must show your passport. You should go to the gate now.  
15. I must have my passport and ticket. I should arrive early.

</details>

---

## Resumen rápido

| Forma | Uso | Ejemplo |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **must** | obligación | You **must** show your passport. |
| **should** | consejo | You **should** go to the gate early. |
| **check-in** | mostrador | Get your boarding pass at check-in. |
| **gate** | embarque | Gate twenty-two. |
| **boarding** | subir al avión | Boarding starts in ten minutes. |

---
